entries.title: Organizing International Cooperation and Global Documentation Efforts
entries.overview: A Belgian lawyer received this honor for his work establishing structures to support peaceful international relations and managing global information.
entries.background: During the early twentieth century, various political figures sought ways to manage foreign affairs through organized cooperation. As a socialist parliamentarian, Henri La Fontaine focused on social policy and building systems for global communication.
entries.work: Between 1907 and his death, Henri La Fontaine served as president of the International Peace Bureau. He established an institute dedicated to gathering worldwide documentation regarding international issues. In 1910, he coordinated a large-scale world conference intended to build an intellectual parliament for all people. These efforts were part of his leadership within the European peace movement.
entries.significance: His actions helped create centralized resources and forums designed to facilitate structured dialogue between different international organizations.

entries.title: Research into Matter Properties and Liquid Helium Production
entries.overview: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes studied how substances behave when cooled to extreme temperatures, specifically focusing on the creation of liquid helium.
entries.background: In a modern laboratory at the University of Leiden, scientists sought to understand how different materials change when they are chilled. This work involved exploring the physical characteristics of matter under intense cold.
entries.work: In 1908, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes used a specialized apparatus to successfully produce liquid helium. He used this fluid to study various substances and map their properties at low temperatures. Later, in 1911, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes found that mercury's electrical resistance vanishes when cooled to just above absolute zero, a discovery called superconductivity.
entries.significance: These investigations established the ability to produce liquid helium and identified the phenomenon of superconductivity, where current flows through a material without any resistance.

entries.title: Improving the precision of atomic-weight measurements
entries.overview: Theodore W. Richards developed highly precise methods for determining atomic weights, reducing experimental errors and correcting values used to calculate the proportions involved in chemical reactions.
entries.background: Chemists need reliable mass relationships to determine how much of one substance reacts with another. Small impurities or unnoticed moisture can distort measurements. Improving accuracy therefore requires careful preparation and handling of samples as well as precise weighing.
entries.work: Richards refined experimental methods for determining atomic weights and investigated sources of systematic error. Removing the effects of moisture was one important part of this work. By around 1904, the improved methods had enabled him to correct previously accepted values for several elements. The achievement lay in reliable quantitative comparisons across a large number of chemical substances, rather than in assuming that a rough measurement was sufficient because the general identity of an element was already known.
entries.significance: More accurate atomic weights strengthened the quantitative basis of chemistry. They improved calculations involving reaction proportions and showed how progress can come from identifying and reducing small experimental errors, as well as from discovering entirely new substances.

sources.title: Theodore W. Richards — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Researching Inner Ear Functions and Balance Mechanisms
entries.overview: Robert Bárány investigated how the vestibular apparatus in the inner ear influences body balance and eye movements during temperature changes.
entries.background: The parts of the inner ear are vital for maintaining equilibrium. Problems within these structures can lead to vertigo and involuntary, rhythmic eye movements known as nystagmus.
entries.work: In his earlier research, Robert Bárány studied how injecting water at different temperatures into a patient's ear affects vision. He observed that using cold water caused eye movements in one direction, while warm water triggered movement in the opposite way. This occurred because temperature fluctuations cause the fluid within the ear's canals to move up or down.
entries.significance: These findings provided new insights for managing diseases affecting the inner ear by explaining the relationship between ear fluid movement and physical balance.

sources.title: Robert Bárány — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Crystals reveal the wave behaviour of X-rays
entries.overview: Max von Laue proposed that the regular structure of crystals could diffract X-rays. Experiments confirmed the idea, linking the nature of X-rays with the arrangement of atoms.
entries.background: Waves passing through closely spaced openings can form diffraction patterns. A crystal contains a regular internal arrangement of atoms, suggesting a possible equivalent on a much smaller scale. Testing that comparison could reveal whether X-rays exhibited the expected wave behaviour.
entries.work: In 1912, while working in Munich, von Laue proposed sending X-rays through crystals to look for such patterns. The resulting experiments confirmed his prediction. The regular crystal structure affected the rays in a way that produced an observable diffraction pattern. The result supplied evidence that X-rays could be described as waves. It also suggested that the pattern contained information about the structure responsible for producing it, connecting a radiation experiment with the study of solid matter.
entries.significance: The discovery opened a way to investigate crystal structures through X-ray diffraction. It joined two previously difficult questions: what kind of radiation X-rays are, and how atoms are arranged inside a crystal.

sources.title: Max von Laue — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Researching the Chemical Structure of Green Plant Pigments
entries.overview: Richard Willstätter investigated how green plant pigments are composed, specifically looking at how they help plants create nutrients using sunlight and carbon dioxide.
entries.background: Between 1906 and 1914, scientists studied chlorophyll, the substance responsible for the green color in leaves. This pigment is vital because it allows plants to convert water and gases into oxygen and carbohydrates.
entries.work: During his research, Richard Willstätter determined that the chemical makeup of chlorophyll remains consistent across various plant species. He identified that this substance is actually a combination of two distinct types, which he successfully isolated in pure forms. Furthermore, he demonstrated that magnesium serves as a necessary component within the structure and noted how chlorophyll relates to the hemoglobin found in red blood cells.
entries.significance: Willstätter's work provided clarity on the chemical identity of plant pigments and revealed specific structural connections between plant chemistry and animal blood components.

sources.title: Richard Willstätter — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Literature explores the search for meaning and human sympathy
entries.overview: Romain Rolland was recognised for idealistic writing and sympathetic portrayals of human beings, with novels, drama and essays exploring the pursuit of happiness, meaning and truth.
entries.background: Rolland trained in Paris and Rome before developing a career across several literary forms. His interests extended beyond storytelling to questions about spiritual life and the social role of the arts. These concerns informed works centred on people struggling to live meaningfully.
entries.work: In the sequence Jean-Christophe, Rolland followed Jean-Christophe Krafft’s struggles for material and spiritual survival. He used the term roman-fleuve, or river novel, for a sustained narrative extending across a sequence of books. His essay The People’s Theatre argued that theatre should become accessible to a wider public. These forms let him connect the portrayal of individual lives with broader questions about society and culture, while maintaining an emphasis on sympathy for different kinds of people.
entries.significance: The prize acknowledged both literary idealism and humane observation. Rolland’s work offered readers extended explorations of character and purpose, while his writing about theatre treated access to artistic experience as a public concern.

sources.title: Romain Rolland — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Determining Atomic Positions Within Crystals Using X-ray Diffraction
entries.overview: William and Lawrence Bragg developed a method to map the internal arrangement of atoms by analyzing how X-rays scatter when passing through crystals.
entries.background: After Max von Laue discovered that X-rays create diffraction patterns in crystals, researchers sought to use this phenomenon for deeper analysis. The work was performed in Great Britain by William and Lawrence Bragg during the early 1900s.
entries.work: The Braggs established a mathematical connection between X-ray wavelength, incident angles, and the spacing of atomic layers within a crystal. While working together, they utilized diffraction pattern methods to determine specific atomic positions. This research converted X-ray observations into a functional technique for measuring the distances between individual layers inside crystalline structures.
entries.significance: This discovery provided a practical tool for analyzing crystal structures, making it possible to calculate exactly where atoms are located within a solid material.

entries.title: Romantic poetry and Swedish history reshape a literary era
entries.overview: Verner von Heidenstam was recognised as a leading figure in a new period of Swedish literature, with writing that emphasised romance, sensual experience and national history.
entries.background: Realism and naturalism had become prominent literary approaches. Heidenstam offered a different emphasis, giving greater scope to personal experience and romantic imagination. His work became influential in the literary movement of the 1890s, alongside other Swedish writers and artists.
entries.work: Heidenstam gained recognition with his 1888 poetry collection Vallfart och vandringsår. He later explored Sweden’s past as a great power, including the soldiers of Charles XII, in the short-story collection Karolinerna. His interest in that history included travels in the king’s footsteps in 1896. The stories romanticised the period and became widely read, including in Swedish schools. Across these works, historical material and the individual’s sensory and emotional experience supplied alternatives to prevailing literary models.
entries.significance: The award recognised Heidenstam’s role in changing the direction of Swedish writing. His influence lay in both the distinctive qualities of his own work and its place within a wider literary generation.

sources.title: Verner von Heidenstam — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Spiritual searching and social change in two Danish authors
entries.overview: Karl Gjellerup was honoured for idealistic poetry, and Henrik Pontoppidan for depictions of Danish life. Their shared prize recognised distinct bodies of writing rather than a collaboration.
entries.background: Denmark’s political struggles and industrialisation supplied material for Pontoppidan’s fiction. Gjellerup pursued questions of belief and spiritual transformation, moving from a Christian upbringing through atheism to an interest in Buddhism. Their subjects and literary approaches therefore differed substantially.
entries.work: Gjellerup’s first novel, An Idealist, appeared in 1878 and reflected his break with Christianity. The Pilgrim Kamanita, published in 1906, drew on reincarnation and an Indian setting. He eventually wrote in German as well as Danish. Pontoppidan’s novels and stories examined social and political life in Denmark. Lucky Per, published between 1898 and 1904, follows a gifted man who leaves his religious family background to become an engineer, confronting the possibilities and limits of personal independence.
entries.significance: The award brought together literature concerned with spiritual ideals and literature rooted in contemporary social experience. Each author explored the relationship between individuals and the beliefs or institutions shaping their lives.

entries.title: Helping wounded soldiers and prisoners during the First World War
entries.overview: The International Committee of the Red Cross was honoured for wartime humanitarian work, particularly assistance to wounded soldiers, prisoners of war and their families.
entries.background: Founded in 1863 on Henry Dunant’s initiative, the committee promoted assistance to people harmed by war. The first Geneva Convention followed in 1864. Its principle of protecting the wounded and those caring for them applied across opposing sides of a conflict.
entries.work: When the First World War began in 1914, the scale of suffering placed enormous demands on the committee. Alongside work connected with the Geneva Convention’s protections for wounded combatants, it took up the interests of prisoners of war. The award explicitly recognised assistance to prisoners and their families as well as wounded soldiers. The red-cross emblem on a white background expressed the protection of humanitarian care, rather than allegiance to one army or nation.
entries.significance: The prize recognised practical humanitarian action during a continuing war. It showed how an organisation could work across national divisions to address the needs of people in captivity or wounded in combat, even when the conflict itself continued.

entries.title: Discovering Unique X-ray Patterns for Every Chemical Element
entries.overview: Charles Glover Barkla identified that different atoms produce their own distinct patterns of secondary X-rays when hit by radiation.
entries.background: After X-rays were first discovered, researchers noticed that irradiated compounds emitted secondary X-rays. These emissions displayed various lines at specific wavelengths, prompting investigations into whether these patterns changed based on a substance's physical state or chemical makeup.
entries.work: Around 1906, Charles Glover Barkla conducted experiments showing that the secondary spectrum of an element remains unique. He demonstrated that this pattern does not change regardless of an atom's temperature, structure, or chemical composition. This finding established that these specific radiation patterns are a permanent characteristic of individual atoms rather than temporary features of their surroundings.
entries.significance: This discovery turned X-ray spectra into a reliable tool for atomic research, providing a way to identify elements through their unique radiation signatures.

sources.title: Charles Glover Barkla — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Producing ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen
entries.overview: Fritz Haber developed a practical synthesis of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen, making atmospheric nitrogen available for the manufacture of fertilisers and other chemical products.
entries.background: Although air contains abundant nitrogen, plants cannot directly use its gaseous form. They need nitrogen in suitable compounds. Producing ammonia offered a route from an enormous atmospheric resource to chemically usable material, but the reaction required carefully controlled conditions.
entries.work: Haber found conditions of temperature, pressure and catalysis that allowed nitrogen and hydrogen to combine effectively. Controlling the gas flow and reaction apparatus made the synthesis practical at laboratory scale. Developing reliable industrial manufacture required subsequent engineering work, associated particularly with Carl Bosch, rather than the laboratory discovery alone. Separately, Haber organised chemical-warfare attacks and defences during the First World War, an activity documented in his Nobel biography and distinct from the synthesis honoured by the prize.
entries.significance: The reaction enabled large-scale nitrogen fertiliser production and remains a major chemical achievement. Haber’s wartime role raises an ethical question about the scientist and the uses of chemistry; it does not overturn the validity of ammonia synthesis.

entries.title: Energy quanta explain the spectrum of thermal radiation
entries.overview: Max Planck introduced discrete energy elements into the explanation of black-body radiation, beginning the quantum account of energy exchange between matter and electromagnetic radiation.
entries.background: Physicists could measure how the spectrum of thermal radiation changes with temperature, but existing theory could not correctly reproduce its full shape. A successful explanation needed to account for the observed distribution of energy across frequencies without predicting unphysical results.
entries.work: In 1900, Planck obtained a formula matching the measured spectrum. To derive it, he treated the energy of the material oscillators exchanging radiation as divided into finite elements. The size of an element was proportional to frequency, with the proportionality set by the quantity now called Planck’s constant. This was a change in how energy entered the calculation. The later proposal that freely travelling light itself behaves as quanta was a further step associated with Einstein.
entries.significance: Planck’s result provided a successful radiation law and introduced a new fundamental constant. It opened the path toward quantum physics by showing that continuous energy assumptions could fail in the description of microscopic processes.

entries.title: The Epic Poetry and Allegorical Writing of Carl Spitteler
entries.overview: In 1919, Carl Spitteler received the Nobel Prize in Literature for his large-scale allegorical poem that combines various thematic elements.
entries.background: After studying law and theology, the Swiss writer turned from a potential career in the church to focus on journalism and poetry. He lived in Russia as a tutor before settling in Luzern to pursue his literary interests.
entries.work: Between 1900 and 1905, Spitteler composed the epic poem Olympian Spring using iambic hexameter. This allegorical work integrates mythological, religious, naturalistic, and fantastic themes. Additionally, he wrote the novel Imago in 1906. His earlier poetic output included the 1881 collection Prometheus und Epithemus, which he originally published using the pseudonym Carl Felix Tandem.
entries.significance: Spitteler's writing combined diverse thematic traditions into a single epic work and provided a linguistic basis for Jungian psychoanalysis through his novel.

entries.title: Antibodies and complement work together to destroy bacteria
entries.overview: Jules Bordet showed that the destruction of bacteria by blood serum involves cooperation between specific antibodies and a different set of factors known as complement.
entries.background: Immunity involves several kinds of defence rather than one uniform process. Investigators studying blood needed to distinguish substances formed after exposure to a particular infection from protective components already present. Separating these contributions could explain how the blood acts against bacteria.
entries.work: In studies of cholera in 1896, Bordet demonstrated that bacterial destruction depended on two cooperating components. One was the antibodies produced following immunisation against particular bacteria. The other was complement, also present in blood from an unimmunised organism. Their interaction explained the action being investigated. This was a finding about an important mechanism of serum defence, rather than a claim that all immune responses depend on the same combination of components.
entries.significance: The work clarified the relationship between specific immune recognition and other protective factors in blood. The interaction also became useful in laboratory tests for disease, including syphilis, linking an experimental account of immunity with diagnostic methods.

entries.title: The Establishment of the League of Nations for Global Peace
entries.overview: Woodrow Wilson received this award for acting as the primary architect behind the creation of an international organization intended to prevent future conflicts.
entries.background: Following the First World War's massive loss of life, leaders sought ways to maintain stability. Although Woodrow Wilson initially maintained American neutrality in 1914, German submarine warfare eventually drew his nation into the global struggle in 1917.
entries.work: In 1918, Woodrow Wilson introduced his Fourteen Points program. This plan advocated for national self-governance for oppressed groups and a more forgiving approach toward defeated nations. His specific goal was to found the League of Nations. During the Paris negotiations, however, his vision faced challenges as Britain and France pushed for heavy German reparations and war guilt.
entries.significance: Wilson's efforts focused on creating a formal structure to ensure post-war peace through international cooperation and diplomacy.

sources.title: Woodrow Wilson — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Motion and electric fields alter the spectra of atoms
entries.overview: Johannes Stark investigated light emitted by moving ions and discovered that an electric field can split spectral lines, revealing how motion and surroundings affect atomic radiation.
entries.background: An electrical discharge through gas at low pressure can produce rapidly moving charged atoms, or ions. Their emitted light provides information about both motion and atomic behaviour. Spectral lines allow small changes in the light’s frequency to be detected and compared.
entries.work: In 1905, Stark demonstrated a Doppler effect in canal rays: light observed in the direction of the emitting atoms’ motion had a higher frequency than light emitted in the opposite direction. He also discovered the effect now bearing his name, in which an applied electric field splits a spectral line into several components. These were distinct findings about changes in atomic spectra, one associated with movement and the other with the influence of an external electric field.
entries.significance: The results gave physicists additional experimental evidence for interpreting atomic radiation. They showed that spectra carry information about the physical conditions of their sources, providing further tests for developing theories of atomic structure.

entries.title: Using thermal measurements to predict chemical equilibrium
entries.overview: Walther Nernst’s work in thermochemistry connected low-temperature behaviour with the calculation of chemical equilibrium, helping researchers predict the balance reached by chemical reactions.
entries.background: A reaction does not always convert all its starting material into products. It can reach an equilibrium whose position changes with temperature. Reactions also release or absorb heat, creating a question about how thermal measurements can help predict that final balance.
entries.work: Nernst investigated the behaviour of substances at very low temperatures and developed the heat theorem associated with the third law of thermodynamics. This provided a basis for connecting thermal data with equilibrium calculations. His work concerned the balance between reactants and products, rather than a direct microscopic picture of each atom’s path during a reaction. It made the release or absorption of heat part of a broader quantitative explanation of chemical change.
entries.significance: The research strengthened the connection between chemistry and thermodynamics. With suitable thermal information, scientists gained a more systematic way to calculate equilibria, extending what could be predicted about reactions beyond observing whether they happened in a particular experiment.

entries.title: The Literary Recognition of Norwegian Author Knut Hamsun
entries.overview: Knut Hamsun received this award for his writing, specifically highlighting a book that explores the connection between human labor and the natural world.
entries.background: Before his 1920 recognition, Hamsun gained fame with his 1890 novel, Hunger. Regarded as a landmark of the modern Norwegian novel, it focuses on survival and individual experience.
entries.work: Hamsun was honored for his book Growth of the Soil. In this work, he depicts settlers working to farm the wilderness. He portrays these agricultural efforts with heroic qualities similar to the ancient poet Hesiod. His writing often focuses on a preference for simple living and a rejection of modern civilization, emphasizing how people interact with nature through physical toil.
entries.significance: The award specifically cited his epic portrayal of human cultivation. His writing style offered a unique perspective on the relationship between humanity and the environment.

entries.title: Investigating how muscle activity changes oxygen supply
entries.overview: August Krogh investigated the regulation of oxygen delivery to muscles, emphasising the role of the smallest blood vessels, capillaries, as demands change during activity.
entries.background: Working muscles need oxygen delivered by the circulation. Understanding how supply adjusts requires examining blood at the scale of the tissues themselves, as well as considering overall flow. Krogh developed precise methods for measuring oxygen and used them to study this regulation.
entries.work: During the 1910s, Krogh concluded that changes in the number of capillaries carrying blood were important to the response to muscular work. He described relatively few open capillaries at rest and greater recruitment as activity increased. This account placed the fine network of blood vessels at the centre of the investigation. It challenged an explanation based simply on faster blood movement and provided an influential model for studying how circulation responds locally to tissue needs.
entries.significance: The prize recognised the capillary regulating mechanism that emerged from these experiments. The work helped make local oxygen delivery a measurable physiological problem, providing a foundation for further investigation of the relationship between circulation and metabolism.

entries.title: Seeking international institutions with the power to preserve peace
entries.overview: Léon Bourgeois advocated international arbitration and legal institutions and played a prominent part in the establishment of the League of Nations after the First World War.
entries.background: Bourgeois took part in the Franco-German War of 1870–71 before pursuing law and politics. Later, as Paris police chief, he helped prevent a military coup by a general seeking revenge against Germany. These experiences formed part of a career increasingly concerned with international peace.
entries.work: At the Hague conferences of 1899 and 1907, Bourgeois promoted arbitration and an international court as alternatives to armed conflict. During the First World War, he proposed a global organisation with substantial authority over its member states. His design sought stronger supranational powers than Woodrow Wilson was prepared to support. The League that emerged followed Wilson’s approach more closely, although Bourgeois also saw the establishment of an international court at The Hague.
entries.significance: The award recognised sustained work toward peace and justice through institutions. Bourgeois’s efforts illustrate both the ambition to replace force with law and the compromises involved when governments negotiate how much authority an international organisation should possess.

sources.title: Léon Bourgeois — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Discovering Nickel Steel Alloys for Precise Physical Measurements
entries.overview: Charles Edouard Guillaume found a specific metal mixture that stays nearly the same size even when temperatures fluctuate, allowing for much more accurate scientific measurements.
entries.background: To establish standard lengths, scientists used the metric system and a German legal meter. However, conducting very exact measurements was difficult because most materials expand or shrink as their temperature changes.
entries.work: In 1896, Charles Edouard Guillaume identified unusual thermal behavior in nickel-steel alloys. He developed invar, whose very small thermal expansion made it valuable for precision instruments. His wider nickel-steel research also supported the manufacture of incandescent lamps.
entries.significance: This work enabled much more precise measurements in physics by providing materials that remain stable despite thermal changes, benefiting both scientific tools and everyday technology.

entries.title: Researching Radioactive Elements and the Discovery of Isotopes
entries.overview: Frederick Soddy identified that certain radioactive substances are actually versions of existing elements that differ in atomic weight despite sharing chemical traits.
entries.background: Following the 1896 discovery of radioactivity, researchers studied how unstable atoms behave. Scientists needed to understand if radioactive materials were entirely unique or related to known elements on the periodic table.
entries.work: Frederick Soddy investigated radioactive preparations and determined they were not all unique elements. He found that some substances are variants of known elements that possess different weights. In 1913, he created the term isotopes to describe these atoms, which maintain identical chemical properties but differ in their radioactive characteristics and mass.
entries.significance: This work changed the understanding of atomic structure by proving that atoms of the same element can have different masses.

entries.title: Social criticism and humane storytelling across literary forms
entries.overview: Anatole France was honoured for a wide literary achievement, with fiction, poetry and journalism combining social concerns, sympathy for human experience and a distinctive prose style.
entries.background: France grew up around his father’s Paris bookshop and later became a librarian for the French Senate. His early work included poetry and journalism. Political controversies also entered his writing, linking literary activity with debates about justice in French society.
entries.work: He achieved major success with Le Crime de Sylvestre Bonnard in 1881 and continued writing novels and stories while exploring other forms. During the Dreyfus affair, he supported Émile Zola’s intervention; the controversy informed Monsieur Bergeret, published in 1901. After 1900, social concerns became more prominent in his fiction. The First World War deepened his pessimism and encouraged a turn toward childhood memories, reflected in Le Petit Pierre, which appeared in 1918.
entries.significance: The award recognised the range and character of France’s writing rather than a single book. His career connected storytelling with public argument and personal recollection, using different forms to explore human experience and the society surrounding it.

entries.title: Strengthening the League of Nations and organised internationalism
entries.overview: Hjalmar Branting and Christian Lange were recognised for sustained support of peace and international cooperation, including their efforts to strengthen the newly created League of Nations.
entries.background: The peaceful separation of Norway and Sweden and the later destruction of the First World War formed important settings for their work. Both supported institutions through which countries could cooperate and settle disagreements, although they acted through different political and organisational roles.
entries.work: Branting defended Norway’s cause in 1905 and pursued social reform through peaceful democratic means in Sweden. As prime minister and League delegate, he accepted its decision recognising Finland’s sovereignty over the Åland Islands. Lange became secretary-general of the Inter-Parliamentary Union in 1909 and kept that organisation functioning through the war. In 1920, his knowledge of internationalism led to his participation as an expert at the League’s first meeting. Both continued their international work after the award.
entries.significance: The prize honoured long-term commitment rather than one shared negotiation. Their efforts linked parliamentary cooperation and democratic politics with acceptance of international procedures, including decisions that did not favour a government’s preferred outcome.

Christian Lange — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Light quanta explain the law of the photoelectric effect
entries.overview: Albert Einstein proposed a quantum explanation of the photoelectric effect, relating the energy of electrons released from a metal to the frequency of the incident light.
entries.background: Light falling on a metal can release electrons, but the effect depends on frequency rather than brightness alone. A classical picture spreading energy continuously through a wave did not readily explain the observations. The problem called for a different account of how light transfers energy.
entries.work: In 1905, Einstein proposed treating light as discrete quanta, later called photons, each with energy proportional to its frequency. A quantum must supply enough energy to free an electron from the material. This explains why a threshold frequency is required, while increasing the intensity of lower-frequency light does not provide the necessary energy in a single quantum. The contribution was a theoretical explanation and quantitative law, subsequently tested through experiments.
entries.significance: The award singled out the photoelectric law within Einstein’s contributions to theoretical physics. The work connected observations of electron emission with the emerging quantum picture, extending ideas about discrete energy from matter to light itself.

entries.title: Separating isotopes by their motion in electric and magnetic fields
entries.overview: Francis W. Aston developed the mass spectrograph to identify isotopes, showing that many non-radioactive elements contain atoms with different masses despite sharing an elemental identity.
entries.background: Chemical analysis alone cannot readily distinguish isotopes because they behave very similarly in chemical reactions. A method sensitive to their mass was therefore needed. Charged atoms moving through electric and magnetic fields offered a way to compare them physically.
entries.work: In 1919, Aston developed a mass spectrograph that directed beams of ions through electric and magnetic fields. Ions are atoms carrying an electrical charge. Under the controlled conditions of the instrument, their paths differed according to mass, allowing different isotopes to be distinguished. Aston used the apparatus to identify isotopes in many elements not known for radioactivity. He also formulated the whole-number rule: isotopic masses were close to whole-number multiples of a common unit.
entries.significance: The research showed that isotopes were a widespread feature of matter rather than a peculiarity confined to radioactive substances. It provided a powerful technique for investigating atomic masses and a quantitative pattern requiring explanation by atomic theory.

entries.title: Realistic social comedy renews Spanish theatrical traditions
entries.overview: Jacinto Benavente was honoured for continuing Spanish dramatic traditions through plays that emphasised credible social observation, often using comedy, humour and satire.
entries.background: Benavente turned from legal studies to travel, journalism and literature. As a dramatist, he sought to give a convincing account of life beyond the theatre. This meant putting recognisable social situations ahead of theatrical effects pursued chiefly for their own sake.
entries.work: His plays often depict upper-class society in Madrid or in the fictional town of Moraleda, while also including other social groups. Many are comedies in the sense that their plots reach happy endings. Humour and satire let him examine behaviour within those settings. Over his career, he produced a large body of writing, most of it for the stage. The Nobel citation recognised the manner in which his dramatic work carried forward an established literary tradition.
entries.significance: Benavente’s contribution lay in adapting theatrical inheritance to close observation of contemporary social life. His work offered audiences situations and characters they could recognise while using the possibilities of comedy to expose tensions within their society.

entries.title: Discoveries Regarding Energy Use and Heat in Muscle Tissue
entries.overview: Researchers identified how muscles use oxygen and chemical processes to generate energy and heat during movement and recovery periods.
entries.background: During the early twentieth century, scientists sought to understand how chemical reactions provide the necessary power for physical muscle movement and the subsequent production of heat.
entries.work: In the 1910s, Archibald Hill studied frog muscles to show that heat generation lags behind mechanical movement, revealing a work phase independent of oxygen and a recovery phase requiring it. At the end of the 1910s, Otto Meyerhof measured oxygen use and heat trends in frogs, mapping how carbohydrates convert into lactic acid during work and how this acid is processed or burned during rest.
entries.significance: These findings established a clear link between oxygen consumption, lactic acid metabolism, and the specific chemical stages required for muscle function.

entries.title: Repatriating prisoners and creating practical protection for refugees
entries.overview: Fridtjof Nansen organised the return of prisoners of war, famine relief and assistance for refugees, connecting international diplomacy with practical responses to displacement after the First World War.
entries.background: The war and its aftermath left large numbers of people stranded outside their homes. Some were prisoners awaiting repatriation; others had lost nationality or faced famine. Helping them required cooperation across borders as well as documents, transport and material relief.
entries.work: Nansen led postwar efforts to return more than 400,000 prisoners from Russia, Germany and the former Austria-Hungary. In 1921, he became the League of Nations’ first High Commissioner for Refugees and helped organise relief for famine in Russia. Nansen passports, introduced in 1922, gave stateless refugees identity and travel documents recognised by participating countries. These measures addressed different obstacles: captivity, hunger and the inability to cross borders lawfully without recognised papers.
entries.significance: The prize honoured both emergency relief and the development of international responsibility for refugees. Nansen’s work showed how diplomatic coordination could become concrete assistance, while the travel documents gave some displaced people greater freedom to rebuild their lives.

entries.title: Discrete atomic energies explain hydrogen’s spectral lines
entries.overview: Niels Bohr proposed a quantum model of the hydrogen atom, connecting permitted electron energies with the specific wavelengths of radiation emitted or absorbed by atoms.
entries.background: The discovery of electrons and radioactivity had made older pictures of the atom inadequate. A successful model also needed to explain why atoms produce characteristic spectral lines rather than an unrestricted range of frequencies. Emerging quantum ideas offered a possible way forward.
entries.work: In 1913, Bohr proposed that the electron in hydrogen could occupy only certain allowed states, represented in his model as prescribed orbits around the nucleus. A transition to a lower-energy state released radiation corresponding to the energy difference. This connected the atom’s possible energies with its observed spectrum. The model was an early application of quantum theory, preceding the fuller quantum mechanics developed later, and provided a new framework for investigating atomic structure.
entries.significance: Bohr’s account successfully explained important features of hydrogen’s spectrum and made energy transitions central to atomic physics. Its historical orbit picture became a stepping stone toward more complete descriptions, while discrete atomic energies remained a fundamental idea.

entries.title: Determining chemical composition from much smaller samples
entries.overview: Fritz Pregl developed microanalysis methods for organic substances, allowing chemists to determine composition accurately when only a very small amount of material was available.
entries.background: Organic chemistry studies a diverse range of carbon-containing compounds, many of which occur in living organisms. Determining their composition is a basic step toward understanding them. Conventional analysis could require more material than researchers could readily obtain from a particular biological source.
entries.work: During the 1910s, Pregl developed apparatus and procedures that substantially reduced the quantity needed for precise analysis. The achievement depended on adapting the experimental method to very small samples while retaining reliable measurements. This allowed composition to be investigated even when a substance was available only in limited amounts. The work concerned organic substances specifically, rather than implying that every compound present in an organism contains carbon.
entries.significance: Microanalysis expanded the range of materials accessible to quantitative chemistry. It was particularly valuable in physiological research, where isolating large quantities of a substance could be difficult. Better use of small samples helped connect chemical measurement with the investigation of biological processes.

entries.title: Irish folklore and experimental theatre inform a poetic career
entries.overview: William Butler Yeats was honoured for poetry that the Swedish Academy regarded as giving artistic expression to a nation, within a career closely connected to Ireland’s literary revival.
entries.background: Yeats’s childhood experiences in Dublin and Connaught brought him into contact with landscapes, folklore and local customs that shaped his writing. In London he also encountered symbolism, mysticism and spiritualism, influences that contributed to his approach to poetry and drama.
entries.work: Yeats began publishing poetry in the 1880s, while theatre occupied a substantial part of his early career. With Lady Gregory, he helped establish the Irish theatre movement that led to the Abbey Theatre. His plays drew on Irish legends and spiritual themes. After 1910, his drama became more experimental, incorporating masks, dance and music under the influence of Japanese Noh. His increasing return to poetry belonged to the final decades of his life, extending beyond the 1923 award.
entries.significance: The prize recognised a poetic achievement connected with cultural renewal. Yeats brought local traditions into dialogue with wider artistic influences, helping make the Irish Literary Renaissance both a national and an international literary development.

entries.title: Developing insulin into an effective treatment for severe diabetes
entries.overview: Frederick Banting and John Macleod received the insulin prize for research that made pancreatic extracts therapeutically useful, with essential contributions from Charles Best and James Collip.
entries.background: Researchers had linked the pancreas with the control of blood sugar, but obtaining a consistently useful preparation was difficult. The Toronto work aimed to extract the substance responsible and test whether it could counter the severe effects of diabetes.
entries.work: In 1921, Banting and Best conducted experiments with dogs in Macleod’s laboratory. Macleod supplied facilities, advised on methods and supervised the developing research. The extracts lowered blood sugar, but improving purity was necessary for clinical use. Collip joined the team and produced a preparation used successfully in Leonard Thompson in January 1922, following an earlier, less effective injection. The development therefore involved animal experiments, biochemical purification and clinical investigation rather than one isolated act of extraction.
entries.significance: Insulin transformed the prospects of patients with severe insulin deficiency. The Nobel award went to Banting and Macleod; both shared their prize money with colleagues, Banting with Best and Macleod with Collip, reflecting the wider team’s contributions.

entries.title: Measuring electron charge and testing the photoelectric law
entries.overview: Robert A. Millikan was honoured for precise work on the elementary electric charge and the photoelectric effect, connecting measurements of electrons with emerging quantum ideas.
entries.background: Identifying electrons raised a quantitative question: how much charge does one carry? A separate question concerned the relationship between light frequency and the energy of electrons released from matter. Both required unusually careful experiments to test ideas about microscopic quantities.
entries.work: Millikan used electrically charged oil droplets between metal plates. By comparing their movement under gravity with the opposing electrical force, he could determine their charges. Around 1910, these measurements established that the observed charges occurred in multiples of a fixed elementary amount. He also carried out sustained measurements of the photoelectric effect, confirming Einstein’s law with high accuracy in 1916. This second contribution tested the quantitative relationship between incident light frequency and emitted electron energy.
entries.significance: The award recognised both achievements. Oil-drop measurements supplied a precise value for electron charge, while the photoelectric experiments gave strong support to a law central to quantum physics, even though interpretation of light quanta remained debated.

entries.title: The National Epic Regarding Polish Peasant Life
entries.overview: Władysław Reymont received this literary honor in 1924 for his expansive novel, The Peasants, which focuses on the lives of common people.
entries.background: Following his time in provincial theatre and starting publication work in 1892, the Polish author focused his life on writing. His creative approach was influenced by naturalism, a style emphasizing detailed environmental descriptions within his narrative.
entries.work: In The Peasants, Reymont structured his story around the four seasons: autumn, winter, spring, and summer. This seasonal cycle links human existence to the natural world. He populated the novel with many characters from the masses, using episodic plots that reflect both the repetitive nature and the continuous novelty found in rural peasant life.
entries.significance: The work serves as a Polish national epic, utilizing rich character development and environmental detail to portray the connection between people and their surroundings.

entries.title: Making the heart’s electrical activity readable as an ECG
entries.overview: Willem Einthoven developed sensitive measurement and interpretation of the electrocardiogram, enabling the heart’s electrical activity to be recorded as a useful clinical trace.
entries.background: Each heartbeat is associated with weak electrical signals detectable at the body’s surface. Recording their variation can reveal aspects of cardiac function, but the signals are small. Doctors needed reliable instruments and a way to relate the recorded patterns to the working heart.
entries.work: Einthoven’s string galvanometer precisely measured tiny electrical currents and became a key tool in the early twentieth century. His work developed the electrocardiogram, or ECG, as a record of changing electrical activity. Such a trace is different from an anatomical picture: its features provide information about the timing and behaviour of the heart’s electrical processes. Einthoven helped connect those recorded features with cardiac functions and illnesses, making the instrument’s output useful to medicine.
entries.significance: The achievement joined sensitive physical measurement with physiological interpretation. It gave doctors a practical way to investigate heart function through electrical signals at the body’s surface and established a foundation for the continuing development of electrocardiography.

entries.title: Advancements in Measuring X-ray Spectra Through New Methods
entries.overview: Manne Siegbahn created new tools and techniques to more accurately map how different elements interact with X-rays during spectral analysis.
entries.background: After X-rays were discovered, Charles Barkla found that elements emit unique secondary X-rays. Later, Henry Moseley used these findings to update the periodic table of elements.
entries.work: During his research, Manne Siegbahn built specialized apparatus and measurement methods. These tools improved the precision of mapping X-ray spectra. By refining how scientists record these light patterns, he increased the accuracy of elemental identification during spectroscopic experiments.
entries.significance: These improved measurement techniques provided important advancements for the developing fields of quantum physics and atomic physics.

entries.title: Scattered light reveals particles in colloidal mixtures
entries.overview: Richard Zsigmondy developed an approach to observing extremely small dispersed particles, helping establish that colloidal solutions contain distinct particles rather than being uniform at every scale.
entries.background: A colloid contains very small particles dispersed through another substance. Ordinary microscopy may not resolve these particles, making a mixture appear more uniform than it actually is. Detecting their presence requires taking advantage of how they interact with light.
entries.work: In 1902, Zsigmondy introduced an idea that led to the ultramicroscope. The sample was illuminated from a direction perpendicular to the viewing direction, allowing scattered light from very small particles to be observed. This made particles detectable even when their detailed shapes could not be resolved. Zsigmondy used the method to investigate the heterogeneous nature of colloids. Heterogeneity refers to dispersed particles within a surrounding medium, rather than simply to differences in the sizes of the particles.
entries.significance: The work supplied both evidence about colloidal structure and methods for studying it. It helped turn apparently uniform liquids into experimentally accessible systems of dispersed particles, providing techniques that became fundamental to colloid chemistry.

entries.title: Satirical drama makes social questions part of the theatre
entries.overview: George Bernard Shaw was honoured for work combining social concerns, idealism and stimulating satire, using drama to provoke discussion about human behaviour and institutions.
entries.background: Shaw moved from Dublin to London and established himself as a critic before becoming a leading playwright. His criticism of contemporary theatre accompanied a belief that art should teach and engage with social issues, rather than provide dramatic effects alone.
entries.work: Plays Pleasant and Unpleasant, published in 1898, collected work reflecting this approach. Shaw used satire, provocation and allegory to explore social injustice and other public questions. Pygmalion became one of his best-known plays, while his dramatic output eventually exceeded sixty works across his career. His political thinking included advocacy of women’s rights and socialism, alongside troubling positions such as support for eugenics. These elements complicate the relationship between his humane literary aims and some of his expressed beliefs.
entries.significance: The award recognised the literary force of Shaw’s drama and satire. His plays gave audiences arguments to confront as well as stories to follow, making the theatre a setting for sustained debate about society.

entries.title: Efforts Toward Franco-German Reconciliation and Financial Stability
entries.overview: Two individuals worked separately to reduce international tensions between France and Germany through diplomatic support and a specialized economic repayment plan.
entries.background: After the First World War, Germany resented French troops occupying its territory to enforce reparation payments. This occupation increased friction between the two nations, creating significant instability in post-war Europe.
entries.work: In 1924, Charles Dawes led a committee that created the Dawes Plan, providing American loans so Germany could pay indemnities and France could end its occupation. Meanwhile, during his time as Foreign Secretary, Austen Chamberlain provided British support for negotiations initiated by Gustav Stresemann in Locarno.
entries.significance: These actions aimed to ease the conflict between France and Germany by addressing both military presence and the financial ability to meet war-related debts.

entries.title: Electron collisions reveal discrete energy changes in atoms
entries.overview: James Franck and Gustav Hertz showed that atoms absorb energy from colliding electrons in specific amounts, providing experimental evidence for discrete atomic energy states.
entries.background: Bohr’s atomic model proposed that an atom could occupy certain allowed energies rather than any value in a continuous range. A way to test this idea was to send electrons through a gas and measure how their collisions affected the electrical current.
entries.work: In 1914, Franck and Hertz applied a voltage across a tube containing gas at low pressure. As the accelerating voltage rose, the current initially increased but then fell at a particular threshold. Electrons had acquired enough kinetic energy to excite atoms through collisions. In transferring that energy, they lost the energy needed to contribute to the measured current. The threshold therefore revealed a specific amount that the atoms could absorb, rather than a gradual response at every possible energy.
entries.significance: The results supported the idea of quantised atomic energies. They connected electrical measurements in a gas tube with the internal states of atoms, offering an experimental counterpart to theories developed to explain atomic spectra.

entries.title: Weighing molecules by spinning dispersed mixtures
entries.overview: The Svedberg studied tiny particles dispersed in liquids. His work connected their random motion with evidence for molecules and developed a powerful method for measuring molecular mass.
entries.background: A dispersed system contains small particles distributed through another substance. Their seemingly erratic movement, known as Brownian motion, raised a fundamental question: could unseen molecules striking those particles account for what researchers observed?
entries.work: Svedberg tested ideas about Brownian motion and helped confirm Einstein’s explanation in terms of molecular collisions. He also developed the ultracentrifuge in 1925. This instrument spins a mixture at very high speed, making its components move outward at different rates. Measurements of that separation allow researchers to calculate molecular weights. The machine therefore turned a process resembling accelerated settling into a quantitative way of studying extremely small objects.
entries.significance: The prize recognised work on dispersed systems, linking experimental evidence for molecules with a practical technique for investigating them. Molecular mass could be measured through the behaviour of substances in a liquid, rather than by seeing individual molecules directly.

entries.title: Literary Achievements Centered on Sardinian Life and Human Struggles
entries.overview: Grazia Deledda received this prize for writing that uses clear imagery to depict life on her home island while exploring universal human difficulties.
entries.background: Growing up in Nuoro, Sardinia, Deledda was influenced by local traditions and family history. Her early education included private Italian lessons, and she began publishing stories in newspapers as a young teenager.
entries.work: Deledda authored various novels, poems, plays, and articles. Her 1892 novel, Fior de Sardegna, preceded her 1903 work, Elias Portolu, which gained international recognition. Her writing frequently explores themes such as moral choices, passion, human fragility, and the influence of destiny or uncontrollable forces.
entries.significance: Her literary contributions provided a vivid portrayal of Sardinian existence through stories that connect specific regional experiences to broader, shared human problems.

entries.title: A claimed experimental cause of cancer was later overturned
entries.overview: Johannes Fibiger received the prize for experiments interpreted as showing that a parasitic worm caused stomach cancer in rats. Later investigation overturned that interpretation.
entries.background: An experimental animal model seemed to offer a way to investigate cancer’s causes under controlled conditions. If a particular exposure reliably produced malignant disease, researchers could study the process rather than relying only on observations of naturally occurring human cancers.
entries.work: Fibiger fed rats cockroaches carrying worm larvae and observed abnormal tissue growth. He interpreted these changes as cancer caused by the parasite. Subsequent investigations, including Hitchcock and Bell’s controlled work in 1952, did not confirm the claimed malignant lesions. They identified nonmalignant changes and showed that vitamin A deficiency affected the results. The correction therefore concerns both the diagnosis of the tissue changes and the causal interpretation of the experiments, not merely an unsuccessful application of a sound discovery.
entries.significance: The case illustrates the importance of independent replication, accurate pathology and control of nutritional factors. It does not overturn the separate, well-established finding that some infections can cause cancer; Fibiger’s particular claimed model was the failure.

entries.title: Diplomacy and the Locarno Treaty of 1925
entries.overview: Two foreign ministers received this award for negotiating an agreement to improve relations between Germany and France following World War I.
entries.background: After World War I, Germany faced harsh peace terms. The French occupation of German territories to collect war debts created tension. Both leaders sought to move past these conflicts to avoid future wars driven by revenge or territorial disputes.
entries.work: In 1925, Aristide Briand helped negotiate the Locarno agreements. As French Foreign Minister, Briand opposed harsh German penalties and criticized military occupations. Meanwhile, German Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann, who previously supported territorial annexations, shifted toward initiating reconciliation with France to stabilize post-war negotiations.
entries.significance: The 1925 treaty represented a major effort toward Franco-German reconciliation through diplomatic negotiation rather than military force or economic retaliation.

entries.title: Proving Atomic Existence Through Liquid Particle Movement
entries.overview: Jean Baptiste Perrin demonstrated that matter consists of individual atoms and molecules by studying how tiny particles distribute themselves within a liquid.
entries.background: During the 1880s, scientists debated whether atoms and molecules were real physical objects or merely theoretical concepts. This uncertainty regarding the actual existence of these microscopic building blocks persisted for decades.
entries.work: In 1908, Jean Baptiste Perrin conducted experiments to show that particles in a liquid do not all sink to the bottom but instead distribute themselves through sedimentation equilibrium. He also used this method to support Einstein’s theory regarding Brownian motion. This random movement of small particles occurs because they are being struck by molecules within the liquid, providing physical evidence for molecular collisions.
entries.significance: Perrin's findings provided experimental substantiation for the existence of molecules, confirming that matter possesses a discontinuous structure made of distinct, individual particles.

entries.title: Investigating the Chemical Structure of Bile Acids and Related Toxins
entries.overview: Heinrich Wieland explored how certain substances are built, focusing specifically on the chemical makeup of bile acids produced by the liver.
entries.background: The body uses many different substances to perform vital functions. During the early 1920s, it was necessary to understand the composition of bile acids that move from the gallbladder into the intestine.
entries.work: Working in the early 1920s, Heinrich Wieland mapped out the chemical structure of bile acids. He also examined bufotoxin, a poison found in various toads that shares a chemical relationship with these acids. His research helped clarify how bile acids assist the body in absorbing different nutrients from the digestive tract.
entries.significance: Wieland's findings provided clarity regarding how the body processes and assimilates substances from the intestine through the action of bile acids.

entries.title: The Philosophical Writing of Henri Bergson
entries.overview: Henri Bergson received this award for presenting vibrant ideas through skilled writing, utilizing expressive imagery and metaphors to interpret life.
entries.background: An educated philosopher from Paris, Bergson taught at the Collège de France. He later served as president of a League of Nations commission regarding intellectual cooperation between nations.
entries.work: In his 1889 book, Time and Free Will, Bergson described consciousness through two levels: internal introspection and external projection. Later, in the 1907 publication Creative Evolution, he expanded on his specific theories of time and applied these concepts to examine living organisms using analogies and powerful imagery.
entries.significance: His contributions provided a fresh way of looking at life by connecting deep psychological experiences with the biological processes of evolution.

entries.title: Malaria fever therapy for a devastating form of syphilis
entries.overview: Julius Wagner-Jauregg was recognised for a historical treatment of general paralysis caused by syphilis: deliberately inducing malaria to produce repeated bouts of fever.
entries.background: General paralysis, also called dementia paralytica, damages the brain and can cause profound mental and physical deterioration. Before modern antibiotic treatment, its often fatal course gave physicians few effective options. Reports that fever sometimes improved psychiatric symptoms suggested a possible intervention.
entries.work: In 1917 Wagner-Jauregg exposed patients to malaria-infected blood and reported improvement or remission in some cases of general paralysis. He selected a form of malaria considered comparatively manageable at the time. The therapeutic claim concerned this particular complication of syphilis; it did not establish fever as a general cure for mental illness. Deliberately causing another infection was itself a serious medical intervention.
entries.significance: The prize marked an important episode in the search for a treatment for neurosyphilis. Malaria inoculation is historical practice; current treatment guidance uses antibiotics such as penicillin, rather than deliberately infecting patients with malaria.

entries.title: Building public support for Franco-German reconciliation
entries.overview: Ferdinand Buisson and Ludwig Quidde worked to change public attitudes in France and Germany, making peaceful cooperation a cause that citizens could support across national boundaries.
entries.background: The Franco-German war of 1870–71 and the First World War left deep hostility. Both men opposed policies that could turn defeat and resentment into another war, although they worked within different national political settings.
entries.work: Buisson combined campaigning for democracy, women’s suffrage and equal rights with meetings aimed at reconciliation. He condemned German aggression during the First World War but also criticised the harsh treatment of Germany afterward. Quidde was a member of the International Peace Bureau and became president of the German Peace Society. He opposed German territorial annexations during the war, despite political surveillance, and continued campaigning against rearmament and demands for revenge.
entries.significance: The award recognised sustained efforts to make international cooperation acceptable to the public. Their contribution was advocacy and organised discussion, rather than the negotiation of a single treaty or a claim that lasting peace had already been achieved.

entries.title: Visualizing Particle Paths and Observing Photon Energy Transfer
entries.overview: These discoveries enabled scientists to see charged particle tracks and proved that light behaves like particles during interactions with matter.
entries.background: In 1911, researchers sought ways to observe tiny particles. Meanwhile, existing theories suggested light travels in energy packages called photons, but physical evidence of momentum transfer was needed to confirm this particle-like behavior of radiation.
entries.work: In 1911, C.T.R. Wilson built a cloud chamber using air and water vapor to make charged particles visible through droplet formation. In 1922, Arthur Compton directed X-ray photons at metal, causing electrons to be released. This process increased the X-rays' wavelength because energy transferred from the photons to the electrons, demonstrating that electromagnetic radiation follows mechanical laws.
entries.significance: Wilson's chamber provided a tool for photographing particle traces, while Compton’s work confirmed that light consists of discrete quanta that can transfer energy during collisions.

entries.title: Connecting sterol chemistry with vitamin D
entries.overview: Adolf Windaus investigated the structure of sterols and their relationship to vitamins. His work helped explain a chemical route by which ultraviolet light produces vitamin D.
entries.background: Sterols include cholesterol, a substance important in cells and other biological processes. Understanding their composition offered a way to connect apparently different substances in the body. Vitamin D deficiency was associated with rickets, a disease that weakens the developing skeleton.
entries.work: During the 1920s Windaus studied cholesterol and related sterols and established their relationship to bile acids. He also investigated ergosterol. Exposure to ultraviolet light converted this sterol into material with vitamin D activity, connecting a chemical transformation with the prevention of deficiency disease. Vitamin D activity appeared following irradiation; the transformation, rather than simply the presence of ergosterol, was central.
entries.significance: The research showed that vitamins could be investigated through their chemical relationships and formation, rather than only through the symptoms of a missing dietary factor. It linked structural chemistry to a specific biological function, explaining why irradiation could change the nutritional properties of a substance.

entries.title: Making medieval Norwegian lives feel immediate
entries.overview: Sigrid Undset was honoured principally for her portrayals of northern life in the Middle Ages, combining historical knowledge with close attention to characters’ feelings and choices.
entries.background: Undset’s early fiction explored contemporary women seeking independence. Her interest in the past drew on her upbringing as an archaeologist’s daughter and her study of medieval literature and society. This knowledge became the setting for stories about love, obligation and faith.
entries.work: Her trilogy Kristin Lavransdatter follows a woman through fourteenth-century Norway. Published in 1920–1922, it places family relationships, religious belief and conflicting loyalties within a carefully realised historical world. Undset makes social rules matter through their consequences for individual lives, rather than treating the past as decorative scenery. Her vivid language and psychological insight give both communities and their inhabitants a sense of immediacy.
entries.significance: The prize recognised the literary achievement of bringing an unfamiliar age into human focus. Readers encounter a society different from their own while recognising its emotional conflicts, and historical detail supports the force of the characters’ experiences.

entries.title: Identifying body lice as the carriers of typhus
entries.overview: Charles Nicolle showed that body lice transmit epidemic typhus. His finding explained a route by which a devastating illness spread during wars, disasters and crowded living conditions.
entries.background: Research had already connected several infections with insects, raising the possibility that typhus also had an insect carrier. Nicolle noticed that patients stopped infecting others after washing and changing their conditions of cleanliness, even though they remained ill.
entries.work: In 1909 Nicolle used transmission experiments involving apes and body lice to demonstrate the lice’s role. The key discovery identified the vector connecting infected and uninfected hosts. Modern accounts clarify the mechanism: infected lice shed bacteria in their faeces, which can enter damaged skin, for example when a bite is scratched. Thus the louse carries the infection, while contaminated material provides a route into the body.
entries.significance: Identifying the carrier explained why measures against body lice and infested clothing could interrupt transmission. It shifted attention from the sick person alone to the conditions that enabled lice to move between people.

entries.title: How heat releases electrons from metals
entries.overview: Owen Willans Richardson explained thermionic emission: the release of electrons from a heated metal. He also established a mathematical relationship between temperature and the amount of electron emission.
entries.background: Electrical effects around hot wires had become useful in devices for controlling and amplifying signals. To understand these effects, physicists needed to identify the moving charge and explain why heating a metal changed its electrical behaviour.
entries.work: In work beginning in 1901, Richardson connected the phenomenon to electrons escaping from a hot metal. Thermal energy enables electrons to leave the metal’s surface and behave as free charged particles. He went beyond a qualitative account by formulating a law relating emission to temperature. This provided a way to describe how strongly a heated material would emit electrons as conditions changed.
entries.significance: The work gave a physical and quantitative foundation to a useful electrical phenomenon. Its importance lay in connecting the observable behaviour of hot wires with the microscopic behaviour of electrons, helping researchers understand and predict a source of electric charge.

entries.title: Investigating Sugar Fermentation and Yeast Enzyme Processes
entries.overview: This work explains how yeast fungi convert sugar into alcohol, a fundamental process for making bread, beer, and wine.
entries.background: After Eduard Buchner proved that chemical substances from yeast fungi drive fermentation, scientists needed to clarify the specific details of this biological mechanism to understand how sugar transforms into alcohol.
entries.work: In his research, Arthur Harden used fine filters on yeast extract to identify two necessary components: a primary enzyme and a coenzyme. He also demonstrated that phosphoric acid is vital to the process. During the 1910s and 1920s, Hans von Euler-Chelpin and his associates further built upon these findings to develop a more detailed understanding of the fermentation mechanism.
entries.significance: These investigations clarified the essential chemical elements and specific substances required for yeast to successfully ferment sugar into alcohol.

entries.title: The Literary Achievement of the Novel Buddenbrooks
entries.overview: Thomas Mann received this honor for his writing, particularly for the widely recognized novel titled Buddenbrooks, which details a merchant family's decline.
entries.background: Growing up in a north German merchant family, Thomas Mann chose a life of writing instead of managing a grain firm. His work draws inspiration from his own upbringing and includes various types of fiction and novels.
entries.work: In 1901, the author published Buddenbrooks, a family chronicle that gained significant recognition as a classic. While he produced many works, this specific novel served as a primary reason for his selection. His later writing also includes The Magic Mountain, which is another well-known book focusing on themes of coming of age.
entries.significance: The award highlights the growing importance of Mann's fiction within contemporary literature and notes the lasting recognition of his family chronicle style.

entries.title: Finding essential nutrients beyond proteins, fats and carbohydrates
entries.overview: Christiaan Eijkman and Frederick Hopkins helped establish that healthy growth requires small quantities of substances beyond the main food groups. These substances became known as vitamins.
entries.background: An apparently adequate supply of carbohydrates, proteins and fats did not always prevent illness or support growth. Researchers needed to explain these failures without assuming that every disease came from an infection or a shortage of food overall.
entries.work: Eijkman studied beriberi and noticed that chickens fed polished rice developed similar symptoms, including weakness and paralysis. His investigations connected protection with material removed during rice milling; the relevant nutrient was later identified as vitamin B1. Hopkins approached the question through controlled feeding experiments. Young rats stopped growing on purified basic nutrients, but a little milk restored growth. By around 1910 he concluded that additional substances were necessary in small amounts.
entries.significance: Together the findings made diet-related deficiency a distinct experimental problem. They showed why the quantity of food alone could not explain nutrition: particular missing components could impair growth or produce disease.

Sir Frederick Hopkins — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: The Creation of the Briand-Kellogg Pact Against Aggressive Warfare
entries.overview: United States Secretary of State Frank B. Kellogg helped develop an international agreement intended to outlaw wars used to attack other nations.
entries.background: Following World War I, French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand sought a security agreement between France and America to protect against German revanchism. This period involved high tensions regarding territorial recovery and international stability.
entries.work: In 1928, Frank B. Kellogg expanded upon Briand's original idea to create a broader, less restrictive pact. While Briand initiated the concept, Kellogg proposed including more countries through a looser framework. He also insisted on specific exceptions to ensure the agreement would not interfere with American interests within the American continent.
entries.significance: The resulting treaty, known as the Briand-Kellogg Pact, was signed by nearly every nation in the world and established a formal prohibition against wars of aggression.

entries.title: The Discovery of Wave Properties in Electrons
entries.overview: In 1924, Louis de Broglie proposed that particles like electrons possess wave-like characteristics, moving beyond the idea that energy only exists in fixed amounts.
entries.background: Early twentieth-century quantum physics grew from observations that energy travels in specific increments. Scientists had already established that light behaves as both a particle and a wave.
entries.work: In 1924, Louis de Broglie introduced the concept that electrons could be described by waves rather than just as particles. This theory was supported by observing how electron streams interacted with matter, specifically when they were reflected by crystals or passed through thin metal foils to spread out.
entries.significance: This discovery provided a crucial foundation for the ongoing development of quantum mechanics by expanding the known nature of subatomic particles.

entries.title: Researching Hemin Structures and Creating Artificial Hem Groups
entries.overview: Hans Fischer investigated the chemical makeup of pigments like hemoglobin and chlorophyll, eventually successfully synthesizing the hem group component in a laboratory.
entries.background: Cells require oxygen for metabolism, which is carried through our blood by hemoglobin. This substance contains a specific part called the hem group that gives blood its characteristic red color.
entries.work: During his research, Hans Fischer mapped out the chemical structure of the hem group. In 1929, he achieved the creation of this substance using artificial methods. Additionally, he performed studies on other important biological pigments, such as chlorophyll, which is a key part of how plants perform photosynthesis.
entries.significance: Hans Fischer's work provided a clear understanding of the chemical composition of vital biological pigments used in both humans and plants.

entries.title: Satire and sharply observed American characters
entries.overview: Sinclair Lewis was recognised for vivid description and for creating memorable types of characters through humour. His fiction made familiar American settings subjects of searching social observation.
entries.background: Lewis began publishing stories and poems while studying at Yale and built a career in fiction. Main Street, published in 1920, brought major commercial success by turning attention to the routines and attitudes of a small American town.
entries.work: Main Street depicts town life in the 1910s with both detail and satire. Lewis’s achievement depended on how he described people and their surroundings: habits, speech and expectations become material for comedy and criticism. Other novels established his reputation during the 1920s. Arrowsmith, published in 1925, was selected for the Pulitzer Prize in 1926, which Lewis declined. The Nobel award followed in 1930, recognising the descriptive power and inventiveness of his writing.
entries.significance: The prize highlighted how humour and close observation can reveal a society through its characters. Lewis’s later books extended his career, but the award concerned the work already achieved by 1930.
