entries.title: The Discovery of Human Blood Groups and Transfusion Safety
entries.overview: In 1930, Karl Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize for identifying that different types of red blood cells exist in humans.
entries.background: Before his findings, transferring blood between individuals to treat heavy blood loss from accidents or illnesses frequently caused dangerous, fatal reactions during the transfusion process.
entries.work: In 1901, Karl Landsteiner identified that mixing blood from different people could cause red blood cells to clump together. He determined that humans possess distinct blood groups based on these varying cell types. This discovery provided the explanation for why previous attempts at transferring blood between patients often resulted in disastrous medical outcomes.
entries.significance: This work made transfusions safer by identifying a major source of incompatibility between donor and recipient blood.

entries.title: Promoting International Peace Through Christian Church Unity
entries.overview: Swedish Archbishop Nathan Söderblom worked to unite different Christian denominations to foster a global mindset focused on preventing conflict between various nations.
entries.background: During his career, Söderblom addressed the challenges of nationalism, racism, and militarism. He believed that religious communities could help establish an international system for justice and arbitration through the League of Nations.
entries.work: After serving as a professor of theology and becoming archbishop in 1914, Söderblom organized the 1925 Universal Conference on Life and Work in Stockholm. As the primary organizer, he led this church meeting to create a shared platform for peace. He encouraged churches to use pulpits and newspapers to spread messages of love and oppose oppression, aiming to build widespread Christian support for peaceful international relations.
entries.significance: His efforts sought to establish a unified religious movement that would actively oppose aggressive nationalism and promote global justice across national borders.

entries.title: The Discovery of Light Scattering and Energy Transfer
entries.overview: In 1928, Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman found that light changes wavelength when it hits small particles, such as molecules within a gas.
entries.background: When light packets, or photons, encounter particles smaller than their own wavelength, the light spreads out in multiple directions. This process is known as scattering, which occurs during interactions between light and matter.
entries.work: During his 1928 research, Chandrasekhara Venkata Raman observed that a tiny fraction of scattered light shifts to different wavelengths from the original source. He demonstrated that this happens because some photons transfer a portion of their energy to molecules, increasing the molecules' energy levels. This discovery showed how light and matter exchange energy during physical collisions.
entries.significance: This finding provides a method for analyzing various types of material by observing how light behaves when interacting with different molecular structures.

entries.title: Developing Chemical Processes Using High Pressure Methods
entries.overview: Two scientists created distinct industrial methods that utilize extremely high pressure and heat to transform chemical substances into useful liquids or fertilizers.
entries.background: Producing ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen requires significant pressure. Similarly, turning solid coal into liquid oil necessitates exposing the material to hydrogen gas under intense pressure for chemical transformation.
entries.work: Around 1913, Carl Bosch created an industrial apparatus using various steels with different heat and pressure resistances to scale Fritz Haber's ammonia production method. Separately, in 1913, Friedrich Bergius developed a technique to convert solid lignite coal into liquid oil by applying hydrogen gas under high pressure to create hydrocarbons.
entries.significance: Bosch enabled efficient large-scale manufacturing for several chemical processes. Bergius provided a way to produce liquid fuel for vehicles from coal.

entries.title: Dalarna’s traditions as a world of poetry
entries.overview: Erik Axel Karlfeldt was honoured for poetry rooted in the Swedish region of Dalarna. Local traditions became a setting for feelings and experiences that reached beyond that particular place.
entries.background: Karlfeldt grew up in a family with generations of farming and mining behind it. He wrote poetry from childhood and published his first collection in 1895, while his university studies were still in progress. His later work included employment as a librarian.
entries.work: His poems draw on the landscapes, customs and language of his home region. The recurring figure Fridolin acts as an alter ego through whom Karlfeldt explores longing, loss and humour. A strong command of language allows the poems to combine restraint with imaginative energy. Although closely connected to inherited traditions, the writing tests what poetic form and invention can make of that inheritance.
entries.significance: The Nobel recognition concerned this poetic achievement rather than a single discovery or historical argument. Karlfeldt’s regional world functions as a small stage on which broader human experiences can be expressed with particular detail and feeling.

entries.title: Discovering How Cells Use Oxygen Through Specific Enzymes
entries.overview: Otto Warburg identified the specific type of enzyme responsible for facilitating cellular respiration and energy release during the breakdown of nutrients.
entries.background: Cells require energy to build their structures. This biological process depends on respiration, where specialized substances called enzymes act as helpers to facilitate chemical reactions without becoming part of the final cell products.
entries.work: During his 1928 research, Otto Warburg examined how sea urchins and other early-stage organisms perform respiration. By measuring oxygen usage in living cells and analyzing which enzymes reacted, he determined that the respiratory enzyme is a red ferrous pigment. This specific substance is chemically related to hemoglobin, the protein found in blood.
entries.significance: This work clarified the nature and mechanical operation of the respiratory enzyme, revealing how organisms utilize oxygen for energy.

entries.title: Efforts to Promote International Law and Global Disarmament
entries.overview: Two individuals received this award for their separate work attempting to revive peace ideals and strengthen international cooperation during a period of global conflict.
entries.background: During the early twentieth century, world tensions rose through World War I. This era saw intense debates regarding national security, the legitimacy of peace treaties like the 1919 agreement with Germany, and the role of international organizations.
entries.work: In 1915, Jane Addams founded a women's peace league, later chairing a conference in the Netherlands to seek mediation. In 1925, Nicholas Murray Butler began leading the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, working toward the 1928 Briand-Kellogg Pact. While Addams focused on disarmament and supporting immigrants at Hull House, Butler worked to strengthen international law and the Hague's International Court.
entries.significance: These distinct activities sought to reduce war through legal frameworks and diplomatic pressure, even as some efforts faced opposition from national governments or political shifts.

entries.title: Discoveries and Investigations Regarding the Nature of Surface Chemistry
entries.overview: Irving Langmuir studied how chemical reactions occur at contact points between different states of matter, such as solids and gases.
entries.background: Chemical processes frequently happen more efficiently when substances in different phases meet. Researching these interactions involves observing how atoms behave at the boundaries where surfaces and gases touch.
entries.work: While studying light bulbs containing thin hydrogen gas, Irving Langmuir found a single layer of hydrogen atoms forming on the interior surface. In 1917, through examining oil films and various materials, he developed a theory suggesting surfaces act like chessboards. He proposed that each square on this surface can hold only one atom or molecule, meaning nearby particles can react more easily.
entries.significance: This work provided a way to understand how atoms occupy space on a surface, explaining why certain molecules are positioned to interact.

entries.title: The Narrative Artistry of The Forsyte Saga
entries.overview: John Galsworthy received this prize for his skilled storytelling, particularly through the creation of his famous series, The Forsyte Saga.
entries.background: Originally a law student, Galsworthy traveled globally to manage family businesses. He initially published short stories using the name John Sinjohn before finding success writing under his own name.
entries.work: After his novel The Island Pharisees criticized the self-centered nature of England's upper class, Galsworthy transitioned from using satire as a tool for social critique toward more detailed character studies. His work evolved through The Forsyte Saga, a collection including three novels and two short stories, which moved away from radical criticism to present warmer, intricate portraits of people.
entries.significance: His writing style shifted from attacking contemporary culture via satire to mastering the art of complex, humanized storytelling within his most recognized literary works.

entries.title: Discoveries Concerning How Nerve Cells Function
entries.overview: This prize honors how the nervous system manages bodily functions through connections between the brain, spinal cord, and various organs.
entries.background: The nervous system uses nerve cells with extensions called fibers to connect the brain and spinal cord to the rest of the body. These cells process signals to control physical movements.
entries.work: During the 1890s, Charles Sherrington demonstrated how the spinal cord and brain transform impulses into muscular contractions and relaxations through complex reflex interplays. Separately, in 1928, Edgar Adrian created techniques to measure electrical currents in nerves. He discovered that while individual signals maintain a consistent size, stronger stimuli increase the frequency of signals and the number of nerve fibers activated.
entries.significance: These findings clarified how nerve impulses trigger reflexes and revealed that the nervous system communicates intensity through signal frequency rather than signal strength.

entries.title: Development of Quantum Mechanics and the Uncertainty Relation
entries.overview: Werner Heisenberg developed new mathematical methods to describe how electrons behave within atoms, helping scientists understand more complex atomic structures.
entries.background: Niels Bohr's existing atomic theory explained hydrogen spectrums through electrons jumping between orbits. However, this model lacked the necessary framework to accurately describe the behavior of larger, more complicated atoms and molecules.
entries.work: In 1925, Werner Heisenberg created a version of quantum mechanics using matrices. Later, in 1927, he introduced the uncertainty relation. This principle established specific mathematical limits on how precisely one can simultaneously measure both the position and the velocity of a particle.
entries.significance: These advancements allowed for the discovery of different hydrogen forms and provided a functional way to apply quantum mechanics to diverse chemical structures.

entries.title: Classical Russian Prose Traditions and the 1933 Literature Prize
entries.overview: Ivan Bunin received this award for maintaining strict artistic standards within the established traditions of classical Russian prose writing.
entries.background: Raised on Russian estates, Ivan Bunin was exposed to folklore by his mother. After traveling extensively through Europe and the Middle East, he left Russia in 1920 due to the Bolshevik regime.
entries.work: Starting with poetry collections between 1887 and 1891, Ivan Bunin later transitioned into prose. His novels, including The Village (1910) and Sukhodol (1912), used realism to depict the decline of landowners and the harshness of rural life. His writing style is noted for being concentrated, reserved, and elegant, often conveying a sense of melancholy through descriptions of the Russian countryside.
entries.significance: His literary contribution preserved classical Russian prose techniques while providing unadorned, realistic depictions of a changing social landscape and the fading era of landed estates.

sources.title: Ivan Bunin — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: Discovering How Chromosomes Carry Genetic Information
entries.overview: Thomas Hunt Morgan identified how chromosomes act as the physical carriers for genes that determine an organism's inherited traits.
entries.background: During the early 1900s, scientists sought to understand the mechanical process of inheritance. The biological connection between cellular structures and passing traits remained unproven until detailed observations were made using specific organisms.
entries.work: Starting in 1910, Thomas Hunt Morgan performed statistical analyses on fruit fly inheritance patterns. His research demonstrated that genes reside within chromosomes inside cell nuclei. He determined that genes are arranged in linear rows and that related traits often belong to genes positioned near each other. Additionally, Morgan identified crossover, a process where segments from different chromosomes swap positions.
entries.significance: These findings established the chromosome's role in heredity and provided a concrete understanding of how genetic material is organized and exchanged during reproduction.

entries.title: The Analysis of War and International Cooperation Through Literature
entries.overview: Norman Angell received this award for his written arguments against the profitability of warfare and his advocacy for global collaboration.
entries.background: In 1910, Norman Angell published a book examining how modern interconnectedness could influence conflict. He proposed that increasing free trade and educational improvements would make aggressive military actions irrational and unrewarding for nations.
entries.work: Through his 1910 book, The Great Illusion, Angell argued that the risk of mutual destruction made war unprofitable for both attackers and defenders. Later, as a supporter of the League of Nations, he worked to spread these ideas of peaceful development via various peace societies. His writing reached millions of readers and was translated into many different languages to promote international stability.
entries.significance: Angell's theories, known as angellism, promoted the idea that economic interdependence and education serve as tools to prevent the financial and social costs of armed struggle.

sources.title: Sir Norman Angell — Nobel Prize facts and background

entries.title: New Mathematical Descriptions of Atomic Energy Levels
entries.overview: Physicists developed new equations to describe how electrons behave and move within atoms using wave-like properties and relativity.
entries.background: Earlier models explained hydrogen atom radiation through fixed electron orbits, but these descriptions failed for more complex atoms. Scientists needed better mathematical frameworks to understand energy transitions in larger molecules and structures.
entries.work: In 1926, Erwin Schrödinger created a wave equation treating electrons as both particles and waves to calculate atomic energy levels. Between 1925 and 1926, other theories also emerged for these levels. In 1928, Paul Dirac formulated a quantum theory incorporating Einstein’s relativity. His specific equations suggested the existence of a positively charged particle, known as the positron, which matched the electron's properties.
entries.significance: These discoveries provided productive forms of atomic theory, allowing for more accurate calculations of energy states and predicting new particles.

entries.title: The Discovery of Heavy Hydrogen Through Liquid Distillation
entries.overview: Harold C. Urey identified a version of hydrogen, known as deuterium, which possesses twice the atomic weight of standard hydrogen atoms.
entries.background: Scientists were investigating isotopes, forms of the same element with different atomic masses. Urey sought evidence that hydrogen also existed in a heavier form.
entries.work: In work published in 1932, Urey and colleagues identified deuterium after concentrating liquid hydrogen and examining its spectrum. Deuterium has about twice the mass of ordinary hydrogen. Water containing deuterium has properties that differ from ordinary water.
entries.significance: The identification of deuterium provided a new substance with different chemical behaviors, which became useful for various applications in nuclear technology.

entries.title: Theatre that questions identity and its own conventions
entries.overview: Luigi Pirandello was recognised for renewing drama through daring theatrical invention. His plays combine comic and tragic elements while examining identity, psychology and the unstable sense of self.
entries.background: Pirandello came from a family involved in Sicilian sulphur mining and earned a doctorate in philology. Flooding of the family’s mines in 1903 brought financial and personal upheaval. His literary career encompassed stories and novels as well as an extensive body of plays.
entries.work: Six Characters in Search of an Author, first staged in 1921, became a central example of his experimental approach. As a play concerned with the making of theatre itself, it unsettled ordinary expectations about dramatic presentation. The first audience reacted so strongly that Pirandello left by a side exit. His wider work repeatedly questions how an individual’s identity is understood and presented to others.
entries.significance: The award recognised a transformation in the possibilities of stage art. The plays continued to be performed and later helped prepare the ground for the theatre of the absurd, rather than belonging to that later movement themselves.

entries.title: Liver therapy opened a route to treating pernicious anaemia
entries.overview: George Whipple, George Minot and William Murphy showed that liver-based treatments could restore blood formation, leading to an effective historical treatment for pernicious anaemia.
entries.background: Anaemia means that the blood cannot carry oxygen normally because of a shortage or problem with red blood cells. Pernicious anaemia was a particularly serious illness. Researchers investigated whether substances in food could help the body make new blood cells.
entries.work: Whipple studied dogs recovering from blood loss and compared different diets, finding that liver and certain other foods stimulated blood formation. In 1926 Minot and Murphy used these findings to develop liver therapy for patients with pernicious anaemia. Their patients’ improvement pointed toward a necessary substance in liver. That substance was later identified as vitamin B12; the early experiments did not themselves isolate the vitamin.
entries.significance: The work turned a previously devastating condition into a treatable one and opened a path to identifying its missing factor. Modern treatment replaces vitamin B12 directly and addresses its impaired absorption; the historical liver diet is not today’s standard treatment.

entries.title: Chairing the League of Nations Disarmament Conference Negotiations
entries.overview: Arthur Henderson received this honor for leading international efforts to reduce military armaments during the early 1930s.
entries.background: During the inter-war years, global tensions rose. As a prominent British Labour Party founder and politician, Arthur Henderson utilized his leadership roles in government to support the League of Nations' mission.
entries.work: Between 1931 and 1934, Arthur Henderson served as Chairman of the League of Nations Disarmament Conference. He directed these complex negotiations through a period of significant resistance. While facing opposition from major world powers and his own British administration, he worked to maintain progress in the discussions regarding the reduction of weapons.
entries.significance: His leadership provided a central mechanism for managing international disarmament talks during a period of intense geopolitical disagreement among powerful nations.

entries.title: The Artificial Synthesis of New Radioactive Elements
entries.overview: In 1934, researchers successfully transformed stable aluminum atoms into a new, man-made radioactive form of phosphorus through particle bombardment.
entries.background: During the early twentieth century, scientists used radiation from natural substances to study atomic structures. Researchers sought to understand how hitting atoms with energetic particles might alter their fundamental chemical properties.
entries.work: In 1934, Frédéric Joliot and Irène Joliot-Curie bombarded thin aluminum with alpha particles, which are helium atom nuclei. Using a cloud chamber to track movements, they observed a new type of radiation. They found that the aluminum atoms had been converted into a radioactive isotope of phosphorus, meaning the radiation persisted even after the initial source was removed.
entries.significance: This work demonstrated that radioactive elements could be created artificially for the first time, rather than only being found naturally in the environment.

entries.title: The embryonic organiser and the influence of neighbouring cells
entries.overview: Hans Spemann received the prize for discovering the organiser effect: a region of an early embryo can influence nearby cells to form an organised set of body structures.
entries.background: An embryo begins as a dividing cell, but its descendants eventually take different roles. The question was whether each cell’s fate was fixed from the outset or could be shaped by its surroundings. Transplanting tiny pieces of embryonic tissue offered a way to test this.
entries.work: Working in Spemann’s laboratory, Hilde Mangold performed crucial grafting experiments on newt embryos in the early 1920s. Tissue from a particular region could induce neighbouring tissue in another embryo to contribute to a second body axis. Their results were published jointly in 1924. The graft did more than grow by itself: it changed how surrounding cells developed, demonstrating the organiser effect.
entries.significance: The discovery showed that development depends on interactions between cells and tissues. It gave experimental embryology a way to investigate how a body’s overall arrangement emerges. Although the Nobel award went to Spemann, Mangold’s experimental contribution is essential to the story.

entries.title: Journalism and Political Criticism During Germany's Interwar Years
entries.overview: A journalist received this honor because of his efforts to defend freedom of expression and his work supporting global peace efforts.
entries.background: During the years between the two World Wars, Carl von Ossietzky actively criticized German political shifts. He utilized journalism to expose secret military rearmament that violated the terms of the Versailles Treaty, leading to a treason conviction.
entries.work: As a socialist journalist, Carl von Ossietzky reported on illegal German military activities. Following the Nazi rise to power in 1933, he was detained and placed in a concentration camp. To support his release, an international movement nominated him for this peace distinction, highlighting his commitment to free thought despite his imprisonment.
entries.significance: The award drew global attention to his situation, though Hitler responded by banning Germans from accepting future prizes and preventing the ill recipient from traveling.

entries.title: The Discovery of the Neutral Subatomic Particle
entries.overview: James Chadwick identified the neutron, a neutral particle found within the atomic nucleus that possesses a mass similar to a proton.
entries.background: In 1930, Herbert Becker and Walter Bothe observed strong radiation emitted when directing alpha particles at beryllium. Scientists initially hypothesized this emission was high-energy electromagnetic radiation, though Ernest Rutherford had previously suggested a neutral particle might exist in nuclei.
entries.work: During his 1932 research, James Chadwick demonstrated that the radiation from the beryllium experiments actually consisted of neutral particles. He proved these particles were not electromagnetic waves but possessed a mass roughly equal to that of a proton. This evidence confirmed the existence of what became known as the neutron, settling the debate regarding the nature of the penetrating radiation observed by Becker and Bothe.
entries.significance: This discovery provided concrete proof of the neutron's existence, confirming Rutherford's earlier theoretical idea about the composition of atomic nuclei.

entries.title: Investigating Molecular Structure Through Electrical Charges and Radiation
entries.overview: Peter Debye researched how molecules are shaped by studying electrical charge distributions and the way radiation interacts with gases.
entries.background: A primary goal in chemistry is discovering the physical arrangement of atoms within a molecule. Scientists needed reliable ways to map these complex internal structures.
entries.work: In 1912, Peter Debye created a technique to measure how electrical charges spread across a molecule, known as dipole moments. Additionally, he created methods for using X-ray radiation and electron beams to map the structures of molecules found in gases.
entries.significance: These developments provided new tools for determining molecular arrangements and understanding the distribution of electrical charges within various substances.

entries.title: A modern American theatre of tragedy
entries.overview: Eugene O’Neill was recognised for dramatic work that combined emotional force with an original approach to tragedy. His plays explored the pressures within families and the conflict between hopes and experience.
entries.background: O’Neill grew up around his actor father’s touring life and later worked at sea and in other temporary occupations. Family addiction and his unsettled early years supplied experiences that informed the emotional world of his writing.
entries.work: Beyond the Horizon brought major recognition in 1920. In Strange Interlude, recognised with a Pulitzer Prize in 1928, O’Neill pursued an ambitious account of a woman’s emotional life. Mourning Becomes Electra, completed in 1931, reworked Greek tragedy in the setting of New England after the American Civil War. These pre-award achievements demonstrate his range in adapting tragic form to modern lives. His better-known later works should be understood as part of his continuing career.
entries.significance: The 1936 award recognised an already established transformation of American drama: characters’ inner conflicts and difficult relationships could carry the intensity associated with classical tragedy.

entries.title: Chemical messengers between nerves and organs
entries.overview: Henry Dale and Otto Loewi established that chemical substances help transmit nerve signals. Their findings explained how an electrical event in a nerve can influence another tissue through a released messenger.
entries.background: Electrical impulses were already known to travel along nerves. What remained uncertain was how a nerve passed its effect to an organ: was the connection wholly electrical, or could a chemical carry the message across?
entries.work: In 1914 Dale showed that acetylcholine produced effects resembling those of the parasympathetic nervous system, including slowing the heart. In 1921 Loewi stimulated the nerve supplying a frog heart and transferred the surrounding fluid to another heart. The second heart responded similarly, showing that the first preparation had released a substance into the fluid. Subsequent work identified acetylcholine’s role and clarified chemical transmission.
entries.significance: The experiments distinguished transmission along a nerve from communication between a nerve and its target. They established a chemical component in nervous-system signalling and gave researchers a concrete messenger to investigate, rather than treating all nerve action as electricity alone.

entries.title: Diplomatic Mediation and the Argentine Antiwar Pact
entries.overview: Carlos Saavedra Lamas earned recognition for creating a South American agreement against aggression and helping negotiate peace during regional conflicts.
entries.background: During the 1930s, international tensions rose. Following his appointment as Argentina's Foreign Minister in 1932, Saavedra Lamas worked within the League of Nations to address territorial disputes and aggressive military actions occurring across different continents.
entries.work: In 1933, Carlos Saavedra Lamas developed the Argentine Antiwar Pact, which by 1936 included thirty-one nations and established legal condemnation of aggressive wars. Additionally, in 1935, he acted as a mediator to assist in negotiations between Paraguay and Bolivia following their Chaco War conflict. He also participated in the League of Nations' efforts to condemn Italy's military campaign in Ethiopia.
entries.significance: His work established a regional legal principle regarding international law and provided a framework for attempting to resolve specific South American border disputes through diplomacy.

entries.title: Cosmic rays and the first observed antiparticle
entries.overview: Victor Hess discovered radiation arriving from space, while Carl Anderson identified the positron in cosmic-ray tracks. The shared prize recognised two distinct discoveries connected by the investigation of this radiation.
entries.background: Radiation can knock electrons from atoms, producing electrically charged ions. Measurements of ionisation therefore offered a way to detect radiation that could not be seen directly. Later, quantum theory suggested that a counterpart to the electron might exist.
entries.work: In 1912 Hess carried instruments in balloons and measured how ionisation changed with altitude. It first fell, then rose at greater heights. Night-time and eclipse measurements showed that the Sun could not account for the effect. In 1932 Anderson examined cosmic-ray tracks in a cloud chamber and identified a particle with positive charge and a mass like the electron’s: the positron.
entries.significance: Hess established an extraterrestrial source of penetrating radiation; his experiments did not by themselves locate its precise astronomical origins. Anderson supplied the first experimental identification of an antiparticle, giving physical evidence for a new class of particles.

entries.title: Investigating the Molecular Structures of Sugars and Essential Vitamins
entries.overview: This award honors research into the chemical compositions of various carbohydrates and several important vitamins required for human growth and health.
entries.background: Human bodies require more than just fats, proteins, and carbohydrates to function. To grow properly, organisms also rely on water, salts, and specific substances known as vitamins.
entries.work: Around 1928, Norman Haworth mapped the structures of cellulose, starch, and various sugars. In 1933, Haworth determined the molecular structure of vitamin C. Separately, Paul Karrer extracted vitamin A from cod-liver oil and identified its composition in 1931, marking the first time a vitamin's structure was mapped. Karrer also determined the structure of vitamin B2 in 1933.
entries.significance: Haworth’s findings enabled the artificial production of vitamin C. Similarly, Karrer’s work on vitamin B2 made its man-made production possible.

entries.title: The Realist Portrait of Human Conflict in French Literature
entries.overview: Roger Martin du Gard received this award for his detailed and truthful depiction of modern life and human struggles within a large-scale novel series.
entries.background: Rooted in realist and naturalist writing traditions, the author utilized his training as an archivist-paleographer to bring historical precision to his fiction. His work explores themes like pacifism and humanist socialism through meticulous scholarly detail.
entries.work: Beginning in 1922, Roger Martin du Gard published The Thibaults, a novel-cycle following brothers Antoine and Jacques from a prosperous Catholic family into the upheavals surrounding the First World War. Its already published volumes prompted the 1937 award; the cycle was not completed until 1940. His earlier success, Jean Barois, appeared in 1913 and demonstrated his detailed approach to contemporary life.
entries.significance: The author's writing provided an artistic look at human conflict and the fundamental elements of modern life using scrupulous realism and attention to small details.

entries.title: Vitamin C and the chemistry of biological oxidation
entries.overview: Albert Szent-Györgyi investigated how cells release energy through controlled chemical reactions. The award recognised contributions involving vitamin C and the catalytic role of fumaric acid.
entries.background: Cells do not simply burn their nutrients in one step. Biological oxidation releases energy through a sequence of reactions, making it important to identify both the intermediate substances and the factors that help those reactions proceed.
entries.work: Szent-Györgyi investigated reactions involved in cellular respiration and showed how small amounts of certain organic acids, including fumaric acid, could promote oxidation. His experiments studied how these substances participate in chemical transformations within cells. He also isolated the substance identified as vitamin C and investigated its role in biological oxidation. In his Nobel lecture he described energy release as a succession of transfers rather than a single direct reaction between food and oxygen.
entries.significance: The research helped connect nutrition with the chemical machinery of living cells. It revealed particular substances that researchers could isolate and test, making the breakdown of nutrients an experimentally tractable sequence rather than an unexplained property of living tissue.

entries.title: Diplomatic Efforts Toward Global Disarmament and Collective Security
entries.overview: Robert Cecil received this award for his persistent work promoting international cooperation, reducing military arms, and strengthening a global organization to prevent conflict.
entries.background: Following World War I, the Versailles peace conference established new rules for international relations. During the inter-war period, political leaders sought methods to manage foreign policy and prevent future wars through organized diplomatic structures.
entries.work: After serving as Minister of Blockade during the Great War, Robert Cecil helped create the League of Nations rules. In 1919, he helped found the League of Nations Union to influence British foreign policy. By 1937, Robert Cecil led a large-scale petition urging the League to use economic and military penalties against those breaking peace agreements. He also held leadership roles in the International Peace Campaign to promote disarmament.
entries.significance: His actions focused on using organized pressure groups and international sanctions to encourage nations to follow established peace treaties and reduce military buildup.

entries.title: Experimental Proof of Electron Wave Properties Through Crystal Diffraction
entries.overview: This award recognizes the separate experimental findings showing that electrons behave like waves when interacting with certain materials.
entries.background: Early quantum physics suggested energy exists in fixed amounts. While scientists knew light behaves as both particles and waves, researchers later proposed that matter, including electrons, possesses these dual characteristics.
entries.work: In 1927 Clinton Davisson and George Paget Thomson obtained independent experimental evidence for electron waves. Davisson studied electrons scattered from a nickel crystal; Thomson studied electrons transmitted through thin films. The resulting patterns showed diffraction, a characteristic wave effect. Their different experimental arrangements therefore supported the same conclusion about the nature of electrons.
entries.significance: These separate experiments provided the experimental discovery of electron diffraction by crystals, confirming the dual particle-wave nature of matter.

entries.title: Research on Carotenoids and Essential Vitamin Structures
entries.overview: Richard Kuhn investigated carotenoids, a family of coloured substances that includes carotene, and carried out important work on vitamins B2 and B6. Some carotenoids are precursors from which the body makes vitamin A.
entries.background: In 1933, scientists sought to understand substances found in plants, such as carrots, that are necessary for bodily growth through the study of carotene components.
entries.work: Working with other researchers, Richard Kuhn identified two types of carotene before finding a third type in 1933. He also explored related carotenoid substances and investigated vitamins B2 and B6. To isolate and produce pure substances, he developed chromatographic techniques, which are methods used to separate different components within a mixture.
entries.significance: Kuhn's work established the existence of specific carotene types and provided the technical methods needed to extract and purify these important nutritional substances.

entries.title: Literary Descriptions of Chinese Peasant Life and Biographies
entries.overview: Pearl Buck received this honor for her detailed writing about the daily lives of Chinese farmers and her creation of significant biographical works.
entries.background: Raised in China as a bilingual child of missionaries, Pearl Buck lived there until 1934. Her writing explores characters navigating the tension between ancient traditions and modern changes.
entries.work: In 1930 Pearl Buck published her first novel, East Wind, West Wind. Her breakthrough followed with The Good Earth (1931), Sons (1932) and A House Divided (1935), a trilogy chronicling the Wang family. These stories portray everyday life in China through characters whose circumstances bring tradition and modern change into conflict.
entries.significance: Her books achieved widespread popularity during the 1930s by providing epic, detailed accounts of life within the Chinese peasantry.

entries.title: Discovery of Mechanisms Controlling Human Breathing Regulation
entries.overview: Corneille Heymans identified how specific bodily structures and nerve pathways communicate to manage our automatic breathing processes.
entries.background: The body maintains respiration through a respiratory center located within the medulla oblongata. Scientists investigated how muscular reflexes and changes in blood chemistry trigger the signals necessary to sustain this involuntary rhythmic breathing.
entries.work: Heymans, his father and colleagues used animal experiments to investigate how nervous reflexes and blood chemistry regulate breathing. In 1931 Heymans demonstrated an important role for the carotid body, a small structure associated with the carotid artery. Its sensing of the blood’s chemical composition helps trigger signals that influence respiratory activity. This connected changes in the blood with the automatic control of breathing.
entries.significance: This research clarified how the sinus and aortic mechanisms function to regulate breathing by sensing chemical changes in the bloodstream.

entries.title: Assisting Displaced People Through the Nansen International Office
entries.overview: The Nansen International Office for Refugees provided essential humanitarian aid and legal documentation to many displaced individuals throughout much of the 1930s.
entries.background: Following work started by Fridtjof Nansen, a League of Nations resolution led to the office's creation in 1930. This organization addressed the needs of people forced from their homes during this period.
entries.work: The Office helped Armenians fleeing Turkey and influenced the League of Nations Refugee Convention. Operating in Europe, Syria, and China, the group managed refugee camps and distributed food, medicine, and jobs. They also issued Nansen passports to stateless individuals and assisted with visa procurement. These humanitarian activities continued through the decade until the organization closed in 1938.
entries.significance: The agency provided vital resources and legal protections for various groups of refugees across several continents during a time of significant migration.

entries.title: Creating radioactive isotopes with slow neutrons
entries.overview: Enrico Fermi used neutron bombardment to produce radioactive isotopes and discovered that slowing neutrons could greatly increase their interaction with atomic nuclei.
entries.background: In 1932, the discovery of the neutron provided a fresh way to examine atomic structures. This new particle allowed researchers to study how nuclei react when struck by subatomic components.
entries.work: Beginning in 1934, Fermi and his colleagues bombarded different elements with neutrons. Nuclei that captured neutrons could form new, often radioactive isotopes. They also discovered that passing neutrons through material such as paraffin slowed them down and increased their effectiveness in many reactions. The result was a method for investigating nuclei and producing previously unknown radioactive forms of elements.
entries.significance: The research established neutron irradiation as a powerful experimental method. It also showed that a particle’s speed can change its likelihood of interacting with a nucleus, rather than faster particles always being more effective.

entries.title: Chemical Discoveries Regarding Sex Hormones and Terpene Structures
entries.overview: This chemistry prize honors individual research into the chemical makeup of sex hormones and the shared building blocks found in various organic substances.
entries.background: During the 1920s and 1930s, scientists investigated how specific molecules regulate body functions and how complex scents relate to larger chemical families like terpenes.
entries.work: In the 1930s Adolf Butenandt helped establish the chemical structures of several sex hormones, including estriol, and isolated androsterone in pure form. Leopold Ruzicka investigated the structural relationships among terpenes, recognising repeating isoprene building blocks. He also showed how androsterone and testosterone could be produced by modifying cholesterol. Their distinct lines of work clarified both hormone chemistry and relationships within complex organic molecules.
entries.significance: These findings clarified the chemical composition of vital hormones and established a fundamental structural link between diverse substances like fragrances and cholesterol.

entries.title: Literature Prize for Depicting Finnish Peasant Life and Nature
entries.overview: Frans Eemil Sillanpää received this honor for his detailed writing about the Finnish countryside, focusing on the lives of rural people and their connection to the natural world.
entries.background: After studying medicine for five years, Sillanpää moved back to his home village in 1913. He chose to focus on writing instead of pursuing a medical degree, using a scientific perspective to observe human existence within his creative works.
entries.work: Sillanpää wrote seven novels and ten short story collections. His 1916 novel, Life and Sun, utilized a Darwinian approach to describe young love. In his 1919 work, Meek Heritage, he chronicled the life of a crofter and provided an explanation for the Finnish civil war rebellion. Throughout these texts, he portrayed humans as beings tied to elemental forces.
entries.significance: His writing is noted for its careful portrayal of how the peasantry interacts with nature and for providing insight into the historical struggles within his country.

entries.title: The Discovery of Antibacterial Effects in Prontosil
entries.overview: Gerhard Domagk identified how certain chemical substances, known as sulfonamides, could effectively fight off harmful bacteria during controlled animal testing.
entries.background: During the 1800s, medical professionals realized that microorganisms cause various illnesses. This realization sparked a difficult search for chemical methods to stop these microscopic attacks, though many believed finding such treatments was an impossible goal.
entries.work: In 1932, Gerhard Domagk and his fellow researchers conducted experiments using mice. They demonstrated that sulfonamides could counteract the bacteria responsible for blood poisoning. This specific research identified the antibacterial properties of prontosil, providing a foundation for developing sulfa drugs, an early family of effective antibacterial medicines.
entries.significance: This work helped establish chemical treatment of bacterial infection and led to a family of sulfonamide medicines. It demonstrated that a substance tested in the laboratory could protect an infected animal, providing a practical route toward new treatments.

entries.title: The Invention of the Cyclotron and Artificial Radioactive Element Creation
entries.overview: Ernest Lawrence created a machine called a cyclotron to speed up particles, allowing scientists to transform atoms into different isotopes through high-speed collisions.
entries.background: To investigate nuclei, researchers needed controllable beams of particles energetic enough to cause nuclear reactions. A central challenge was accelerating the particles without making an impractically long machine or requiring a single enormous voltage.
entries.work: Lawrence conceived the cyclotron in 1929 and developed working machines with colleagues and students in the early 1930s. An electrical field repeatedly accelerates charged particles, while a magnetic field bends their paths so they can return for another acceleration. They spiral outward before striking a target. This made it possible to induce nuclear reactions and produce artificial radioactive isotopes.
entries.significance: The cyclotron gave nuclear physics a reusable source of energetic particles. Its development expanded the range of nuclei and reactions that researchers could study and supplied new radioactive materials for further experiments.

entries.title: Using Radioactive Isotopes to Track Elements Through Chemical Processes
entries.overview: George de Hevesy developed a technique using radioactive isotopes as markers to follow the movement of specific elements through various chemical or biological pathways.
entries.background: Hevesy’s early attempts to separate the substance then called radium D from lead failed. Radium D is a radioactive isotope of lead, so ordinary chemical separation could not distinguish it from the other lead atoms. This difficulty suggested a new use for it.
entries.work: Hevesy realised that radioactive lead could act as a label for ordinary lead. After adding a minute quantity of the radioactive isotope, he could follow the element by measuring radioactivity in different samples. The tracer shares the element’s chemical behaviour while providing a detectable signal. He developed the indicator method in the 1910s and extended it to biological investigations, including work on plants published in 1923.
entries.significance: Radioactive tracers made it possible to follow elements through processes that were otherwise difficult to observe. They became important experimental tools in chemistry and biology because a detectable label could reveal movement and transformation without requiring the element to be seen directly.

entries.title: Discovering the Role and Chemical Structure of Vitamin K
entries.overview: This award honors the identification of a vital nutrient required for blood to clot properly and the determination of its chemical makeup.
entries.background: Human health requires vitamins alongside proteins, fats, and carbohydrates. Early research focused on how specific dietary components prevent abnormal bleeding and support essential bodily functions.
entries.work: In 1934, Henrik Dam observed that chickens fed low-fat diets experienced prolonged bleeding. He found that adding hempseed stopped this effect, identifying a substance called vitamin K necessary for coagulation. Later, in 1939, Edward Doisy produced two pure variants of this substance. This allowed him to define its chemical structure and develop methods for artificial production.
entries.significance: Identifying the properties and structure of vitamin K provided important knowledge for managing bleeding issues, particularly in small children.

entries.title: Molecular beams and the magnetism of the proton
entries.overview: Otto Stern was recognised for developing molecular-beam methods and discovering the proton’s magnetic moment. His work made beams of particles a precise tool for investigating atomic and nuclear properties.
entries.background: Before 1922, classical physics suggested that atoms and electrons moving through magnetic fields would spread out in a continuous distribution. Scientists needed new ways to test emerging theories regarding how particles occupy energy states.
entries.work: In 1922 Stern and Walter Gerlach sent silver atoms through an uneven magnetic field. The beam separated into two parts rather than spreading continuously, supporting the existence of discrete quantum states. Stern went on to develop beam techniques for investigating magnetic properties, including the magnetic moment of the proton. The Nobel citation explicitly recognised that nuclear measurement as well as the wider experimental method.
entries.significance: These experiments linked measurable beam deflections with properties of atoms and nuclei. They gave quantum physics direct experimental tests and established techniques for probing magnetism at scales that could not be examined with ordinary magnets or microscopes.

entries.title: The Discovery of Splitting Heavy Atomic Nuclei
entries.overview: Otto Hahn was awarded the prize for nuclear fission. The discovery joined chemical evidence from Hahn and Fritz Strassmann with the physical explanation developed by Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch.
entries.background: Following the 1932 discovery of the neutron, researchers gained a new method for investigating atomic structures. This tool allowed scientists to probe the interior of atoms by using neutron particles to trigger changes in heavy elements.
entries.work: In December 1938 Hahn and Strassmann identified barium among the products of uranium bombarded with neutrons. Barium was far lighter than the elements they expected, creating a major puzzle. Meitner and Frisch explained the result around the turn of 1939: the uranium nucleus had split into lighter parts, releasing energy. This process became known as nuclear fission. The discovery depended on both the chemical identification and its physical interpretation.
entries.significance: This finding established the concept of nuclear fission, providing the scientific basis for the later development of both nuclear energy production and nuclear weapons.

entries.title: Literary Achievements of a Danish Author and Former Medical Student
entries.overview: Johannes V. Jensen received this award for his creative writing, which blended intense imaginative power with an expansive interest in diverse intellectual subjects.
entries.background: After three years of medical studies, Jensen turned fully to writing. His scientific interests remained important to his fiction, journalism and essays. His travels included Asia and the United States, and he also worked briefly as a newspaper correspondent in Spain.
entries.work: Between 1898 and 1910, Jensen produced Himmerlandshistorier, focusing on his birthplace. In Kongens Fald, he combined historical facts regarding King Christian II with lyrical prose. His eleven-volume series, Myter, utilized similar techniques. Additionally, during the period from 1908 to 1922, he wrote Den lange rejse, a collection of novels exploring themes related to Darwinism and evolutionary philosophy.
entries.significance: Jensen's body of work, including essays, travelogues, and poetry, utilized his scientific background to integrate evolutionary concepts into various literary forms.

entries.title: Discovering How Individual Nerve Fibers Transmit Electrical Signals
entries.overview: Joseph Erlanger and Herbert Gasser investigated the different properties of nerve fibres, showing that their thickness and electrical conduction speeds are related.
entries.background: The nervous system uses extensions called nerve fibers to connect the brain and spinal cord to the rest of the body. These fibers use weak electrical currents and chemical substances to transmit vital bodily signals.
entries.work: In the 1920s, Joseph Erlanger and Herbert Gasser investigated the distribution and properties of these fibers. They categorized them into different groups based on their thickness. Through this study, they demonstrated that thicker nerve fibers are capable of conveying impulses at a faster speed than thinner ones.
entries.significance: This research revealed the specialized functions of single nerve fibers, showing how varying fiber thicknesses influence the speed of nervous system communication.

entries.title: Red Cross Efforts Regarding Prisoners of War
entries.overview: The International Committee of the Red Cross received this honor for actions taken to assist captives during the Second World War.
entries.background: During World War II, the organization operated under the 1929 Geneva Convention. At that time, it sought to maintain neutrality and protect its relationship with the Swiss government while managing humanitarian tasks in conflict zones.
entries.work: During the Second World War, the committee facilitated communication between prisoners of war and their families. It coordinated prisoner exchanges and delivered essential supplies like food, medicine, and clothing to camps. The group also conducted inspections of prison facilities. However, in 1942, the organization chose not to publicly report Nazi atrocities against Jews to avoid potential military retaliation or damage to its neutral status.
entries.significance: The award highlighted humanitarian activities for captives during wartime. While focused on prisoner welfare, later historical evidence revealed that the committee had suppressed information regarding certain war crimes.

entries.title: The Resonance Method for Measuring Magnetic Properties of Atomic Nuclei
entries.overview: Isidor Isaac Rabi developed a resonance method for measuring the magnetic properties of atomic nuclei. Radio waves supplied a precise way to change, and therefore investigate, their quantum states.
entries.background: Atomic nuclei can behave as tiny magnets. In a magnetic field they occupy particular allowed states, so changing between those states requires a matching amount of energy. This makes their response to radiation a source of information about nuclear magnetism.
entries.work: In 1938 Rabi and his collaborators combined molecular beams, magnetic fields and radio-frequency radiation. When the radiation frequency matched a transition between nuclear magnetic states, it could change the states of particles in the beam. Detecting the resonance allowed the nuclear magnetic moment to be measured with much greater precision than earlier beam methods.
entries.significance: The method turned a precisely controlled frequency into a probe of nuclear properties. It established molecular-beam magnetic resonance as an experimental technique and formed part of the foundation on which later magnetic-resonance methods developed.

entries.title: Chemical Methods for Preserving Nutrients in Agricultural Fodder
entries.overview: Artturi Virtanen created a chemical process to protect vital nutrients in grass, helping maintain high-quality animal feed during seasons when fresh crops are unavailable.
entries.background: In cold climates, keeping livestock well-nourished throughout the winter is difficult because natural pastures disappear. Maintaining the nutritional value of stored fodder is necessary to ensure cattle can produce milk consistently without relying on expensive imported feed.
entries.work: During his 1932 research, Artturi Virtanen studied the chemistry of nutrients within dairy processes. He developed a technique to protect proteins and vitamins in green fodder by applying hydrochloric and sulfuric acids. This chemical application interrupted specific natural processes that usually degrade food quality, allowing the grass to remain nutritious for much longer periods.
entries.significance: The method helped preserve winter feed supplies and support the nutritional quality of dairy products. It could reduce reliance on imported fodder.

entries.title: The Literary Achievement of Gabriela Mistral in Poetry
entries.overview: Gabriela Mistral received this honor for creating lyric poetry that uses intense feelings to represent the idealistic goals found throughout Latin America.
entries.background: A former teacher from Chile, Lucila Godoy Alcayaga used a pseudonym for her writing. Her creative style was shaped by the modernist movement and various roles she held in Latin American education and diplomacy.
entries.work: Writing with direct language and strong emotion, Mistral published Desolación in 1922. Her later collections included Ternura in 1924, featuring nursery rhymes, and Tala in 1938, which utilized free verse and unique imagery. Her poems explored themes such as nature, sorrow, travel, and affection for children. Beyond poetry, she contributed opinion pieces to Chilean newspapers and engaged with sociopolitical matters.
entries.significance: Mistral became the first person from South America to win this specific literary prize, establishing her name as a symbol of regional aspirations.

entries.title: The Discovery and Development of Antibacterial Penicillin
entries.overview: This work details how a mold substance was identified and later transformed into a stable, mass-produced medication to combat bacterial infections.
entries.background: Microorganisms compete with one another, and some produce substances that inhibit their rivals. Turning such an observation into a useful medicine requires identifying the substance and finding a way to prepare it reliably.
entries.work: In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed a mold fungus inhibited bacteria in a culture bowl, identifying the substance penicillin. During the early 1940s, Ernst B. Chain and Howard Florey worked with colleagues to systematically produce pure penicillin. Their efforts focused on investigating its properties and overcoming instability to create a version that could be manufactured in much larger quantities for medical use.
entries.significance: These findings established a way to create pharmaceutical treatments that effectively inhibit the growth of various infectious bacterial diseases.

entries.title: Establishing the United Nations and Promoting International Understanding
entries.overview: Cordell Hull received this honor for his persistent efforts toward global cooperation and his central role in creating the United Nations organization.
entries.background: During World War II, as Norway faced Nazi-German occupation, the world sought a new international body. This effort followed the previous League of Nations, aiming to foster better relations between different countries through organized diplomacy and trade.
entries.work: Serving as US Secretary of State from 1933 to 1944, Hull implemented policies involving cooperation with Latin American nations. He also negotiated various free trade agreements. During the Second World War, he participated in the planning stages required to establish the United Nations, which was established in 1945 after the League of Nations had failed to prevent another world war.
entries.significance: Hull's actions provided a foundation for the new world organization, helping to transition international diplomacy from the defunct League of Nations toward a different global structure.

entries.title: The Discovery of the Atomic Exclusion Principle
entries.overview: Wolfgang Pauli established that two electrons in an atom cannot occupy the same complete quantum state. Electrons may share an energy level while still differing in other quantum properties.
entries.background: In Niels Bohr's early atomic model, electrons traveled in set paths around a nucleus. Scientists used specific numbers to describe these electrons' energy levels and movements as the model evolved.
entries.work: In 1925 Pauli formulated the exclusion principle using the quantum numbers that describe an electron’s state. No two electrons in an atom can have the same complete set of these numbers. This restricts how electrons are arranged among available states. The principle also applies to other particles of the same quantum class, including identical protons or identical neutrons.
entries.significance: The exclusion principle helps explain the organisation of electrons in atoms and, consequently, patterns in atomic structure. Its application to protons and neutrons also makes it important for understanding nuclei.

entries.title: Isolating Crystals of Enzymes and Virus Proteins
entries.overview: Scientists demonstrated that specific biological substances like enzymes and certain viruses can be extracted from cells in a pure, crystallized form.
entries.background: By the late 1800s, researchers understood that enzymes drive biochemical processes without needing living cells. However, scientists lacked a method to isolate these substances in their pure, individual forms for study.
entries.work: In 1926 James Sumner isolated active urease crystals from beans; subsequent investigation established that urease is a protein. Beginning around 1929, John Northrop extended the purification and crystallisation approach to digestive enzymes, including pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin. In 1935 Wendell Stanley obtained crystalline preparations of tobacco mosaic virus. Further research established that this virus contains both protein and RNA.
entries.significance: The work made enzymes and virus material accessible to chemical investigation in purified form. It helped establish the protein nature of the enzymes studied, while the tobacco mosaic virus proved to be a combination of protein and nucleic acid.

entries.title: Literary Achievements Featuring Themes of Human Spirit and Balance
entries.overview: Hermann Hesse received this prize for writings that demonstrate increasing boldness while illustrating classical humanitarian ideals through high-quality stylistic elements.
entries.background: After leaving seminary education, Hesse worked in bookstores. His early poetic debut occurred in 1896. Following the 1904 publication of Peter Camenzind, he earned enough from writing to live independently.
entries.work: Influenced by figures like Buddha and Nietzsche, Hesse explored authenticity and spirituality. Demian, written in 1917 and published in 1919, used symbolism to examine the duality of body and spirit. His 1927 work, Steppenwolf, addressed the tension between instinct and piety. Additionally, his 1943 novel, The Glass Bead Game, presented an intellectual order using a complex game to test beauty and knowledge.
entries.significance: Hesse's compositions provided deep explorations of individual enlightenment, focusing on the persistent human struggle to find internal balance and spiritual meaning.

entries.title: Discovering How X-ray Radiation Causes Genetic Mutations
entries.overview: Hermann Muller identified how exposing organisms to X-rays increases the frequency of sudden changes in their genetic code, known as mutations.
entries.background: The term mutation describes a change in an organism's hereditary material. These changes are a key mechanism that allows species to evolve over time and enables new species to emerge.
entries.work: In 1927, Hermann Muller conducted research using fruit flies to study hereditary traits. He determined that X-ray irradiation leads to higher rates of mutation. Specifically, Muller observed that as the dose of X-rays or other ionizing radiation increased, the quantity of genetic mutations within the fly population also grew larger.
entries.significance: This work demonstrated a direct link between radiation exposure and the production of mutations, providing a way to explain how genetic changes occur in organisms.

entries.title: International Peace Efforts through Social Activism and Religious Cooperation
entries.overview: This award honors individual efforts toward global stability through anti-war activism, social reform, and fostering international religious connections during the early twentieth century.
entries.background: During the World Wars, global tensions rose alongside growing movements for disarmament. This era featured intense struggles against fascism, colonial oppression, and racial discrimination, alongside efforts to promote reconciliation across diverse national and religious boundaries.
entries.work: In 1946, Emily Greene Balch was recognized for lifelong peace advocacy, including wartime work with Jane Addams to influence neutral nations and leading the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom. John R. Mott was honored for establishing a cross-border religious brotherhood through the YMCA. He organized international youth camps and exchanges while performing prisoner of war relief work during both World Wars.
entries.significance: These actions sought to promote understanding, warn against aggression, and create networks intended to foster cooperation and mitigate conflict between different nations and peoples.

entries.title: High Pressure Physics Apparatus and Related Material Discoveries
entries.overview: Percy Bridgman created a machine capable of generating massive pressure to observe how different substances change their physical forms and properties.
entries.background: In 1905, Percy Bridgman attempted to study how light behaves under intense pressure. During his initial experiments, his existing laboratory equipment failed and broke apart due to the extreme forces involved.
entries.work: While attempting to fix broken instruments, Bridgman designed a new sealing mechanism. This invention evolved into specialized apparatus that could generate extremely high pressures. Using this technology, he investigated how materials and various substances undergo structural changes or adopt new characteristics when subjected to much higher levels of force than those found in ordinary environments.
entries.significance: This work enabled scientists to examine the altered structures and physical properties of matter under extreme pressure conditions.

entries.title: Investigating Nitrogenous Plant Substances and Their Chemical Formation
entries.overview: This chemistry prize honors research into alkaloids, which are nitrogen-containing plant substances that can strongly influence human physiology.
entries.background: Plants produce various nitrogenous compounds known as alkaloids, such as morphine and quinine. Understanding how these biological products are constructed was a key challenge in chemical science.
entries.work: Robert Robinson proposed ways that plants could build alkaloids from amino-acid precursors. In 1917, he developed a method to synthesize the tropinone alkaloid by combining three simpler molecules. This approach replaced older production techniques that required many complex chemical reaction steps.
entries.significance: Robinson's findings provided new insights into the relationship between chemistry and biology, affecting the fields of medicine and biological sciences.

entries.title: Literature Award for Psychological Insight and Truthful Human Portrayals
entries.overview: In 1947, André Gide received recognition for his extensive writings that explored human circumstances through a lens of psychological depth.
entries.background: Gide’s writing champions individual desire and freedom from moral convention. That theme also calls for critical scrutiny: Nobel’s biographical account notes his sexual abuse of minors and the exploitation of vulnerable people underlying aspects of his ideal of freedom.
entries.work: Gide wrote fiction, criticism, plays and poetry, and translated authors including Shakespeare and Whitman into French. The Counterfeiters is formally experimental: it is a novel concerned with the creation of a novel and the conditions of writing. His wider body of work explores motives, desires and conflicts through close psychological observation.
entries.significance: The award recognised literary form and psychological insight. Understanding the work also requires distinguishing its artistic influence from the harm described in the author’s own accounts and in subsequent assessments of his conduct.

entries.title: Discoveries Regarding Glycogen Conversion and Pituitary Hormone Regulation
entries.overview: Scientists identified how the body transforms sugar and studied how specific brain hormones regulate glucose levels to provide energy.
entries.background: The body requires constant energy, necessitating efficient processes to convert sugars into usable fuel. Researchers sought to understand the metabolic pathways involving glycogen and how various organs coordinate sugar metabolism.
entries.work: Carl and Gerty Cori described the cycle linking sugar metabolism in muscle and liver in 1929, then investigated the enzymes involved in glycogen breakdown and synthesis. In 1938–1939 they identified a key enzyme and demonstrated glycogen formation in a test tube. Separately, Bernardo Houssay used animal experiments to investigate hormonal regulation. Removing parts of the pituitary made animals more sensitive to insulin, showing that anterior-pituitary activity could oppose insulin’s effects.
entries.significance: These findings clarified how glycogen converts into glucose for muscle cells and demonstrated how the pituitary gland regulates sugar metabolism through hormonal interactions.

entries.title: Humanitarian Aid by British and American Quaker Organizations
entries.overview: Two Quaker aid groups received this award for their international peace efforts and work helping people suffering through various global conflicts.
entries.background: The Quakers held long-standing traditions of supporting the poor, sick, and marginalized. Since the early 1800s, they participated in forming peace societies and campaigned against slavery, intolerance, and social injustice to prevent war.
entries.work: Established in 1927, the Friends Service Council performed missionary and aid work for British Quakers. Founded in 1917, the American Friends Service Committee assisted France with livestock, seeds, and healthcare after World War I. This American group also provided relief to the Soviet Union, Germany, and Spanish Civil War victims, while helping interned Japanese-Americans during World War II.
entries.significance: The committee recognized these organizations for their humanitarian efforts that served people regardless of their nationality or race during periods of intense global warfare.

entries.title: Discovering Atmospheric Layers Through Radio Wave Interference
entries.overview: Edward V. Appleton identified specific layers in the upper atmosphere by studying how radio waves interact and overlap while traveling across long distances.
entries.background: During the early 1900s, scientists noticed radio signals curved around the Earth. They believed a layer of the atmosphere, created when solar ultraviolet light releases electrons from atoms, reflected these waves.
entries.work: In 1924, Edward Appleton proved this layer exists by analyzing the interference patterns of radio waves traveling different paths. He later showed in 1927 that a second, outer layer also resides in the atmosphere. These investigations focused on the physics of the upper atmosphere to confirm the presence of what is now called the ionosphere.
entries.significance: Appleton's findings confirmed the existence of the ionosphere. His experimental methods for studying wave superposition also provided useful techniques for developing radar technology.

entries.title: Separating proteins by their movement in an electric field
entries.overview: Arne Tiselius created a technique to pull different substances apart from a mixture by using electrical fields to move charged molecules.
entries.background: During the 1930s, scientists needed ways to distinguish between various components found within complex biological liquids like blood serum. This era required new chemical analysis tools to study how specific particles behave under electrical influence.
entries.work: Tiselius developed precise methods for observing the movement of dissolved substances in an electric field. His moving-boundary apparatus followed the separation of components in solution, revealing that blood-serum proteins were a complex mixture rather than a single uniform substance. Different molecules have different electrical mobilities, making their movement useful for analysis. His work also encompassed adsorption methods, another approach to separating the components of mixtures.
entries.significance: This work established an important tool for chemical analysis. It allowed researchers to identify and separate distinct molecular components based on their movement through an electric field.

entries.title: Modernist Poetry and the Evolution of Twentieth Century Verse
entries.overview: T.S. Eliot received this honor for his pioneering role in developing contemporary poetic styles through innovative writing techniques.
entries.background: During the early twentieth century, poets sought new ways to express the complicated nature of modern civilization. This era required fresh literary approaches to capture a changing world.
entries.work: Beginning with his 1915 poem, “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock,” Eliot introduced daring innovations to English verse. He produced notable works including “The Hollow Men” (1925), “Ash Wednesday” (1930), and “The Waste Land” (1922). His writing focused on representing the intricate layers of contemporary life, establishing him as a central figure in the Modernist movement through his unique poetic contributions.
entries.significance: Eliot's work provided a new framework for twentieth-century poetry by using experimental methods to reflect the complexities of the modern age.

entries.title: Discovery of Insecticide Effectiveness for Controlling Disease Vectors
entries.overview: In 1948, Paul Müller received recognition for finding that DDT acts as a powerful contact poison to kill various arthropods.
entries.background: Many illnesses are transmitted by insects. For instance, mosquitoes spread malaria, while lice in clothing carry typhus fever. Such outbreaks often occur when hygiene levels drop during wartime periods.
entries.work: In 1939, Paul Müller identified that the chemical DDT could successfully kill insects. Using this substance, it was possible to reduce the transmission of malaria and stop typhus epidemics. However, later observations showed that DDT accumulates within food chains, causing harm to humans and other wildlife through environmental concentration.
entries.significance: This discovery provided a method to limit the spread of specific insect-borne diseases by targeting the organisms responsible for carrying them.

entries.title: Developing Cloud Chamber Methods for Studying Nuclear Particles and Radiation
entries.overview: Patrick Blackett refined the cloud-chamber method to study charged particles and used it to make discoveries about nuclear reactions and cosmic radiation.
entries.background: Scientists needed reliable ways to observe and record the movement of microscopic, electrically-charged particles originating from nuclear reactions and cosmic radiation sources throughout the universe.
entries.work: In 1932, Patrick Blackett and Giuseppe Occhialini joined a cloud chamber with a Geiger counter to capture images exactly when particles passed through. Using this improved method, Blackett demonstrated that applying high energy can transform photons into pairs of electrons and positrons. This technique allowed for detailed observation of tracks left by various particles during nuclear processes.
entries.significance: This method provided a precise way to visualize and detect the behavior of subatomic particles and cosmic rays during physical reactions.

entries.title: Studying Substance Behavior at Extremely Low Temperatures
entries.overview: William F. Giauque studied how heat moves and transforms through chemical thermodynamics, specifically looking at how substances act when cooled to extreme lows.
entries.background: Thermodynamics involves using statistical descriptions of atomic and molecular movements to understand energy transformations. A central, complex concept in this field is entropy, which serves as a measure of disorder within a system.
entries.work: In 1933 Giauque and D. P. MacDougall achieved exceptionally low temperatures through adiabatic demagnetisation. After magnetising a material and removing heat, they thermally isolated it and reduced the magnetic field, causing further cooling. This extended the temperature range available for experiments. Giauque’s low-temperature measurements provided important evidence supporting the third law and its account of entropy.
entries.significance: Giauque's work provided experimental evidence for the validity of the third law of thermodynamics regarding entropy levels in crystals.

entries.title: Literary Achievement in Modern American Novel Writing
entries.overview: William Faulkner received this honor for his distinct and influential style within the tradition of modern American fiction.
entries.background: Growing up in Mississippi, Faulkner drew inspiration from his local surroundings. His early life experiences provided the foundation for creating a fictional universe known as Yoknapatawpha County, which reflected real-world environments.
entries.work: Originally a poet, Faulkner authored novels and numerous short stories. In his breakthrough work, The Sound and the Fury, he utilized stream of consciousness to depict internal thought processes. His writing frequently employs multiple character perspectives, using long, imagery-heavy sentences and regional dialects alongside surreal linguistic elements to portray his characters' lives.
entries.significance: His creative approach introduced experimental techniques to the American novel, using unique narrative structures and language to explore complex human perspectives.
