entries.title: Revealing unusual bonds in boron–hydrogen compounds
entries.overview: William Lipscomb determined structures of boranes, compounds made from boron and hydrogen. His studies showed how these molecules hold together and expanded chemists’ understanding of chemical bonding.
entries.background: Boranes presented a structural puzzle: familiar pictures of bonds between pairs of atoms did not readily explain their compositions and shapes. Many are highly reactive, which also made experimental investigation difficult. Knowing their ingredients was not enough to understand their behaviour.
entries.work: From the 1950s onward, Lipscomb used X-ray methods to locate atoms in borane structures and combined those results with quantum-mechanical analysis. His work described arrangements in which bonding extends over several atoms, including three-centre bonds. Structural information and calculations together provided a way to reason about the molecules’ stability and reactions.
entries.significance: The award recognised research on a particular family of compounds that illuminated a general chemical problem. Boranes demonstrated that useful models of bonding must accommodate structures beyond simple pairs of atoms joined by conventional bonds, connecting measured molecular geometry with electronic explanations.

entries.title: Consumption, money and the limits of economic stabilisation
entries.overview: Milton Friedman was recognised for research on consumption, monetary history and theory, and the difficulties of stabilisation policy. The prize covered analytical and empirical contributions across these connected areas.
entries.background: Economists sought to explain household spending, fluctuations in economic activity and inflation. Policy also raised a timing problem: an intervention could take effect after the conditions that prompted it had changed. Friedman questioned assumptions about both spending behaviour and the effectiveness of discretionary intervention.
entries.work: His consumption analysis distinguished temporary income changes from more lasting income expectations. In monetary economics he argued that the money supply has important effects on economic activity and prices. Historical research, including A Monetary History of the United States written with Anna Schwartz, supported his examination of monetary forces and policy. He also emphasised the complexity and uncertainty involved in efforts to stabilise an economy.
entries.significance: These contributions reshaped debates about spending, inflation and monetary policy. The award recognised the research; it did not establish that every broader political position or policy recommendation associated with Friedman was correct.

entries.title: Human lives amid the pressures of contemporary culture
entries.overview: Saul Bellow was recognised for fiction that combines close attention to individual people with analysis of the culture surrounding them. His novels helped renew the forms and voices of American fiction.
entries.background: Born near Montreal and raised in Chicago, Bellow studied anthropology and sociology before establishing his literary career. Chicago repeatedly became a setting for his work. His interest in people within their social environments remained central to his writing.
entries.work: Bellow’s first novel, Dangling Man, appeared in 1944. The Adventures of Augie March, published in 1953, brought his major breakthrough. Herzog (1964) and Humboldt’s Gift (1975) were further prominent works available before the Nobel award. Across his fiction, the committee valued the combination of human understanding and scrutiny of contemporary life, rather than identifying a single book as the sole achievement.
entries.significance: The prize recognised a body of novels that makes cultural questions inseparable from the lives of particular characters. Bellow’s importance rests on both his treatment of those people and the literary invention through which their experiences are presented.

entries.title: Discovering New Ways Infectious Diseases Spread and Originate
entries.overview: Two scientists identified unique methods by which certain viruses and agents move through populations, uncovering previously unknown biological transmission patterns.
entries.background: Before these studies, the specific mechanisms for how some diseases traveled between humans and animals remained mysterious. Researchers sought to understand how infectious agents could cause illness or linger undetected within a host.
entries.work: Blumberg’s investigations of blood proteins led to the discovery of the Australia antigen and its connection with hepatitis B. The virus could be carried by people without obvious illness, making detection important for blood transfusions. Separately, Gajdusek and colleagues investigated kuru among the Fore people of New Guinea and its spread through mortuary practices involving deceased relatives. Transmission to chimpanzees demonstrated an infectious process with a long incubation period.
entries.significance: Blumberg’s work enabled new blood transfusion tests and vaccines. Gajdusek's findings pointed toward a previously unknown type of infectious agent that causes brain cell degeneration.

entries.title: Founding a Movement to End Violence in Northern Ireland
entries.overview: Two women established an organization aimed at stopping the intense religious and political conflict between Protestants and Catholics in Northern Ireland.
entries.background: In August 1976 three children died after a car struck their family in Belfast. Its driver, an IRA member, had been shot while fleeing British soldiers. The tragedy became a catalyst for a movement opposing violence across the divided community.
entries.work: After witnessing the tragedy, Betty Williams launched an appeal against violence. She joined Mairead Corrigan, whose sister lost the three children, to found the Community of Peace People in 1976. They organized large protest marches and local groups focused on confidence-building measures between former opponents. While Williams previously participated in a priest's anti-violence campaign, she and Corrigan worked together to build this grassroots movement.
entries.significance: Their movement brought thousands into peace marches and local confidence-building efforts during 1976 and 1977. The reserved 1976 prize was awarded in 1977, recognising their attempt to build peace through community participation.

entries.title: Discovering the J/psi and evidence for charm
entries.overview: Two scientists separately identified a massive new particle, which provided experimental evidence for a fourth type of quark known as charm.
entries.background: By the early 1970s many particles once regarded as elementary were understood as combinations of quarks. The growing classification raised questions about whether further quark types existed and how they could be detected.
entries.work: In 1974 teams led independently by Richter and Ting discovered the same heavy particle. Ting’s group used proton collisions with a target at Brookhaven; Richter’s group worked at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center. Named J by one team and psi by the other, it became known as J/psi. It is a bound state of a charm quark and its antiquark, rather than an elementary particle in the modern sense.
entries.significance: The discovery provided decisive evidence for charm and transformed the picture of subatomic matter. It linked experimental observations with a quark type that had already been proposed theoretically.

entries.title: Developing Theory Regarding Orderly Systems Within Irreversible Thermodynamic Processes
entries.overview: Ilya Prigogine developed the theory of dissipative structures: organised patterns that can arise and persist in systems driven away from thermodynamic equilibrium.
entries.background: Thermodynamics describes energy transformations and entropy production. A system exchanging energy or matter with its surroundings can remain far from equilibrium. Understanding such systems requires going beyond the conditions used to describe small departures from equilibrium.
entries.work: Prigogine investigated how irreversible processes can produce ordered structures under suitable conditions. Rather than appearing only as a temporary stage on the way to balance, these structures can be maintained by continuing flows through an open system. His work examined the stability of such states and how new patterns emerge when a previous state becomes unstable.
entries.significance: The theory connected irreversible processes with the emergence of organised behaviour. Such local order does not overturn thermodynamics: sustaining it involves dissipation and exchanges with the surroundings. The framework opened ways to study pattern formation beyond equilibrium.

entries.title: Theories Regarding Global Trade Patterns and International Economic Policy
entries.overview: This work explores how countries exchange goods and manage money flows across borders, focusing on resource allocation and the effects of government policies.
entries.background: Before these developments, understanding how trade affects a nation's income and resources was complex. The research addressed how openness to foreign markets influences domestic prices and stability within economies that rely heavily on global commerce.
entries.work: In 1933, Bertil Ohlin published work identifying factors that shape the international division of labor and trade patterns. He showed how trade affects income distribution and resource use. Later, in his 1951/55 writings, James Meade examined how economic policies influence trade and investigated stabilization methods for open economies, whose domestic activity is connected with trade and financial flows across borders.
entries.significance: These contributions established foundational frameworks for studying international macro-theory, helping to explain the relationship between national policy decisions and global market interactions.

entries.title: Spanish Poetic Renewal and the Human Cosmic Condition
entries.overview: Vicente Aleixandre received this honor for poetic writings that explore human existence within the universe and modern society through updated Spanish traditions.
entries.background: Part of the Generation of ‘27, Aleixandre moved from studying law to literature. His early career faced challenges, including a period when his poetry was banned by the fascist regime in Spain following the Spanish Civil War.
entries.work: Influenced by Surrealism, Aleixandre debuted in 1928 with Ambito. During the 1930s, he wrote Espadas como labios and La destruccion o el amor. While his early style was more complex, the war led him toward simpler imagery. After the ban on his work ended in 1944, he published Sombra del paraíso, which addresses finding new meaning after wartime struggles.
entries.significance: His writing represents a major renewal of Spanish poetic traditions and provides a way to view humanity's place in the cosmos.

entries.title: Discovering Brain Hormones and Measuring Body Substances
entries.overview: Scientists identified how the brain produces specific signaling molecules and created a precise method to measure tiny amounts of substances within the human body.
entries.background: Hormones act as signals that regulate various bodily functions. Previously, researchers struggled to study these substances because they exist in extremely small quantities, making them difficult to isolate or detect accurately.
entries.work: Guillemin’s team used sheep hypothalamus tissue and Schally’s used pig tissue to isolate tiny quantities of brain hormones. In 1969 both groups identified the structure of thyrotropin-releasing hormone. Separately, Yalow and Solomon Berson developed radioimmunoassay: in a laboratory sample, a measured hormone competes with a radioactively labelled version for antibody binding. This allows extremely low concentrations to be measured; the assay does not require injecting the patient with radioactive material.
entries.significance: The hormone discoveries explained chemical control linking the hypothalamus and pituitary. Radioimmunoassay made such scarce molecules measurable and revealed that some people with diabetes still produced insulin, challenging the idea that all diabetes resulted from its complete absence.

entries.title: Global Human Rights Advocacy via Amnesty International
entries.overview: Amnesty International is an independent, member-run group that investigates human rights breaches and organizes campaigns to protect individuals from various violations.
entries.background: Amnesty began in 1961 following an appeal by British lawyer Peter Benenson. It developed as a membership organisation independent of governments, political ideologies and religious creeds, campaigning for people whose rights were being violated.
entries.work: Amnesty investigated cases, published reports and mobilised members to press for change. Campaigns for prisoners of conscience and against torture made individual suffering an international concern. In 1977 it declared a Prisoners of Conscience Year and organised pressure on governments concerning torture and the death penalty. Its method combined documenting abuses with sustained action by ordinary members.
entries.significance: The organization works to bring worldwide respect to human rights by exposing truth and mobilizing members to end various forms of mistreatment across different nations.

entries.title: Theoretical Investigations of Electronic Structure in Disordered and Magnetic Systems
entries.overview: Three scientists explored how electron movement determines the electrical and magnetic characteristics of various solid materials, including those with irregular or random structures.
entries.background: In many solids, properties depend on electrons interacting with atomic nuclei. While some materials possess regular crystalline patterns, others, such as glass or certain alloys, feature disordered compositions or lack a consistent structural arrangement.
entries.work: In 1949, Nevill Mott explained how electron interactions allow crystals to transition between insulators and conductors. During the 1930s, John Van Vleck developed theories regarding how electrical fields affect foreign atoms in crystals and how electron movements create local magnetic moments. In 1958, Philip Anderson identified specific conditions determining if an electron moves freely or remains bound within a disordered system.
entries.significance: These theoretical studies provided a deeper understanding of electrical phenomena and the behavior of electrons within both regular and disordered solid materials.

entries.title: The Chemiosmotic Theory of Biological Energy Transfer
entries.overview: Peter Mitchell developed a theory explaining how living organisms move and store energy using molecules called adenosine triphosphate, also known as ATP.
entries.background: All life depends on energy. While scientists knew that ATP provides power by releasing phosphate groups to become ADP, the specific mechanisms for building up these molecules remained unclear during the early 1960s.
entries.work: In 1961 Mitchell proposed that electron-transfer reactions drive protons across a biological membrane, creating an electrochemical gradient: a difference in both proton concentration and electrical potential. The return flow of protons can then power the formation of ATP from ADP and phosphate. In mitochondria this coupling takes place across the inner membrane. The gradient links the energy-releasing reactions with ATP synthesis, rather than requiring a direct chemical intermediate between them.
entries.significance: Chemiosmotic theory explained how cells conserve energy in ATP through membrane processes. It connected electron transport, proton movement and ATP formation in a single framework, changing the understanding of biological energy conversion.

entries.title: Researching How People Make Decisions Inside Economic Organizations
entries.overview: Herbert Simon studied how individuals and companies make choices, moving beyond the idea that everyone always acts with perfect logic to maximize profits.
entries.background: Many economic models describe a decision-maker who compares all available alternatives and chooses the best one. In real organisations, information, time and the ability to process complex choices are limited. Simon investigated how decisions are actually made under these constraints.
entries.work: Simon combined economics with insights from psychology and organisational research. His account of bounded rationality explained how decision-makers search for satisfactory alternatives when they cannot calculate a global optimum. Organisations shape that search through their rules, information channels and division of responsibility. He treated firms as adaptive systems involving people, social relationships and physical resources.
entries.significance: The work made the processes and limits of decision-making central to the study of organisations. It offered an account of purposeful choice under constraints, rather than simply describing people as illogical or assuming complete information.

entries.title: Yiddish Narrative Art Rooted in Polish-Jewish Cultural Traditions
entries.overview: Isaac Bashevis Singer received this honor for his passionate storytelling that uses Polish-Jewish traditions to explore universal aspects of the human experience.
entries.background: Singer grew up in a Yiddish-speaking Jewish environment in Warsaw and initially studied to become a rabbi. He chose writing instead and emigrated to the United States in 1935, settling in New York, where he worked as a writer, journalist and translator.
entries.work: Writing primarily in Yiddish, Singer made his literary debut with Af der elter in 1925. His body of writing includes novels, short stories and books for children. He utilized Jewish folklore and legends to depict Polish Jewish life prior to the Holocaust. Many of his stories examine how families are changed by secularism, modernity, and assimilation, often following multiple generations through their changing social landscapes.
entries.significance: Singer's writing brought specific cultural histories and legends to a global audience, using the Yiddish language to connect traditional Polish-Jewish life with broader human themes.

entries.title: Discovery and Application of Enzymes That Cut DNA Molecules
entries.overview: Scientists identified specific proteins called restriction enzymes that break DNA strands at particular nucleotide sequences, providing tools to study genetic material.
entries.background: DNA molecules are composed of long rows of building blocks known as nucleotides. Understanding how these genomes are organized and how individual genes are arranged within chromosomes was a central challenge in molecular genetics.
entries.work: Arber investigated how bacteria restrict invading viral DNA and protect their own DNA through modification, predicting enzymes that recognise particular sequences. Smith and colleagues isolated a bacterial restriction enzyme and established its specific cleavage pattern in 1970. Nathans used restriction enzymes to cut and map the DNA of the SV40 virus. Their contributions linked a natural bacterial defence mechanism with precise experimental tools for genetics.
entries.significance: These discoveries allowed researchers to investigate the chemical composition of genes, determine the order of genes on chromosomes, and combine DNA into new arrangements.

entries.title: Negotiating Peace Between Egypt and Israel
entries.overview: Anwar al-Sadat and Menachem Begin shared the prize for negotiating peace between Egypt and Israel. The 1978 Camp David Accords established a framework for the treaty signed the following year.
entries.background: Following the 1967 war, tensions remained high. Anwar al-Sadat sought to regain Egyptian territory through United States support, while Menachem Begin led Israel as Prime Minister following his history with various Zionist movements.
entries.work: Sadat visited Jerusalem in 1977, opening a direct route to negotiations with Begin. At Camp David in September 1978, US President Jimmy Carter mediated talks between the two leaders. The resulting agreements set out a framework for peace, including an Egypt–Israel treaty and Israeli withdrawal from Sinai. The Nobel award followed these accords; the final bilateral treaty was signed in March 1979.
entries.significance: The negotiations transformed relations between states that had repeatedly fought one another. Distinguishing the 1978 framework from the later treaty is important: the prize recognised a major diplomatic breakthrough while detailed agreement and implementation still lay ahead.

entries.title: Discoveries in Low Temperature Physics and Cosmic Radiation
entries.overview: This award honors findings regarding how substances behave at extreme cold and the detection of leftover radiation from the early universe.
entries.background: In the mid-twentieth century, scientists investigated how cooling matter alters its physical properties. Simultaneously, researchers examined cosmic radiation falling toward Earth to understand the strength of different wavelengths in space.
entries.work: Pyotr Kapitsa created a way to produce large amounts of liquid helium in 1934 and identified its resistance-free flow, called superfluidity, in 1937. Separately, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson studied cosmic radiation in 1964, finding that seven-centimeter microwaves were stronger than expected, ruling out measurement errors.
entries.significance: Kapitsa’s work made low-temperature experiments possible and revealed an unusual state of liquid helium. Penzias and Wilson’s detection was identified as cosmic microwave background radiation, providing evidence for a hot early universe.

entries.title: Developing New Methods for Creating Complex Carbon Compounds
entries.overview: Two scientists created new ways to use boron and phosphorus atoms to build specific carbon molecules in laboratory settings.
entries.background: Building a complex organic molecule requires choosing reactions that create or transform particular bonds. Chemists need reagents that make those changes predictably, so that a planned series of steps can reach the desired structure.
entries.work: Brown developed organoboron chemistry, including hydroboration, in which boron and hydrogen add across a carbon–carbon multiple bond. The products can be transformed into other useful organic compounds. Wittig developed phosphorus-containing reagents that convert the carbon–oxygen double bond of an aldehyde or ketone into a carbon–carbon double bond. The resulting control over molecular construction became valuable in synthesis, including the manufacture of vitamin A.
entries.significance: These developments provided important reagents for organic synthesis, enabling the artificial production of biologically active substances and other essential chemical products.

entries.title: Researching Economic Development Challenges in Developing Nations
entries.overview: These researchers studied how certain economic structures and agricultural conditions contribute to the persistent problems of underdevelopment found within various growing nations.
entries.background: During the mid-twentieth century, economists sought to understand why some regions remained impoverished. The focus was on identifying the specific mechanisms that cause imbalances between urban industrial productivity and rural agricultural income levels.
entries.work: Schultz treated agriculture as part of the wider economy and emphasised investment in people’s skills and knowledge as a source of productivity growth. Lewis developed a model with a subsistence sector and an expanding capitalist sector. Under its assumptions, workers can move into more productive employment while reinvested profits support further expansion. Lewis also studied trade between poorer and richer countries.
entries.significance: Their work placed rural livelihoods, labour and investment at the centre of development economics. It offered different ways to analyse growth and persistent poverty, while leaving the relevance of each model’s assumptions to be tested in particular economies.

entries.title: Greek Poetry Blending Surrealism and Ancient Literary Traditions
entries.overview: Odysseus Elytis received this prize for writing poems that use sensory imagery and clear thought to portray the human struggle for liberty and creativity.
entries.background: Drawing from Greek literary heritage, his writing emerged during a period of significant change. After publishing in the 1930s, he experienced World War II combat and lived in Paris during the Greek military dictatorship that began in 1967.
entries.work: In his 1959 book Axion esti, Elytis blended prose and poetry using styles from Byzantine liturgy. His early writing features sunlight, the sea, and rocky landscapes. However, his time fighting Mussolini’s troops in Albania during World War II added darker themes to his later verse. He successfully combined surrealist influences with the traditional literature of his homeland.
entries.significance: His literary contribution provides a depiction of modern humanity's quest for freedom by merging contemporary surrealism with long-standing Greek cultural and religious stylistic elements.

entries.title: Developing Computer Assisted Tomography for Internal Body Imaging
entries.overview: This achievement involves using X-ray beams and computer calculations to create detailed cross-sectional and three-dimensional images of the body's interior.
entries.background: After X-rays were discovered, doctors could see parts of the body's inside. However, expanding this technology required new ways to process radiation data into clear, layered pictures of internal structures.
entries.work: Around 1957, Allan Cormack created the required calculation methods. During the 1960s, Godfrey Hounsfield built a device that captures X-ray beams passing through the body from various angles. Together, these developments allow computers to use measurement data from different perspectives to generate slice-like images and three-dimensional views.
entries.significance: These advancements expanded X-ray technology beyond simple shadows, enabling the production of detailed cross-sections and volumetric visual representations of human anatomy.

entries.title: Humanitarian Aid Efforts and the Missionaries of Charity Organization
entries.overview: Mother Teresa received this honor for her efforts to provide assistance to people experiencing intense suffering throughout the world.
entries.background: After moving to Calcutta, India, Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu felt a religious calling to assist impoverished populations. She established the Missionaries of Charity to live directly among those in need.
entries.work: Mother Teresa and the Missionaries of Charity established homes for children, facilities for people with leprosy and hospices for the dying in Calcutta, alongside aid work elsewhere. The prize recognised help for people experiencing severe poverty and suffering. The official Nobel background also records criticism: allegations that hospice patients lacked adequate pain relief, and objections to her opposition to abortion. Those criticisms concern aspects of the care and her wider public position.
entries.significance: Her work established a global network of care for vulnerable groups, including orphans and the sick, through organized religious service.

entries.title: The Unified Theory of Electroweak Fundamental Interactions
entries.overview: Glashow, Salam and Weinberg contributed to a common theoretical description of electromagnetic and weak interactions. The resulting electroweak theory explained how apparently different forces can arise within one framework.
entries.background: Nature contains four fundamental forces. Two of these are the electromagnetic interaction and the weak interaction, which is the process responsible for the beta decay of atomic nuclei.
entries.work: Glashow proposed an important gauge-theory structure in 1961. Weinberg in 1967, and Salam independently, incorporated a mechanism that allows the weak force carriers to have mass while the photon remains massless; Salam’s account was published in 1968. The theory predicted weak neutral-current interactions, in which the weak interaction acts without transferring electric charge. Their subsequent observation supported the framework.
entries.significance: Electroweak theory connected previously separate descriptions of elementary-particle interactions and made testable predictions. The prize recognised distinct theoretical contributions developed over the 1960s, not a single joint discovery made in 1968.

entries.title: Methods for Manipulating and Sequencing Nucleic Acid Molecules
entries.overview: Scientists developed techniques to combine DNA from different organisms and identify the specific order of building blocks within genetic material.
entries.background: DNA contains an organism's genome, consisting of long rows of nucleotides. Understanding these sequences and learning how to manipulate these molecules allows for mapping genomes and creating new biological characteristics.
entries.work: In 1972 Berg and colleagues joined SV40 viral DNA with a DNA segment containing bacteriophage genes and bacterial genes, constructing a recombinant DNA molecule in the laboratory. Gilbert and Allan Maxam developed a sequencing method using labelled DNA and selective chemical cleavage. Sanger developed a different method in 1977, using chain-terminating nucleotides. Separating the resulting fragments by length made it possible to read the sequence of DNA bases.
entries.significance: These advancements allowed researchers to map genomes and provided a way to engineer bacteria to produce substances used in various medicines.

entries.title: Developing Mathematical Models to Study Economic Changes and Policies
entries.overview: Lawrence R. Klein developed mathematical frameworks known as econometric models to analyze how economies fluctuate and to evaluate different economic policies.
entries.background: Growing up during the Great Depression influenced Klein's professional focus. After studying in Berkeley and earning a doctorate from MIT in 1944, he worked at various universities and served as an advisor during the 1976 presidential campaign.
entries.work: In 1950, Klein published research attempting to define specific models of the American economy from the interwar period. Through his writings and by guiding international research groups, he promoted the use of forecasting models. His work focused on using these mathematical structures for the practical study of economic shifts and the potential effects of different government policies.
entries.significance: Klein's efforts stimulated global research into economic forecasting models and demonstrated how these tools could be applied to analyze various economic policies.

entries.title: Poetry and Prose Exploring Human Vulnerability and Conflict
entries.overview: Czesław Miłosz received this award for writing about the human condition while facing a world filled with intense and difficult conflicts.
entries.background: Born in Lithuania, Czesław Miłosz lived through significant historical shifts, including participating in the Warsaw resistance during World War II. He later worked as a cultural attaché in Paris before seeking asylum in France due to his dissatisfaction with the Communist regime.
entries.work: Miłosz’s early poetry collections appeared in the 1930s, often marked by a sense of impending catastrophe. His later writing explored life and death, faith and doubt, and questions of moral responsibility. The Captive Mind (1953) is a work of essays and analysis, not a novel. Drawing on the experiences of writers under a repressive regime, it examines pressures that lead intellectuals to accommodate political power. His Nobel award recognised a wider literary achievement, particularly his poetry.
entries.significance: The work provides a clear-sighted look at how individuals exist within a period of severe global struggles and political repression.

entries.title: Genetic Cell Surface Structures Controlling Immune System Reactions
entries.overview: The laureates identified inherited differences in cell-surface molecules that help regulate immune responses. The discoveries explained important aspects of tissue compatibility and why transplanted material can be rejected.
entries.background: The human body must distinguish between its own healthy cells and harmful, damaged, or foreign substances. Understanding how the immune system recognizes these different entities is necessary for managing biological rejections during medical transplants.
entries.work: Snell’s work with genetically similar strains of mice connected tissue rejection with a particular group of genes. Dausset identified related cell-surface differences in humans, laying foundations for tissue typing. Benacerraf’s studies in guinea pigs showed that responses to particular antigens also depend on inherited factors linked to this genetic region. Together the findings connected transplant compatibility with broader regulation of the immune response.
entries.significance: The work made inherited tissue differences central to understanding immune recognition. It helped explain why donor and recipient compatibility matters in transplantation and how genetic variation influences responses to particular substances.

entries.title: Nonviolent Human Rights Activism During the Argentine Military Dictatorship
entries.overview: Adolfo Pérez Esquivel promoted nonviolence and social development through human rights networks across Latin America during periods of intense political repression.
entries.background: Argentina’s military coup in 1976 brought a dictatorship marked by severe repression. Across Latin America, human-rights activists confronted political violence and restrictions on freedom. Pérez Esquivel pursued a nonviolent response within this setting.
entries.work: Since the 1960s, Adolfo Pérez Esquivel practiced nonviolent liberation to aid social development. In the 1970s, he led the human rights group SERPAJ. He traveled throughout Latin America to build activist networks. While serving as an opponent of violence, his activities led to his arrest and torture by Argentine military rulers in 1977. He remained imprisoned for fourteen months until external pressure helped secure his release.
entries.significance: His nonviolent struggle provided a source of inspiration for oppressed populations globally, particularly within the context of Latin American political violence.

entries.title: Discovery of Symmetry Violations in Neutral K-Meson Decay
entries.overview: James Cronin and Val Fitch discovered that neutral kaon decays violate CP symmetry: the combined operation of replacing particles with antiparticles and reflecting space does not always leave the process unchanged.
entries.background: Physicists already knew that left–right reflection alone, called parity, was not respected by the weak interaction. Many expected that combining reflection with an exchange of matter and antimatter would restore the symmetry. Neutral kaons offered a way to test that expectation.
entries.work: In 1964 Cronin, Fitch and their collaborators observed long-lived neutral kaons decaying into two pions, a process that would be forbidden if CP symmetry held exactly. Careful checks established a small but real symmetry violation. Under the additional assumption of CPT symmetry, the result also implies time-reversal violation; the experiment was not a direct comparison of a process with its time reverse.
entries.significance: The discovery showed that a symmetry thought to connect matter and antimatter was not exact. It opened a new problem for particle theory and the study of fundamental interactions.

entries.title: Frontier orbitals help explain the course of chemical reactions
entries.overview: Kenichi Fukui and Roald Hoffmann independently developed theories connecting molecular electron orbitals with chemical reactivity, explaining why particular reaction pathways are favoured over others.
entries.background: Chemical reactions rearrange bonds, so their course depends on the electrons involved. Quantum theory describes those electrons through orbitals rather than miniature planetary paths. Chemists needed ways to extract useful predictions from this picture without calculating every detail of a molecule.
entries.work: Fukui identified the importance of frontier orbitals: the most loosely bound occupied orbitals and the most accessible unoccupied ones. Their interactions help explain how molecules react. In the 1960s, Fukui and Hoffmann independently showed how orbital symmetry could explain reaction patterns. Hoffmann’s work with Robert Woodward developed the conservation of orbital symmetry into a powerful approach. The two prize-winning contributions supplied related but independently developed ways of reasoning about molecular change.
entries.significance: The theories gave chemists practical explanations for reactions that had seemed puzzling. By focusing on orbital interactions and symmetry, they connected quantum descriptions of electrons with predictions that could guide experiments and the synthesis of new molecules.

entries.title: Connecting choices about assets with spending and employment
entries.overview: James Tobin analysed how financial markets influence consumption, investment, production and employment, placing decisions about assets and debts within a broader account of economic activity.
entries.background: Households and firms can hold many kinds of assets while also borrowing. They compare expected returns and risks, and changes in financial conditions can alter their choices. Understanding the wider economy therefore requires more than examining money balances or one interest rate.
entries.work: Tobin developed portfolio-selection ideas to explain how people and firms choose combinations of assets and liabilities. He then connected those decisions with markets for goods and services. His analysis examined how financial changes affect spending and investment, providing channels through which monetary and fiscal policy can influence economic activity. One important relationship concerns firms’ incentives to invest when the market value of existing capital differs from the cost of acquiring new capital.
entries.significance: The research joined financial decisions with questions about output, jobs and prices. Its contribution was an analytical framework for investigating these connections, helping economists examine how developments in financial markets can reach the wider economy.

entries.title: Literary Achievements of a Multidisciplinary German Language Writer
entries.overview: Elias Canetti received this prize for his diverse writings, which feature wide-ranging perspectives, numerous creative ideas, and strong artistic ability.
entries.background: Although he earned a doctorate in chemistry, the Bulgarian-born author chose to focus on literature. Writing primarily in German, he lived across England, Austria, and Switzerland throughout his nomadic life.
entries.work: Canetti produced various literary forms, including three plays, memoirs, and several author profiles. His 1935 novel, The Deception, was initially planned as a multi-book series influenced by Honoré de Balzac. Later, he spent many years researching the dynamics of large groups, producing the 1960 book titled Crowds and Power.
entries.significance: His contributions spanned several genres, ranging from fictional narratives and dramatic plays to deep analytical studies regarding how mass movements function.

entries.title: Distinct brain functions and the processing of visual information
entries.overview: Roger Sperry investigated functional differences between the cerebral hemispheres. David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel separately explained important stages of visual processing and their development.
entries.background: The brain’s two hemispheres communicate through connecting nerve fibres. Patients whose connections had been cut to treat severe epilepsy offered a way to investigate their functions. A different question concerned how signals from the eyes become organised representations in the visual cortex.
entries.work: Sperry’s studies revealed differences in the tasks the separated hemispheres could perform, including language and spatial processing. These were findings about specialised functions under particular experimental conditions, rather than two fixed personality types. Hubel and Wiesel studied cells in the visual system that respond to features such as contrast, orientation and movement. Their work showed how visual information is analysed through successive stages and how early experience matters to the development of those abilities.
entries.significance: The shared prize recognised two distinct research programmes. Together they made aspects of brain organisation experimentally accessible, connecting observable behaviour and perception with the different functions of neural systems, without assigning every mental activity exclusively to one hemisphere.

entries.title: Protecting Fundamental Rights and Supporting Displaced People Worldwide
entries.overview: The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees received this honor for defending the basic rights of individuals forced to flee their homes.
entries.background: By 1981, global displacement had grown significantly. While refugee issues were once primarily European concerns, they became critical in Africa and other developing regions, involving roughly ten million people needing assistance.
entries.work: During the 1970s, the UNHCR worked to return refugees to their home countries across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The agency also upheld principles from the international Refugee Convention, which gained importance after thousands of Vietnamese refugees faced extreme hardships in the South China Sea.
entries.significance: This recognition supported United Nations principles and highlighted the vital connection between providing humanitarian aid to displaced populations and maintaining global peace.

entries.title: Laser and electron spectroscopy reveal precise energy levels
entries.overview: Nicolaas Bloembergen and Arthur Schawlow advanced laser spectroscopy, while Kai Siegbahn developed high-resolution electron spectroscopy. Both approaches extract information about the energy structure of matter.
entries.background: Atoms and molecules absorb or emit light at characteristic frequencies as their energies change. Photons can also eject electrons whose measured energies reveal how strongly they were bound. These effects offer different ways to investigate the same underlying quantum structure.
entries.work: Bloembergen developed the understanding of nonlinear optical processes, including mixing three light waves to generate a fourth. This extended the wavelengths available for laser spectroscopy. Schawlow developed methods that removed spectral broadening caused by atomic motion, allowing much more precise measurements. Siegbahn’s separate approach illuminated a sample and measured the energies of electrons released by the photoelectric effect. Improvements in resolution made those electron measurements informative about the sample’s electronic structure.
entries.significance: The award recognised complementary measurement techniques rather than one shared instrument. Laser methods sharpened and extended optical spectroscopy, while electron spectroscopy supplied another sensitive probe of atoms, molecules and materials through the electrons they emit.

entries.title: Reconstructing the structures of nucleic acid–protein complexes
entries.overview: Aaron Klug developed crystallographic electron microscopy and used structural methods to investigate viruses and chromatin, explaining how nucleic acids and proteins are organised together.
entries.background: Electron microscopes can image biological material, but weak contrast and radiation damage complicate the task. Increasing exposure or adding heavy-metal stains can distort the structure being studied. Extracting more information from less damaging images offered a different route to reliable structural detail.
entries.work: Klug applied mathematical methods related to crystallography to electron-microscope images. Combining views from different directions allowed three-dimensional structures to be reconstructed from two-dimensional projections. He used these and other structural techniques to investigate nucleic acid–protein assemblies, including tobacco mosaic virus. With colleagues, he also studied fragments of chromatin, the complex of DNA and proteins in chromosomes, using information from those manageable pieces to develop a picture of larger organisation.
entries.significance: The work connected improved imaging with specific biological structures. It showed how mathematical analysis and complementary experimental methods could reveal the organisation of complex molecular assemblies, helping explain how their components come together and support biological functions.

entries.title: Research on Industrial Structures and the Effects of Public Regulation
entries.overview: George J. Stigler analyzed how market processes function and investigated how government laws and regulations influence the behavior and structure of various industries.
entries.background: During his academic career, George J. Stigler focused on examining the relationship between economic activity and legal frameworks. He sought to understand the underlying forces that lead to the creation of official regulatory legislation.
entries.work: George J. Stigler conducted research into the way markets operate and studied industrial organization. His work specifically looked at how economic legislation impacts market processes. By investigating the causes and consequences of public regulation, he established a new field of study located at the intersection of economics and law, focusing on the impact of government rules on competition.
entries.significance: Stigler's investigations provided a way to study how legal interventions affect industries, creating an entirely new area of research regarding the connection between economic systems and law.

entries.title: Magical realism gives form to Latin American lives and conflicts
entries.overview: Gabriel García Márquez was recognised for novels and stories that combine realistic settings with fantastic elements, creating an imaginative literary account of Latin America’s experiences and conflicts.
entries.background: García Márquez developed a career in journalism before concentrating on creative writing. His fiction became a major example of magical realism, in which extraordinary or dreamlike events belong within a recognisable social world rather than being separated into an entirely different realm.
entries.work: One Hundred Years of Solitude, published in 1967, brought him international recognition. The Autumn of the Patriarch followed in 1975. Through such works, he combined narrative invention with questions of history, society and power. The fantastic elements operate alongside the realistic ones within the same imagined world. His achievement lay in a distinctive and influential use of this literary approach, rather than the invention of magical realism as a genre.
entries.significance: The prize recognised the breadth and imaginative force of his fiction. It acknowledged writing that made a continent’s life and tensions accessible through compelling stories, while showing how departures from everyday probability can illuminate recognisable human experience.

entries.title: Prostaglandins reveal chemical signals controlling local body responses
entries.overview: Sune Bergström, Bengt Samuelsson and John Vane explained the chemistry and actions of prostaglandins and related substances, connecting biological signalling with the effects of important medicines.
entries.background: These short-lived signalling substances influence processes including inflammation, blood-vessel behaviour and platelet activity. Understanding them required identifying their structures, tracing how the body makes them and determining how drugs alter the pathways involved. Related molecules can have different, even opposing, effects.
entries.work: Bergström isolated prostaglandins and helped establish their chemical structures. Samuelsson mapped their formation from fatty acids and investigated related compounds, including thromboxanes and leukotrienes. Vane showed in 1971 that aspirin inhibits prostaglandin production. He and colleagues subsequently discovered prostacyclin, which dilates blood vessels and inhibits platelet aggregation—the clumping together of platelets—rather than preventing platelets from being formed. These contributions connected molecular chemistry with specific physiological actions.
entries.significance: The findings explained existing drug effects and supported further therapeutic development. They also showed why treating these substances as one uniform signal is misleading: related pathways can regulate inflammation, clotting and other responses in distinct ways.

entries.title: Diplomatic Efforts Toward Nuclear and Weapon-Free Zones
entries.overview: Two diplomats worked to reduce global arms tension by promoting agreements that create regions free from nuclear weapons and other armaments.
entries.background: During the Cold War, the growing nuclear arms race created intense international fear. Following the 1962 Cuban missile crisis, there was a pressing need for diplomatic frameworks to prevent nuclear proliferation and establish safe, weapon-free territories.
entries.work: As a Swedish minister, Alva Myrdal advocated for nations to ban nuclear weapons on their territories to encourage superpower disarmament. Separately, Alfonso García Robles used his legal and diplomatic expertise to help create a 1967 agreement making Latin America a nuclear-free zone. He also assisted in drafting the 1968 non-proliferation treaty.
entries.significance: These efforts focused on using international law and negotiation to establish zones where nuclear weapons are prohibited, aiming to limit the spread of dangerous weaponry.

entries.title: Explaining critical behaviour by connecting different length scales
entries.overview: Kenneth Wilson developed a theoretical approach to critical phenomena, explaining how the behaviour of matter near certain phase transitions emerges from interactions across many length scales.
entries.background: Near a critical point, effects at small distances can be linked with behaviour over much larger regions. This makes a single-scale calculation inadequate. The difficulty appears in systems such as fluids and magnets, despite their different microscopic constituents.
entries.work: In 1971, Wilson developed a renormalisation approach that handled the problem through successive changes of scale. Instead of trying to include every scale in one step, the method tracked how the description changed as finer details were combined into a coarser picture. This supplied a framework for calculating critical behaviour that earlier approaches could not adequately capture. A critical point is a particular physical condition, rather than simply a moment when any substance changes from solid to liquid.
entries.significance: The work gave physicists a systematic way to connect microscopic interactions with collective behaviour near criticality. It made scaling central to the explanation and helped account for patterns shared by physically different systems.

entries.title: Molecular bridges explain a route for electron transfer
entries.overview: Henry Taube investigated how electrons transfer between metal complexes, demonstrating that a shared bridging group can provide a pathway and revealing details of the reaction mechanism.
entries.background: Metal ions can exist in different charge states and are often surrounded by attached molecules or ions. An electron-transfer reaction changes their charges, but knowing the starting materials and products does not reveal how the electron moved between them.
entries.work: Taube studied complexes involving metals such as cobalt and chromium. By tracing an attached group as the reaction occurred, he found evidence that a bridge formed between the metal centres before electron transfer. He then investigated how changing the bridging group affected the reaction and examined transfer across longer bridges. This established an important class of mechanisms; it did not imply that every electron-transfer reaction requires a bridge of the same kind.
entries.significance: The research shifted attention from merely recording a change of charge to explaining the path and sequence of the reaction. It provided experimental methods and concepts for understanding electron transfer, a process central to many areas of chemistry.

entries.title: Giving general equilibrium a rigorous mathematical foundation
entries.overview: Gerard Debreu developed mathematical foundations for general equilibrium, identifying conditions under which prices can make the plans of consumers and producers mutually consistent across markets.
entries.background: An economy contains many interdependent decisions: firms choose production and inputs, while consumers choose purchases. General-equilibrium theory asks whether prices can coordinate those choices so that supply and demand agree across markets. Writing equations alone does not establish that such a solution exists.
entries.work: Working with Kenneth Arrow in the early 1950s, Debreu proved the existence of equilibrium prices within a model built on explicit assumptions about production and consumer behaviour. His 1959 book Theory of Value presented an influential axiomatic treatment. The achievement established the logical consistency of the model under its stated conditions. It did not prove that every actual economy automatically reaches an equilibrium or that the assumptions always hold in practice.
entries.significance: The work made fundamental economic claims open to precise mathematical examination. It helped economists distinguish what follows from a model’s assumptions from what requires additional evidence about real markets, uncertainty and consumer behaviour.

entries.title: Literary Exploration of Human Nature Through Myth and Realistic Narrative
entries.overview: William Golding received this award for novels that use realistic storytelling and universal myths to examine the complexities of the modern human condition.
entries.background: After studying natural sciences, Golding became a writer. His time serving in the British Navy during World War II battles provided the personal experiences that later informed the themes found within his various published works.
entries.work: Golding released his first poetry collection in 1934. Following World War II, he authored the novel Lord of the Flies, which arrived in 1954. His writing often utilizes adventure plots to investigate how humans can turn constructive impulses into destructive or malicious actions through a blend of myth and clear narrative art.
entries.significance: His novels provide a way to look at the capacity for human destruction by combining diverse myths with straightforward, realistic storytelling techniques.

entries.title: Discovery of Genetic Elements That Change Position on Chromosomes
entries.overview: Barbara McClintock identified mobile genetic components within corn chromosomes that can shift locations, influencing whether specific genes remain active or become inactive.
entries.background: During her studies starting in 1919, Barbara McClintock focused on how hereditary traits are passed down through generations. She investigated the way organisms inherit characteristics via genes stored in cellular nuclei.
entries.work: In the 1940s and 1950s, Barbara McClintock examined the various kernel colors in corn to trace inheritance patterns. Through this research, she demonstrated that certain genetic elements can move between positions on a chromosome. Her work showed that these shifting elements directly cause neighboring genes to either switch on or off, altering the plant's visible traits.
entries.significance: This work revealed that chromosomes are not static structures, providing evidence that genetic elements can change position and regulate gene activity.

entries.title: Nonviolent organising challenges one-party control in Poland
entries.overview: Lech Wałęsa was recognised for the nonviolent struggle for independent trade unions and human rights in Poland, becoming an international symbol of the Solidarity movement.
entries.background: Poland’s communist authorities restricted independent political and labour organisation. Workers protesting conditions had faced deadly repression. Wałęsa, a shipyard electrician, lost his job because of his involvement in demands for independent unions before returning to take part in the 1980 strike.
entries.work: During that strike, he entered the Lenin shipyard in Gdańsk and led negotiations with the authorities. Cooperation among workers, intellectuals and the Catholic Church strengthened the movement that produced Solidarity. The authorities banned the union in 1981 and interned Wałęsa. They claimed that repression was necessary to prevent Soviet intervention; that was their justification, rather than an established fact about what would otherwise have happened. Released before the award, he remained a prominent representative of independent organising.
entries.significance: The prize supported the right to organise outside the ruling party’s control. It recognised nonviolent collective action and negotiation, while the subsequent political changes in Poland remained a longer process extending beyond the award year.

entries.title: Explaining stellar evolution and the formation of chemical elements
entries.overview: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar investigated the structure and evolution of stars. William Fowler studied the nuclear reactions that power stars and produce many of the elements found in the universe.
entries.background: Gravity draws gas together to form a star, raising its temperature until nuclear reactions can begin. The balance between gravity and internal support changes as the star evolves. Understanding that history also requires knowing which nuclear reactions occur and what they produce.
entries.work: Chandrasekhar developed theoretical accounts of stellar structure and stability, including influential studies of compact white dwarfs begun when he was a young researcher. His broader work examined different stages of stellar evolution and the extreme physical conditions reached in later stages. Fowler combined laboratory investigations of nuclear reactions with theoretical calculations. Working with colleagues, he helped develop an account of how successive nuclear processes form elements inside stars and during their evolution.
entries.significance: The two contributions explain related parts of a cosmic story: how stars change and how nuclear processes alter their chemical contents. The shared award recognised complementary research rather than a single theory developed jointly by the laureates.

entries.title: Solid supports simplify the stepwise synthesis of peptides
entries.overview: Bruce Merrifield developed solid-phase synthesis, anchoring a growing molecule to an insoluble support so that excess reagents and soluble by-products can be removed between reaction steps.
entries.background: Peptides are chains of amino acids, and making a particular sequence requires repeated chemical steps. In solution, separating the growing chain from the other materials after every addition can be laborious. Small losses and impurities can accumulate over many repetitions.
entries.work: At the beginning of the 1960s, Merrifield developed a method that attached the initial amino acid to a solid support. Further amino acids could be added while the chain remained attached. Washing then removed soluble material without requiring the desired chain to be isolated in the usual way after each step. Repetition could be mechanised. The technique simplified handling and separation; it did not guarantee that every coupling reaction was perfect or remove all possible errors in an attached chain.
entries.significance: The method made the controlled assembly of peptides more practical and helped automate chemical synthesis. Its central contribution was a new way to organise repeated reactions and purification around a molecule held on a solid matrix.

entries.title: Building consistent systems of national economic accounts
entries.overview: Richard Stone developed national-accounting systems that connect income, spending, production and saving, giving economists a consistent statistical framework for describing and analysing an economy.
entries.background: An economy generates an enormous number of transactions. Useful analysis requires grouping them without losing the relationships between sectors. A payment recorded as one party’s expenditure must also appear as another’s income, allowing the totals to be compared and checked.
entries.work: Working in Britain during the Second World War, Stone and colleagues organised statistics needed to analyse resources and expenditure. He developed integrated accounts covering households, businesses, government and transactions with other countries. The connected structure allowed figures from different sources to be cross-checked, rather than treating each statistic in isolation. Stone continued refining the systems and contributed to international standards, including work associated with the United Nations.
entries.significance: The contribution was a coherent system for economic measurement, not the invention of every individual spending statistic. National accounts made relationships across the economy easier to examine and provided a stronger empirical basis for policy analysis, comparisons and research.

entries.title: The Modernist Poetry of a Czech Writer
entries.overview: Jaroslav Seifert received this literary honor for his inventive poetry that captures human versatility, sensuality, and a sense of freshness through rhythmic verse.
entries.background: Following World War II, Czechoslovakia faced a repressive Communist government that pressured writers to produce political propaganda. Amidst this period, Seifert engaged with movements seeking increased freedom, including the Prague Spring and Charta 77.
entries.work: Starting with his 1921 debut, City in Tears, Seifert produced over thirty collections. His writing utilizes melody, rhythm, and everyday scenes inspired by folk songs and common speech. Through his poems, he criticized totalitarian efforts to limit individual liberty and human potential. Beyond poetry, he also worked as a journalist and translator throughout his career.
entries.significance: As a pioneer of modernist literature in his native country, Seifert used his verse to present a liberating image of the indomitable human spirit.

entries.title: Immune-system theories and a method for making monoclonal antibodies
entries.overview: Niels Jerne developed theories of immune recognition and regulation. Georges Köhler and César Milstein separately established a method for producing large quantities of one specific antibody.
entries.background: The immune system can recognise a great variety of targets, raising questions about how that diversity develops and how responses are controlled. Researchers also wanted a reliable source of identical antibodies, each recognising a chosen target, for experiments and practical applications.
entries.work: Jerne’s 1955 theory proposed that an antigen selects among existing antibody specificities rather than acting as a template for a newly designed antibody. He later proposed theories concerning immune-cell development and networks of interacting antibodies. These were influential theoretical proposals, not a complete modern account of immunity. In 1975, Köhler and Milstein fused antibody-producing cells with tumour cells, creating hybridomas that could multiply while making a selected monoclonal antibody.
entries.significance: The prize recognised distinct contributions to understanding and using the immune system. Jerne’s ideas stimulated research, while hybridoma technology supplied a reproducible biological tool with major applications in investigation, diagnosis and the development of treatments.

entries.title: Nonviolent opposition to apartheid gains international support
entries.overview: Desmond Tutu was honoured as a unifying leader in the nonviolent campaign against apartheid, articulating the suffering and demands of South Africans denied political and social equality.
entries.background: Apartheid imposed racial domination and met resistance with repression. The Sharpeville massacre occurred in 1960, and the Soweto uprising in 1976. Against this history of violence, campaigners faced difficult choices about how to pursue liberation and secure wider support.
entries.work: As an Anglican bishop, Tutu maintained a nonviolent position while speaking openly against the system. He did not condemn Nelson Mandela and others who had chosen different methods. His public leadership helped connect people within the struggle and drew attention to the experiences of the oppressed. The Nobel Committee highlighted his clarity, courage and unifying role, recognising a sustained campaign rather than a peace agreement already reached.
entries.significance: The award increased Tutu’s international prominence and amplified opposition to apartheid. Nobel’s account considers it a contribution toward stronger sanctions in the 1980s, although the broader struggle and eventual political transformation involved many people, organisations and developments.

entries.title: The Discovery of Weak Interaction Field Particles
entries.overview: Physicists identified the W and Z particles, which act as messengers for the fundamental force known as weak interaction.
entries.background: Nature operates through four fundamental forces. One such force, the weak interaction, is responsible for processes like beta decay in atomic nuclei. Scientific theory predicted that specific heavy particles mediate this process.
entries.work: In 1983, researchers verified these particles existed. Simon van der Meer created a technique to collect many high-energy antiprotons within an accelerator ring. Carlo Rubbia then directed experiments using these antiprotons to collide with protons at extreme speeds. These specific high-speed collisions allowed for the detection of the W and Z bosons.
entries.significance: This work provided physical evidence for the existence of particles that communicate the weak interaction, confirming a key aspect of modern physics.

entries.title: Developing Direct Methods for Determining Molecular Crystal Structures
entries.overview: In 1985, researchers were honored for creating a mathematical way to map the internal shapes of molecules by analyzing how X-rays bend.
entries.background: Mapping molecular structures requires studying how X-rays, which are short-wavelength electromagnetic waves, interact with crystals. To understand these structures, scientists must measure the rays' direction, intensity, and phase, which refers to the displacement of wave crests.
entries.work: During the early 1950s, Herbert Hauptman and Jerome Karle created a system of equations designed to solve structural puzzles. Their method utilized measurements of X-ray intensity to calculate the missing phase information. This mathematical approach allowed for the direct determination of molecular structures by using available intensity data to reconstruct the way waves are displaced.
entries.significance: This mathematical development made it possible to directly determine molecular structures, providing a way to map molecules using measurable X-ray intensities.

entries.title: Economic Research Regarding Personal Savings and Financial Market Structures
entries.overview: Franco Modigliani developed theories explaining how individuals manage lifelong savings and how a company's value relates to its financing methods.
entries.background: During his career, Franco Modigliani studied various economic theories with practical uses. His work involved analyzing the way people save money over time and investigating how different types of debt affect businesses.
entries.work: In his life-cycle theory, Franco Modigliani analyzed personal savings to help predict how pension plans might change future behaviors. Additionally, working alongside Merton H. Miller, he researched financial markets. Together, they demonstrated that, given specific assumptions, a firm's total value does not depend on its specific balance of debt and equity.
entries.significance: His research provided tools for evaluating the future consequences of pension systems and understanding how much a company's capital structure influences its overall worth.

entries.title: French Literary Innovation through New Novel Techniques
entries.overview: In 1985, Claude Simon received this award for his unique writing style that merges artistic vision with a deep perception of time.
entries.background: As a key figure in the French "new novel" movement, Simon moved away from traditional storytelling. His writing was shaped by his wartime experiences in 1940 and subsequent involvement in the resistance movement.
entries.work: Starting with Le Tricheur in 1946, Simon developed a style that avoids standard dialogue and linear plots. In works like La Route des Flandres, published in 1960, he utilized cinematic methods. He applied film-like techniques, such as zooming in and out, to create a fluid connection to time while depicting human life.
entries.significance: Simon's contribution was interpreting modernism by blending the creative approaches of painters and poets to represent the human condition through non-traditional narrative structures.

entries.title: Discovering How Cells Control Cholesterol Levels in the Blood
entries.overview: Scientists identified how cells manage cholesterol levels by using specific receptors to absorb particles from the bloodstream, helping regulate vital biochemical processes.
entries.background: Excessive cholesterol in the blood can lead to narrowed blood vessels. Understanding how the body maintains a healthy balance of this substance was necessary for managing biological functions and related health risks.
entries.work: In 1973, Michael Brown and Joseph Goldstein identified a cell surface receptor that absorbs low-density lipoprotein particles containing cholesterol. They clarified how cells balance their internal cholesterol production with amounts provided by the diet and blood supply. Additionally, they demonstrated that certain genetic abnormalities interfere with this regulatory process.
entries.significance: This research explained the mechanisms used to regulate cholesterol metabolism and showed how genetic mutations disrupt the body's ability to manage these levels.

entries.title: Physicians explain the catastrophic consequences of nuclear war
entries.overview: International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War received the prize for communicating the medical consequences of nuclear conflict and building public awareness across Cold War divisions.
entries.background: Doctors could bring professional knowledge of injury, disease and public health to debates often dominated by military strategy. The founders sought cooperation between physicians from opposing political systems, arguing that the consequences of nuclear war demanded attention beyond national rivalry.
entries.work: American cardiologist Bernard Lown and Soviet cardiologist Evgeny Chazov became acquainted in the 1960s and later helped establish IPPNW. Founded in 1980, the organisation had grown to 135,000 members in forty countries by the award. Its congresses explained health risks and the possibility of nuclear winter, in which effects of extensive nuclear war could block sunlight and reduce temperatures. It advocated a nuclear test ban and commitments against first use.
entries.significance: The award recognised communication and professional organising rather than a completed disarmament treaty. IPPNW used the shared responsibilities of physicians to make the potential human and environmental consequences of nuclear war more visible to the public.

entries.title: An exceptionally precise quantum effect in electrical conduction
entries.overview: Klaus von Klitzing discovered that Hall conductance in a two-dimensional electron system forms precise quantised plateaux, revealing a collective electrical effect with fundamental significance.
entries.background: In the ordinary Hall effect, a magnetic field deflects moving charges and creates a voltage across a conductor, perpendicular to the current. At very low temperatures and strong magnetic fields, electrons confined to a thin layer can behave differently.
entries.work: In 1980, von Klitzing found that changing the magnetic field produced plateaux in Hall conductance at values given by whole-number multiples of a fundamental unit. The agreement was unexpectedly precise. The result concerned electrons constrained to move effectively in two dimensions, rather than merely the general purity of a metal. It showed that the electrical response could remain fixed across a range of changing conditions before moving to another quantised value.
entries.significance: The precision made the effect useful for electrical-resistance standards and measurements of fundamental constants. It also opened a major field of research into quantum behaviour in two-dimensional systems, connecting microscopic physics with an exceptionally reproducible electrical measurement.

entries.title: Tracking how molecular collisions distribute energy and form products
entries.overview: Dudley Herschbach, Yuan Lee and John Polanyi developed complementary methods for studying reaction dynamics, revealing what happens during individual chemical encounters rather than only measuring final bulk products.
entries.background: A reaction’s overall chemical equation does not reveal how colliding molecules exchange energy, form temporary arrangements or separate into products. Investigating those details requires controlled collisions or measurements sensitive to the energy carried by newly formed molecules.
entries.work: Herschbach developed crossed molecular-beam methods that brought well-defined streams into collision. Lee extended the approach to a wider range of reactions through improved apparatus and product detection. Measurements of product motion, mass and energy revealed details of the reaction process. Polanyi developed infrared chemiluminescence: analysing the very weak infrared emission from newly formed molecules to determine how the reaction energy had been distributed. The methods supplied different experimental views of molecular change.
entries.significance: The work helped establish reaction dynamics as a detailed experimental science. It connected observations of individual encounters with quantum descriptions of molecular energy, giving chemists more than an inventory of the substances present before and after a reaction.

entries.title: Developing Frameworks for Economic and Political Decision Making
entries.overview: James Buchanan created a system to understand how individuals make choices within the public sector and political structures using contractual and constitutional foundations.
entries.background: While traditional economics focuses on how consumers choose products, labor, or investments, there was a need for a similar theory regarding how decisions are made in government and public institutions.
entries.work: In 1962, James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock co-authored Calculus of Consent. Through various studies, Buchanan established a theory for decision-making in the public sector. His work focused on creating the constitutional and contractual bases needed to analyze political choices and public economics, moving beyond the study of simple consumer behavior.
entries.significance: This contribution provided a new way to apply economic logic to political processes, offering a method to study how rules and agreements shape government actions.

entries.title: Literature Prize for Dramatizing Human Existence Through Cultural Perspectives
entries.overview: In 1986, Wole Soyinka received the Nobel Prize for creating drama that reflects human existence through a wide cultural lens and poetic style.
entries.background: Born in Abeokuta, Nigeria, Soyinka’s writing is influenced by his Yoruba heritage, including local legends and traditions. His career involved working in theaters across Great Britain and Nigeria, alongside academic roles in the United States.
entries.work: As a playwright, poet, novelist, and essayist, Soyinka writes in English while integrating Yoruba culture with Western literary traditions like classical tragedies and modernist drama. He has also performed as an actor. His creative output includes pointed criticism of Nigerian political regimes, which led to him living largely abroad.
entries.significance: Soyinka’s work fashions the drama of existence by blending his native Nigerian roots with diverse international literary influences and poetic overtones.

entries.title: Growth factors reveal signals controlling cell development
entries.overview: Rita Levi-Montalcini and Stanley Cohen discovered growth-regulating signals, including nerve growth factor and epidermal growth factor, helping explain how cells grow, survive and acquire specialised functions.
entries.background: An organism’s cells do more than multiply: they develop different identities and connections in an organised pattern. Researchers needed to understand the signals guiding that organisation. Growth could mean extension and survival of nerve fibres as well as division of cells.
entries.work: Levi-Montalcini observed that mouse tumours promoted nerve growth when transplanted into chick embryos. The effect did not require direct contact, pointing to a released substance. She developed sensitive culture tests for nerve growth factor, and Cohen helped identify and purify it. Cohen later found another activity in salivary-gland extracts: epidermal growth factor, which stimulated cells of the skin and cornea. The discoveries emerged through observation, biological tests and biochemical investigation.
entries.significance: The work established growth factors as important signals in development and tissue behaviour. It opened research into how altered signalling contributes to disease, while distinguishing the regulation of cell growth, differentiation and survival from a single universal command to divide.
