entries.title: Keeping East Timor’s struggle before the international community
entries.overview: Carlos Belo and José Ramos-Horta were honoured for efforts toward a just and peaceful resolution of the conflict in East Timor during Indonesian occupation.
entries.background: Indonesia occupied East Timor in 1975 as Portuguese colonial rule ended. Military repression and human rights violations shaped the struggle over the territory’s future. Belo worked within East Timor’s Catholic church, while Ramos-Horta pursued the cause internationally through diplomacy and advocacy.
entries.work: After becoming head of the Catholic church in East Timor in 1983, Belo publicly denounced the occupation and advocated nonviolent resistance. In 1989 he called for a United Nations plebiscite, and after the 1991 massacre he helped witnesses reach international human rights officials. Ramos-Horta had left East Timor as foreign minister of the government formed by the FRETILIN independence movement. He later promoted dialogue with Indonesia and proposed a 1992 plan involving humanitarian cooperation and a growing international presence.
entries.significance: The award recognised two distinct forms of advocacy for self-determination: local public witness and sustained international diplomacy. It concerned their efforts toward a peaceful solution while the territory’s future remained unresolved, rather than an independence settlement already completed in 1996.

entries.title: An unexpected phase transition reveals superfluid helium-3
entries.overview: David Lee, Douglas Osheroff and Robert Richardson discovered superfluidity in helium-3, showing that this isotope can enter a remarkable collective quantum state at extremely low temperatures.
entries.background: Helium-4 was already known to flow without ordinary viscosity when sufficiently cold. Helium-3 follows different quantum statistics, making its possible superfluid state a harder problem. Theoretical ideas suggested that pairing could allow its atoms to form a collective state, but experiments had not demonstrated it.
entries.work: At Cornell, Lee and Richardson worked with graduate student Osheroff using apparatus capable of reaching temperatures only thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. They were investigating magnetic ordering in solid helium-3 when small changes appeared in their pressure measurements. Their first 1972 report attributed the effect to the solid. Further measurements showed that it instead involved transitions in liquid helium-3, establishing the discovery of its superfluid phases.
entries.significance: The result opened research on a new quantum liquid and showed how careful attention to unexpected measurements can overturn an initial interpretation. Helium-3 became a system for studying collective quantum behaviour, with a richer structure than simply reproducing the already known behaviour of helium-4.

entries.title: Molecular machinery makes ATP and uses it to pump ions
entries.overview: Paul Boyer and John Walker explained how ATP synthase produces the cell’s energy-carrying molecule, while Jens Skou discovered an enzyme that uses ATP to transport ions.
entries.background: Cells must both generate usable chemical energy and spend it on organised work. ATP links these activities. Its production can be driven by hydrogen-ion movement across membranes, while its breakdown can power processes such as maintaining different sodium and potassium concentrations inside and outside a cell.
entries.work: Boyer developed a mechanism in which structural changes in ATP synthase’s catalytic sites enable ATP formation and release. Walker and colleagues determined the structure of its catalytic F1 portion in 1994, supporting the proposed mechanism; this was not yet the structure of every part of the enzyme. Separately, Skou’s 1957 discovery identified sodium-potassium ATPase, a membrane enzyme that couples ATP breakdown to the movement of sodium and potassium ions.
entries.significance: The shared award connected the production of a widely used energy carrier with one of its major uses. It clarified how specific molecular machines convert between chemical energy and ion gradients, supporting functions that include nerve signalling and muscle activity.

entries.title: Pricing options by connecting them with underlying assets
entries.overview: Robert Merton and Myron Scholes developed methods for valuing financial derivatives, working alongside Fischer Black to relate an option’s price to the assets and risks underlying it.
entries.background: An option gives its holder a right to buy or sell an asset under specified conditions. Its value depends on uncertain future prices, time and other factors. A consistent pricing method must account for that uncertainty and the possibility of constructing alternative investments with matching risks.
entries.work: Black and Scholes published their option-pricing formula in 1973. Its logic relates an option to a changing portfolio of shares and borrowing, using the absence of risk-free arbitrage to determine a price under the model’s assumptions. Merton supplied another derivation and extended the method to a wider range of financial claims. Black’s contribution remained central, although he had died before the award and did not share it.
entries.significance: The work provided a common framework for analysing options and other contingent financial claims. Its usefulness depends on the assumptions and inputs, including the behaviour of underlying prices; a model-derived price does not guarantee that an actual investment or hedge is free of risk.

entries.title: Popular theatrical traditions become instruments of political satire
entries.overview: Dario Fo was honoured for theatre that uses comedy to challenge authority and defend people excluded from power, drawing on the traditions of medieval jesters and popular farce.
entries.background: Fo trained in architecture while participating in amateur theatre, then made his acting debut in 1952. He worked closely with Franca Rame and with several theatre groups during the 1960s and 1970s. Their performance practice reached audiences beyond conventional theatre buildings.
entries.work: Mistero Buffo, from 1969, helped establish Fo’s reputation for political and social satire. Accidental Death of an Anarchist followed in 1970, and We Won’t Pay, We Won’t Pay! in 1974. His work drew on medieval farce and the comic performance traditions of commedia dell’arte. Performances in parks, schools and prisons brought this theatre into varied public settings, while its challenges to the police, government and Catholic Church generated controversy in Italy.
entries.significance: The literary achievement included the relationship between writing and live performance. Fo renewed inherited comic forms as tools for examining contemporary power, making satire a way to expose abuses and assert the dignity of people whose voices were often marginalised.

entries.title: Discovery of Prions as a New Principle of Biological Infection
entries.overview: Stanley B. Prusiner identified prions, which are abnormal protein structures that cause brain cell degeneration in diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
entries.background: Certain illnesses affecting both humans and animals cause the destruction of brain cells. Before this discovery, the specific infectious agent responsible for these degenerative conditions remained unknown to the scientific community.
entries.work: In 1982, Stanley B. Prusiner isolated a suspected infectious protein he named the prion. He identified its corresponding gene but noted it exists in healthy organisms. His research demonstrated that prion molecules possess an incorrect shape compared to normal proteins. Crucially, he showed that this abnormal folding pattern can be transferred from a prion to a regular protein, triggering the disease process.
entries.significance: This work established a new biological principle of infection by proving that misfolded proteins alone can drive infectious diseases.

entries.title: A civil-society campaign helps establish a ban on antipersonnel mines
entries.overview: Jody Williams and the International Campaign to Ban Landmines were honoured for mobilising international action to prohibit antipersonnel mines and clear the danger left by existing weapons.
entries.background: Mines can remain active long after fighting ends, injuring civilians and obstructing ordinary life. Humanitarian organisations working with affected communities sought more than changes in military practice: they pressed for a prohibition, clearance of contaminated land and assistance for people harmed.
entries.work: Williams became a driving force in organising the campaign from 1991, and the ICBL was formally launched in 1992. By 1997, it brought together more than a thousand organisations across sixty countries. Working with supportive governments and other partners, it helped bring about the Mine Ban Treaty, adopted in September 1997 and opened for signature that December. The treaty prohibited the use, production, stockpiling and transfer of antipersonnel mines and included clearance and assistance obligations.
entries.significance: The award recognised an international coalition’s ability to turn humanitarian evidence into diplomatic action. The treaty entered into force in 1999; that legal milestone was part of the subsequent implementation of a campaign whose central breakthrough came in the award year.

entries.title: Using light to cool atoms and hold them for study
entries.overview: Steven Chu, Claude Cohen-Tannoudji and William Phillips developed methods for cooling and trapping atoms with laser light, greatly improving experimental access to their quantum behaviour.
entries.background: Temperature is related to atomic motion. A photon carries momentum, so repeated absorption and emission can change an atom’s movement. Carefully chosen laser frequencies and beam directions can slow atoms, while trapping arrangements keep a cold cloud within a limited region.
entries.work: Chu and colleagues developed optical molasses, using opposing laser beams to slow atoms moving in different directions. Phillips developed methods combining lasers and magnetic fields to slow atomic beams, then found temperatures below the expected Doppler-cooling limit. Cohen-Tannoudji and colleagues explained additional cooling processes involving atoms’ internal structure and developed methods to reach still lower temperatures. These were related contributions from different groups rather than one shared experimental apparatus.
entries.significance: The methods made it possible to observe cold atoms for longer and investigate matter-light interactions with exceptional precision. Cooling reduces motion without making atoms permanently motionless. The work supported new research on ultracold gases and precision measurements, including improved approaches to atomic clocks and atom interferometry.

entries.title: Making quantum calculations practical tools for chemistry
entries.overview: Walter Kohn developed density-functional theory, while John Pople developed computational methods and software that made quantum-mechanical calculations increasingly useful for understanding molecules and chemical reactions.
entries.background: Electron behaviour helps determine a molecule’s structure and reactivity, but a full quantum description rapidly becomes mathematically demanding as a system grows. Useful computational chemistry therefore needs approaches that balance tractability with accuracy and whose results can be compared with experiments.
entries.work: Kohn’s work beginning in 1964 showed how a system’s energy could be related to its electron density, providing a different starting point from describing every electron through a many-particle wavefunction. Pople developed and tested practical calculation methods and made them accessible through the Gaussian program, first published in 1970. His work allowed researchers to specify a molecular system and calculate properties or reaction possibilities from quantum-mechanical models, rather than merely fitting a description to experimental observations.
entries.significance: The two contributions helped establish computation alongside laboratory experiments as a way to study chemistry. Their practical success also depended on later refinements by many researchers, and calculated results remained subject to the approximations used in each method.

entries.title: Measuring deprivation and explaining why people cannot obtain food
entries.overview: Amartya Sen connected social choice, welfare measurement and the study of famine, examining how collective decisions and economic arrangements affect people with the least resources.
entries.background: Average income alone can conceal severe deprivation, and simply counting people below a poverty line ignores how far below it they fall. Likewise, the amount of food available in a country does not by itself explain who can actually obtain enough to eat.
entries.work: Sen analysed how individual values and rights can be incorporated into collective decision-making. He developed poverty measures that consider the incidence, depth and distribution of poverty. In his studies of famine, he examined people’s ability to command food through work, production, exchange and other entitlements. His 1981 book showed why famine could occur without an overall decline in food supply: particular groups might lose the income or opportunities needed to secure it.
entries.significance: The work sharpened both the ethical questions and the empirical tools of welfare economics. It shifted attention from aggregate resources to their distribution and people’s real access to them, providing ways to investigate deprivation that a single national average or food total would miss.

entries.title: Literary Achievement Through Allegory and Imaginative Storytelling
entries.overview: José Saramago received this honor for creating parables using irony, compassion, and imagination to help readers understand a difficult reality.
entries.background: Before becoming a full-time author in his fifties, José Saramago worked as a journalist and car mechanic. His political involvement with the Portuguese Communist Party and his atheism influenced his writing, sometimes causing controversy in Portugal.
entries.work: In 1982, he achieved international success with the novel Baltasar and Blimunda. His writing style features long sentences, minimal punctuation, and merged dialogue and narration. He often uses allegory to critique society alongside fantastical elements. For example, his 1995 novel Blindness describes a sudden epidemic of blindness that triggers a total collapse of social structures.
entries.significance: Through his unique prose and use of parable, José Saramago provides a way for people to grasp elusive aspects of our world.

entries.title: A gas carries a signal that relaxes blood vessels
entries.overview: Robert Furchgott, Louis Ignarro and Ferid Murad identified nitric oxide as a biological signalling molecule, explaining a key mechanism by which blood vessels relax and widen.
entries.background: Blood-vessel behaviour depends partly on communication between the endothelial lining and surrounding smooth muscle. Nitroglycerin was known to widen vessels, but its action and the identity of the lining’s own relaxing signal required explanation. The discoveries connected these previously separate questions.
entries.work: Murad’s studies in the 1970s showed that nitric oxide released by nitroglycerin and related compounds could relax smooth muscle through intracellular signalling. In 1980, Furchgott demonstrated that acetylcholine caused relaxation only when the endothelial lining was intact, indicating that the lining released an unknown factor. Removing it prevented that relaxation response, not all vessel contraction. In 1986, Furchgott and Ignarro independently concluded that the factor was nitric oxide.
entries.significance: The work established that a small gaseous molecule can transmit information between cells. It clarified control of vascular smooth muscle and provided a basis for research and medicines affecting the nitric-oxide pathway, connecting a familiar drug effect with the body’s own signalling chemistry.

entries.title: Building support across communities for the Good Friday Agreement
entries.overview: John Hume and David Trimble were honoured for efforts toward a peaceful solution in Northern Ireland, helping develop and secure support for the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.
entries.background: The conflict involved competing constitutional aspirations, political exclusion and sustained violence. A workable settlement required arrangements that could command support among both unionists and nationalists, while also addressing relations between Northern Ireland, the Republic of Ireland and the British government.
entries.work: Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party, promoted dialogue and shared government rather than exclusive control by either community. Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party from 1995, entered negotiations and persuaded a majority of his party to support the agreement reached on 10 April 1998. The settlement involved multiple parties and both governments. It proposed a devolved Assembly and power-sharing Executive, with Northern Ireland’s constitutional status subject to majority consent.
entries.significance: The prize recognised leadership in building a negotiated framework across a deep political division. Hume and Trimble were important participants in a wider process; the agreement created institutions and commitments for resolving disputes peacefully rather than implying that every disagreement or implementation challenge had disappeared.

entries.title: Collective electron behaviour produces fractional electrical charges
entries.overview: Horst Störmer and Daniel Tsui discovered the fractional quantum Hall effect, and Robert Laughlin explained it through a new collective state of electrons with fractionally charged excitations.
entries.background: In the Hall effect, a magnetic field deflects moving charge carriers sideways, producing a voltage transverse to the current. In very cold, effectively two-dimensional electron systems, Hall conductance can settle at precise plateaux. Earlier experiments had found values corresponding to whole-number multiples of a fundamental constant.
entries.work: In 1982, Störmer, Tsui and colleagues found additional plateaux at fractional values while using very strong magnetic fields and low temperatures. Laughlin’s 1983 theory explained key observations through the correlated behaviour of many electrons forming a quantum fluid. Disturbances in that fluid behave as quasiparticles carrying a fraction of an electron’s charge. This does not mean an individual electron has been physically cut into smaller pieces; the fractional charge belongs to a collective excitation.
entries.significance: The discovery demonstrated that interactions among familiar particles can generate unexpected properties of matter. Experiment and theory together established a new quantum state and new concepts for understanding collective behaviour beyond what isolated electrons would suggest.

entries.title: Using Laser Technology to Observe Fast Chemical Reaction Transitions
entries.overview: Ahmed Zewail developed techniques to observe the extremely brief moments when atoms rearrange themselves to form new chemical compounds during a reaction.
entries.background: Chemical reactions involve molecules changing from one structure to another. Because atoms within these molecules vibrate at very high speeds, the period between these movements is incredibly short, lasting only ten to one hundred femtoseconds.
entries.work: During the late 1980s, Ahmed Zewail created methods to map these fast-moving processes. He utilized laser technology to generate incredibly brief flashes of light, measuring durations of just a few femtoseconds. This allowed for the detailed study of transition states, which occur when atoms meet and reorganize into different substances during a chemical change.
entries.significance: This work enabled scientists to observe the specific, rapid transitions that occur as molecules transform from one state into another.

entries.title: Analyzing Currency Exchange Rates and Optimal Monetary Policy Zones
entries.overview: Robert Mundell examined how government fiscal and monetary actions behave under various exchange rate systems and identified conditions for shared currency use.
entries.background: During the early 1960s, the way different national currencies interact through market forces or fixed rates significantly influenced global business stability and economic performance.
entries.work: Starting in the 1960s, Robert Mundell studied the consequences of letting market forces determine exchange rates versus keeping them fixed. He developed a theory suggesting that multiple nations could benefit from adopting one single currency. This specific arrangement works best when workers can move easily between different countries to find jobs.
entries.significance: His research provided a theoretical framework for understanding how common currencies function, which related to the later creation of the euro within the European Union.

entries.title: Satirical fiction confronts Germany’s historical memory
entries.overview: Günter Grass was honoured for fiction that combines imaginative storytelling, personal experience and historical events, using dark humour and satire to recover neglected perspectives on the past.
entries.background: The Second World War, Nazi crimes and the city of Danzig, now Gdańsk, recur in Grass’s work. The city’s changing affiliations supplied a historical setting for his fiction. He also worked as a graphic artist and sculptor and participated actively in political debate.
entries.work: The Tin Drum, published in 1959, established his international reputation. His novels mixed historical circumstances and autobiographical elements with invented events, creating ironic perspectives rather than straightforward documentary accounts. Political commitments also entered his public life, including opposition to the construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961. After the 1999 award, Peeling the Onion, published in 2006, addressed his own wartime membership in the Waffen-SS; that later book was not part of the work available to the awarding committee.
entries.significance: The prize recognised a literary career already built around the relationship between storytelling and historical memory. Grass’s use of satire invited readers to question how societies remember violence, responsibility and ordinary lives within large historical events.

entries.title: Proteins carry signals that direct them to cellular destinations
entries.overview: Günter Blobel discovered that proteins contain signals guiding their transport and location, explaining how newly made proteins reach the compartments where they are needed.
entries.background: A cell’s proteins do different jobs in different places. Many must enter membrane-bound compartments, become part of membranes or be exported. The problem was how a newly made protein could be recognised and directed toward the appropriate route rather than distributed at random.
entries.work: Blobel proposed a signal hypothesis in 1971 and provided biochemical evidence in 1975 for the targeting of proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum. A short sequence of amino acids within a protein could direct its passage into this membrane system. Subsequent work with colleagues and other groups identified the machinery involved and extended the principle to other destinations. By 1980, Blobel had formulated general principles of protein sorting, while molecular mechanisms continued to emerge through work over the following years.
entries.significance: The work connected information in a protein’s sequence with its destination as well as its chemical function. It explained a basic organisational problem shared by many cells and helped researchers understand disorders and practical production problems involving incorrectly located proteins.

entries.title: Independent medical assistance and public witness in humanitarian crises
entries.overview: Médecins Sans Frontières was recognised for pioneering humanitarian work across continents, providing emergency medical assistance while drawing attention to violence and abuses affecting the populations it served.
entries.background: Wars and natural disasters can leave people without accessible medical care. Founded in France in 1971, MSF developed an approach grounded in medical ethics, independence and assistance according to need. Its charter rejects discrimination based on political convictions, religion or race.
entries.work: The organisation brought medical and other personnel into emergencies to conduct consultations, operations and other essential work alongside locally employed staff. It sought freedom to reach affected populations and to make medical decisions independently of political or military interests. MSF also spoke publicly about violence and human rights violations witnessed where its teams worked. That willingness to criticise abuses formed part of its humanitarian role alongside the provision of direct clinical care.
entries.significance: The award honoured the organisation’s contribution to international emergency assistance and its insistence on access to people in distress. Its historical importance lies in combining medical action with independence and public witness, extending the idea of humanitarian responsibility beyond the immediate task of treating individual patients.

entries.title: Making electroweak theory mathematically usable for precise predictions
entries.overview: Gerardus ’t Hooft and Martinus Veltman clarified the quantum structure of electroweak theory, establishing methods that allowed reliable calculations of particle properties and interactions.
entries.background: The electroweak theory connected electromagnetism with the weak interaction, responsible for processes such as beta decay. Yet detailed calculations produced problematic infinities. Earlier methods had made quantum electrodynamics workable, but extending that success to the more complicated electroweak theory required a new mathematical foundation.
entries.work: Veltman developed symbolic computation tools and investigated whether the theory could be renormalised: whether infinities could be handled consistently while retaining finite physical predictions. His student ’t Hooft made a decisive breakthrough in 1971, showing how the relevant theories could meet that requirement. Their subsequent methods enabled quantitative calculations rather than leaving the theory as a promising qualitative framework. Precision comparisons with experiments then tested the framework and constrained properties of particles before direct observation.
entries.significance: The contribution strengthened the mathematical basis of the standard model. It helped transform electroweak theory into a tool for predicting measurable quantities, complementing the earlier formulation of the theory and the separate experiments that discovered its particles.

entries.title: Creating Materials That Conduct Electricity Using Plastic Polymers
entries.overview: In 2000, scientists were honored for showing that certain plastic-like materials, made of long molecular chains, can be made to carry an electrical current.
entries.background: Polymers are massive molecules organized into long chains. Traditionally, these plastic materials act as insulators, meaning they do not allow electricity to flow through them easily during use.
entries.work: During the late 1970s, Alan Heeger, Alan MacDiarmid, and Hideki Shirakawa demonstrated how to produce conductive polymers. They showed that by arranging alternating single and double bonds between carbon atoms and using a process called doping—adding specific atoms to create free electrons or holes—the plastic could conduct electricity.
entries.significance: This discovery allows for the use of these conductive plastics in various electronic devices and other practical technological applications.

entries.title: Analyzing Individual Choices and Statistical Selection in Economic Data
entries.overview: Two economists created mathematical tools to better understand how people make specific choices and how certain data gaps affect the study of human behavior.
entries.background: Researchers often face difficulties when data is incomplete or when studying how individuals select between different options. These statistical challenges can lead to inaccurate conclusions about household and social patterns during economic analysis.
entries.work: In the 1970s, Daniel McFadden developed conditional logit analysis to predict how people choose among finite alternatives, such as using public transit. Separately, James Heckman created the Heckman correction, a method for addressing problems that arise when analyzing selective samples of individual or household behavior.
entries.significance: These methods allow for more accurate studies of labor markets and transportation usage by providing ways to account for selection bias and discrete decision-making processes.

entries.title: Shifting narrative voices join Chinese traditions with modern experimentation
entries.overview: Gao Xingjian was recognised for fiction and drama that combine Chinese literary and performance traditions with modernist experimentation, using language and changing perspectives to explore individual experience.
entries.background: Gao wrote plays, poems and essays in China during the 1980s before settling in France amid increasing official criticism. His work drew from both Chinese popular theatre and Western dramatic experimentation. Questions of memory, personal freedom and the instability of perspective run through it.
entries.work: Soul Mountain, first published in Chinese in 1990, grew from journeys through southern and southwestern China. It mixes encounters, stories, reflections and different narrative voices, making the reader reconsider the relationship between storyteller and experience. His drama likewise allows characters to inhabit a role while also describing it from outside. One Man’s Bible, published in 1999, explored the Cultural Revolution through the different positions of participant, victim and observer.
entries.significance: The prize recognised innovation across novels and theatre rather than a single political message. Gao’s methods expanded the possibilities of Chinese-language writing by connecting inherited forms with experiments in voice, genre and the ways a person can represent or question their own experience.

entries.title: Chemical signalling changes nerve-cell activity and memory
entries.overview: Arvid Carlsson, Paul Greengard and Eric Kandel revealed complementary mechanisms of nervous-system signalling, connecting neurotransmitters, changes in cellular proteins and the modification of synapses during learning.
entries.background: Nerve cells communicate at junctions called synapses. Chemical messengers bind receptors and can change the receiving cell’s activity. Understanding behaviour and memory therefore requires explaining both how messages act inside cells and how the effectiveness of connections changes with experience.
entries.work: Carlsson showed in the late 1950s that dopamine is itself a brain transmitter and is important in movement, helping establish the link between dopamine loss and Parkinson’s disease. Greengard explained how transmitter-activated receptors trigger changes in protein phosphorylation, regulating nerve-cell functions. Kandel used a sea slug’s relatively simple nervous system to study learning. His programme distinguished short-term changes involving existing proteins from longer-lasting memory processes requiring altered protein synthesis and changes to synaptic connections.
entries.significance: The discoveries connected molecular events with movement, learning and memory without reducing them to one mechanism. They supported treatments affecting neurotransmission and established experimentally tractable ways to study how experience changes the strength and structure of neural connections.

entries.title: Democratic advocacy and engagement across the Korean divide
entries.overview: Kim Dae-jung was honoured for advancing democracy and human rights in South Korea and East Asia, alongside efforts toward peace and reconciliation with North Korea.
entries.background: Kim’s political career developed under South Korean authoritarian rule and included imprisonment, house arrest, kidnapping and exile. His election as president in 1997 brought a longstanding democracy advocate into government. Relations with North Korea remained burdened by decades of war, division and hostility.
entries.work: As president, Kim pursued the sunshine policy, seeking engagement with North Korea through dialogue, humanitarian aid and expanded exchanges. His visit for a summit in 2000 helped enable meetings between relatives long separated by the division of Korea. The Nobel Committee also recognised his domestic democratic work and wider advocacy, including support for democracy in Burma and opposition to repression in East Timor. These contributions extended beyond the diplomacy of a single summit.
entries.significance: The award recognised efforts to build conditions for peaceful relations and democratic rights. It supported an opening for reconciliation rather than certifying that Korea had been reunified or that all tensions had been resolved. The historical achievement includes both political opposition and subsequent leadership in government.

entries.title: Layered semiconductors and integrated circuits enable modern electronics
entries.overview: Zhores Alferov and Herbert Kroemer developed semiconductor heterostructures for fast electronics and light-based devices, while Jack Kilby was recognised for his part in inventing the integrated circuit.
entries.background: Electronic technology faced two related challenges: improving the behaviour of individual devices and fitting many components into a small, reliable circuit. Joining different semiconductor materials in thin layers offered new device properties, while integration promised to reduce the need for separately assembled components.
entries.work: Kroemer proposed a heterostructure transistor in 1957. In 1963, he and Alferov independently proposed the principle of a heterostructure laser, setting out a design that later experimental advances would make practical. Alferov’s experimental work helped develop practical layered devices. Separately, Kilby built the first integrated circuit, demonstrating that circuit elements could be made together in one piece of semiconductor. Robert Noyce independently developed the silicon-based approach that became central to practical manufacturing.
entries.significance: The shared award covered distinct foundations of information technology. Heterostructures enabled fast transistors and efficient semiconductor lasers, including those used in optical communications, while integrated circuits made increasingly compact and complex electronic systems possible. The contributions addressed different needs in electronic systems.

entries.title: Making a chosen molecular mirror image
entries.overview: The laureates developed catalysts that favour one mirror-image form of a molecule, helping chemists make substances with the biological effects they want.
entries.background: Many molecules come in two mirror-image forms that can act differently in the body. A synthesis that produces a mixture can therefore be unsuitable for a medicine. Chemists needed ways to guide a reaction toward the desired form.
entries.work: William Knowles showed in 1968 that metal-containing catalysts could select a molecular form during hydrogenation, a reaction that adds hydrogen. Ryoji Noyori subsequently developed more general catalysts for this kind of selective reaction. K. Barry Sharpless pursued a different route, developing selective catalysts for oxidation reactions from the 1970s. Catalysts facilitate a reaction without being consumed; their structure helps determine which molecular form the reaction produces.
entries.significance: The methods made selective synthesis useful in pharmaceutical production. Knowles's approach helped enable manufacture of L-dopa for Parkinson's disease, while the broader catalyst developments gave chemists ways to prepare other medicines in a desired molecular form.

entries.title: Analyzing Markets Where Information Is Unevenly Distributed
entries.overview: This research examines how markets function when one party possesses more knowledge about a product or service's quality than the other party.
entries.background: In many transactions, sellers hold a secret advantage regarding the true value of an item. This imbalance of information can create challenges for buyers who cannot easily verify the actual characteristics of what they are purchasing.
entries.work: George Akerlof studied markets where sellers know more than buyers, using secondhand cars to illustrate quality issues. A. Michael Spence created signaling theory, showing how well-informed people use education to communicate productivity to others. Joseph Stiglitz researched how uninformed parties use screening and self-selection to improve their standing, such as when insurance companies categorize customers into different risk levels.
entries.significance: These studies changed the understanding of how information gaps influence economic behavior and how individuals navigate uncertainty in various marketplace exchanges.

entries.title: Exploring Colonialism and Identity Through Narrative and Travel Writing
entries.overview: V. S. Naipaul received this honor for combining observant storytelling with critical examination to reveal previously hidden historical accounts.
entries.background: Born in Trinidad, V. S. Naipaul moved to the United Kingdom at eighteen. His writing often explores the complexities of post-colonial societies, focusing on themes of alienation and identity within diverse, multicultural environments.
entries.work: Starting with his 1957 debut novel, The Mystic Masseur, Naipaul used travel, reportage, and fiction to document various global locations. In his 1961 breakthrough, A House for Mr. Biswas, he examined colonial life. His literary output integrates detailed observations from his international travels to investigate the presence of suppressed histories through careful narrative scrutiny.
entries.significance: His writing provides a way to perceive overlooked historical truths by connecting personal stories of identity to the broader effects of colonialism and global movement.

entries.title: Discovering the Key Regulators of the Cell Cycle
entries.overview: Researchers identified specific genes and proteins that control how cells divide and manage their growth during development.
entries.background: Multicellular organisms develop as cells divide and take on specialised functions. Their growth depends on controlling the sequence and timing of division. Researchers therefore needed to identify the genes and proteins that regulate the cell cycle and respond when something is wrong.
entries.work: In 1971, Leland Hartwell used yeast to identify hundreds of genes governing division and showed the cycle stops if DNA is damaged. During the mid-1970s, Paul Nurse found a specific gene crucial to several phases, later finding its human version in 1987. In the early 1980s, Tim Hunt studied sea urchins to find proteins that break down during different cell cycle stages.
entries.significance: These findings revealed how cells regulate their own division and how specific components manage the timing of the cycle.

entries.title: The United Nations and Kofi Annan Working Toward Global Cooperation
entries.overview: The 2001 Peace Prize honored the United Nations and Secretary-General Kofi Annan for efforts toward a more organized, peaceful global community.
entries.background: Following World War II, the United Nations was created in 1945 to replace the League of Nations. While intended to protect peace, power disputes prevented the creation of an international armed force, shifting early focus toward economic and social development.
entries.work: The UN's early development work was joined by a growing emphasis on human rights from the 1970s. Kofi Annan led peacekeeping as Under-Secretary-General before becoming Secretary-General in 1997. The Nobel Committee recognised his efforts to renew the organisation, prioritise human rights, combat the spread of HIV in Africa and oppose international terrorism. The joint award connected his leadership with the UN's wider role in cooperation between states.
entries.significance: The award highlighted the importance of multilateralism and organized cooperation between different states to improve global stability.

entries.title: Creating New States of Matter Using Extremely Cold Atoms
entries.overview: Scientists created a unique state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate by cooling specific types of atoms to temperatures near absolute zero.
entries.background: Building on Bose's work, Einstein predicted that bosons could gather in the lowest-energy quantum state at very low temperatures. Related effects were already known in superconductors and superfluids. The challenge recognised in 2001 was producing a condensate in a dilute atomic gas.
entries.work: In 1995, Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman demonstrated this phenomenon using a thin gas of rubidium atoms. During that same year, Wolfgang Ketterle achieved the same result using a sparse gas of sodium atoms. Both groups reached temperatures low enough to force these atoms into the predicted condensed state.
entries.significance: The achievement provided experimental proof for the 1924 predictions and allowed for early studies into the fundamental properties of these atomic condensates.

entries.title: Measuring proteins and revealing their shapes
entries.overview: Fenn and Tanaka made large biological molecules accessible to mass spectrometry, while Wüthrich developed a different method for determining protein structures in solution.
entries.background: Proteins are large, intricate molecules whose identities and shapes help determine what they do in cells. Existing analytical methods faced important limits: mass spectrometry required electrically charged molecules in a gas, and obtaining structural information about proteins was difficult.
entries.work: John Fenn's electrospray method produced charged droplets of protein solution; evaporation left protein ions available for measurement. Koichi Tanaka used soft laser desorption to release large molecules from a sample, rather than simply destroy the proteins into fragments. Separately, Kurt Wüthrich developed nuclear magnetic resonance methods that used signals from nuclei to identify positions and distances within proteins. Those measurements allowed their three-dimensional structures to be calculated.
entries.significance: Researchers gained ways to identify proteins in a sample and, through NMR, study their structures in a solution resembling their cellular environment. The complementary methods expanded biological research and supported the development of pharmaceuticals.

entries.title: Psychological Insights and Laboratory Experiments in Economic Science
entries.overview: This award honors research into how human judgment works during uncertainty and the use of controlled laboratory experiments to study different market structures.
entries.background: Economics traditionally focused on theoretical models, but researchers sought better ways to understand real-world human choices and test how various auction systems or institutions function through empirical observation.
entries.work: Starting in the late 1960s, Daniel Kahneman used cognitive psychology to study judgment and decisions under uncertainty. With Amos Tversky, he formulated prospect theory to describe patterns that standard economic assumptions missed. Separately, Vernon Smith developed methods and standards for reliable laboratory experiments in economics. His experiments examined market rules, including how the choice of auction method changes the revenue a seller can expect.
entries.significance: Kahneman integrated psychology into economic science through his study of decision-making, while Smith founded the field of experimental economics by providing tools for empirical market analysis.

entries.title: Literature Honoring Individual Experience Amidst Historical Chaos
entries.overview: Imre Kertész received this honor for his writing that protects the vulnerable person's perspective against the random and brutal nature of history.
entries.background: Born in 1929, Imre Kertész was deported to Auschwitz at fourteen and later held at Buchenwald. He survived the camps and returned to Budapest after liberation in 1945. Those experiences became a central source for his fiction.
entries.work: Kertész's fiction belongs to witness literature, in which writers draw on personally experienced trauma. He spent many years on his debut novel, Fateless, published in 1975. Through György Köves, a young character who is deported and survives, the novel explores life under an ideological death sentence. His work examines both the experience of persecution and the burden of surviving when so many others died.
entries.significance: His novels examine the struggle to maintain one's humanity and handle the weight of surviving mass death during historical atrocities.

entries.title: Genetic Control of Organ Development and Programmed Cell Death
entries.overview: Scientists discovered how specific genes regulate cell death and organ formation by studying the development and life cycles of the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans.
entries.background: Development involves both making new cells and removing particular cells. Cell death can be part of an organised biological programme rather than simply an accident. Researchers used a small roundworm to investigate how genes govern that process alongside cell division and organ formation.
entries.work: In the mid-1970s, Sydney Brenner used genetic analysis to connect cell division with organ formation. In 1976, John Sulston detailed how roundworm cells divide and mature, proving certain cell deaths are normal developmental steps. In 1986, H. Robert Horvitz identified two genes required for this death process, later finding a gene that prevents it and others that manage dead cell removal.
entries.significance: These findings established the genetic mechanisms that control how cells die and how organs develop within an organism.

entries.title: Efforts Toward Global Peace and Human Rights Advocacy
entries.overview: Jimmy Carter received this honor for his long-term dedication to resolving international disputes, supporting democratic movements, and encouraging social and economic progress.
entries.background: During his presidency, the 1978 Egypt-Israel peace agreement marked a major success. However, later foreign policy challenges included tensions with Iran following the Shah's fall and increased Cold War friction after the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in late 1979.
entries.work: In 1978, Jimmy Carter mediated an agreement between Egypt and Israel. Following his presidency, he continued a campaign of mediation and human rights advocacy. These activities occasionally conflicted with official United States policies. His work also focused on promoting social welfare and supporting the development of democratic institutions and economic stability across various nations throughout several decades.
entries.significance: His actions represented an active pursuit of nonviolent conflict resolution and the advancement of human rights, even when his mediation efforts stood apart from formal government positions.

entries.title: Detecting Cosmic Neutrinos and X-ray Sources in Space
entries.overview: Scientists used underground tanks and satellites to identify elusive particles from the sun and observe high-energy radiation originating outside our solar system.
entries.background: Nuclear reactions, such as protons combining into helium, produce tiny particles called neutrinos. While stars emit visible light, X-rays from space are blocked by Earth's atmosphere, making them difficult to study.
entries.work: Beginning in the 1960s, Raymond Davis Jr. detected neutrinos using a chlorine-rich liquid deep underground: rare interactions produced argon atoms that he could count. Masatoshi Koshiba later used an underground water detector to observe light flashes from neutrino interactions. In a separate programme beginning in the 1960s, Riccardo Giacconi helped develop space-based X-ray astronomy, revealing sources beyond the solar system and objects thought to contain black holes.
entries.significance: These efforts confirmed that nuclear reactions power the sun and revealed new celestial objects through X-ray observations.

entries.title: Discovering How Cells Transport Water and Charged Atoms
entries.overview: Agre identified a protein that lets water cross cell membranes, while MacKinnon revealed the structure of a channel that selectively carries potassium ions.
entries.background: Organisms rely on moving substances across cell surfaces. While processes like nerve signaling and kidney function depend on these pathways, the actual shapes of the canals for water and ions were unknown.
entries.work: Peter Agre isolated a previously unknown membrane protein and demonstrated its water-channel function in experiments reported in 1992; it became known as aquaporin. Separately, in 1998 Roderick MacKinnon used X-ray crystallography to reveal the structure of a potassium ion channel. Diffraction patterns from protein crystals provided the structural evidence, helping explain a molecular pathway for charged atoms to cross a cell membrane.
entries.significance: The work identified molecular routes for water and ions across cell membranes. Such transport underpins processes including the kidneys' recovery of water and the electrical signals used by nerves and muscles.

entries.title: Statistical Methods for Analyzing Fluctuating Economic Time Series
entries.overview: Two researchers created new mathematical techniques to study how economic variables like stock prices and GDP change over time through volatility and common trends.
entries.background: Economic data often follows unpredictable patterns. Many series are nonstationary, meaning temporary disturbances can cause long-lasting effects. Analyzing these fluctuations requires specific tools to avoid incorrect conclusions when looking at trends in wealth, consumption, or exchange rates.
entries.work: In 1982, Robert Engle developed ARCH models to capture how financial variables move between high and low volatility periods. Separately, Clive Granger created cointegration methods to study series with common trends. Granger demonstrated that applying standard stationary statistics to nonstationary data produces misleading results. His approach allows for analyzing relationships between different economic factors, such as price levels and exchange rates.
entries.significance: These developments provided new tools for evaluating the relationship between financial variables and understanding how volatility shifts within economic time series.

entries.title: Portraying the Role of Outsiders Through Analytical Prose
entries.overview: The 2003 prize was awarded to J. M. Coetzee for his literary writing that explores how outsiders interact with various different societies.
entries.background: After working as a programmer in London during the 1960s, J. M. Coetzee moved to Cape Town. He taught English literature there until 2002, following a period of protest against the Vietnam War.
entries.work: Beginning with the 1974 novel Dusklands, Coetzee's writing uses rigorous and analytical prose. In works like Waiting for the Barbarians, he examines moments where morality is tested by human weakness. His stories often feature recurring characters, such as an elderly male academician or a female author named Elizabeth Costello, to illustrate how individuals face difficult situations.
entries.significance: Coetzee's literature focuses on fundamental human struggles and the way people navigate critical circumstances where right and wrong are challenged.

entries.title: Discoveries Enabling Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Human Body
entries.overview: This discovery used the way atomic nuclei act like tiny magnets to produce detailed images of internal body structures by measuring water content.
entries.background: Inside atoms, protons and neutrons behave as small spinning magnets. These particles align within a magnetic field, but specific radio waves can disrupt this orientation based on the type of atom present.
entries.work: During the 1970s, Paul Lauterbur introduced magnetic field variations to help map the body's interior. Separately, Peter Mansfield created calculation methods for this process. Together, these advancements allow scientists to measure hydrogen atom levels and use differences in tissue water content to generate medical images.
entries.significance: These developments provided a way to visualize internal organs and tissues without invasive procedures by utilizing the measurable properties of hydrogen atoms.

entries.title: Efforts for Democracy and Human Rights in Iran
entries.overview: Shirin Ebadi worked toward democratic principles and human rights, focusing specifically on protecting the legal interests of women and children.
entries.background: Following the 1979 revolution in Iran, Shirin Ebadi was removed from her position as a judge. She later faced imprisonment in 2000 after criticizing the nation's religious leadership structure.
entries.work: As a lawyer, Ebadi defended individuals persecuted by authorities and helped create organizations to address human rights issues. She authored books suggesting changes to divorce and succession laws. Her advocacy included promoting the separation of religion and state while seeking to decrease political power held by the clergy.
entries.significance: Her work addressed fundamental rights during a period of high tension between Islamic and Western worlds, while supporting the Iranian reform movement.

entries.title: Theories Regarding Superconductors and Superfluids Under Extreme Cold
entries.overview: The laureates explained two different low-temperature phenomena: electrical currents without resistance in superconductors and the unusual flow of liquid helium in a superfluid state.
entries.background: Certain materials become superconducting when cooled, while liquid helium can become superfluid. These are distinct quantum phenomena. Explaining them required theories of how the constituents behave collectively and, for superconductors, how the material responds to an applied magnetic field.
entries.work: Vitaly Ginzburg and Lev Landau formulated a theory of superconductivity in 1950. Alexei Abrikosov used that framework to explain type-II superconductors, in which magnetic flux enters through vortices while the material remains superconducting. In a separate contribution, Anthony Leggett explained superfluid helium-3: the helium atoms form pairs whose interactions and ordering produce the superfluid state. Helium-3 here is a superfluid liquid, not an electrical superconductor.
entries.significance: The theories clarified how quantum effects govern the collective behaviour of matter. Understanding type-II superconductors is especially useful because they can sustain superconductivity in strong magnetic fields, including those used in research equipment and medical imaging.

entries.title: How Cells Identify and Break Down Unneeded Proteins
entries.overview: Scientists identified how cells use a specific protein called ubiquitin to mark other proteins for destruction, allowing the cell to recycle materials.
entries.background: While cells constantly produce new proteins to function, they also require a system to destroy old or unnecessary ones. Without an effective way to break these down, cellular processes would be disrupted.
entries.work: In the early 1980s, Aaron Ciechanover, Avram Hershko and Irwin Rose showed that ubiquitin helps mark proteins for destruction. Ubiquitin tags direct selected proteins toward the proteasome, a large protein complex that breaks them into smaller pieces. This explained how cells can select proteins for removal rather than indiscriminately destroy their contents. The resulting material can be used in building other cellular substances.
entries.significance: This discovery explained how the cell recycles broken-down protein pieces to help build other necessary substances within the cell.

entries.title: Why policy promises and technology shocks matter
entries.overview: Kydland and Prescott showed how expectations complicate economic policy and developed models linking business fluctuations to the decisions of households and firms.
entries.background: People make decisions today partly by anticipating future policy. Expected taxes can affect saving, and expected inflation can influence wages and prices. Policymakers may later want to change an earlier plan, making a promise difficult to believe from the outset.
entries.work: Their analysis of time consistency explained how an attractive announced policy might not be implemented when the moment arrives unless policymakers can commit to it. They also developed business-cycle models in which changes in technological progress influence output, consumption, investment and working hours. These models treated fluctuations as the combined result of forward-looking decisions by households and firms, and showed that supply-side shocks could have substantial effects.
entries.significance: The work shifted attention toward the credibility and institutions of policymaking, influencing debates about central-bank independence. It also established methods for analysing business cycles alongside long-term growth, without claiming that technology explains every downturn.

entries.title: Literary Writing Exposing Social Clichés and Hidden Power Structures
entries.overview: Elfriede Jelinek won this award for her use of musical rhythms in prose and drama to reveal how societal clichés exert control.
entries.background: During her creative development, Jelinek studied piano, organ, and theater. She moved from musical training toward composing texts that examine the underlying ideologies found within language itself.
entries.work: In her novels, such as The Piano Teacher and Lust, and in her plays, Jelinek utilizes a flow of various voices and counter-voices. Her writing employs a sharp, satirical approach to critique modern consumerism. Through her prose and poetry, she uncovers patterns of sexism, sadism, and submission, using linguistic intensity to expose the absurdity found within common social patterns.
entries.significance: Her work serves as a critique of society by uncovering hidden structures of power and exploring how language carries deep-seated, subjugating ideologies.

entries.title: Discovering How Genetic Code Creates Our Sense of Smell
entries.overview: Scientists identified how specific genes produce proteins that allow our noses to detect and distinguish various different scents through electrical brain signals.
entries.background: Understanding the biological mechanism behind scent perception required identifying the specific genetic instructions responsible for creating sensory proteins within the nose's olfactory neurons.
entries.work: In 1991, Linda Buck and Richard Axel found that hundreds of DNA genes encode odorant sensors in nasal neurons. These receptors are proteins that change shape when a scent molecule attaches to them. This physical change triggers an electric signal sent to the brain. Because different sensors react to slightly different substances, the brain interprets these varying electrical patterns as specific, distinct smells.
entries.significance: This discovery clarified how the organization of the olfactory system works, showing how individual chemical signals are translated into the complex scents we perceive.

entries.title: Tree Planting for Democracy and Sustainable Development in Kenya
entries.overview: Wangari Maathai organized a grassroots movement that used environmental conservation to support women's rights, democratic struggles, and international solidarity.
entries.background: Deforestation threatened the livelihoods of Kenya's farming communities. Maathai, a biologist and university professor, began the Green Belt Movement in 1977 in response. Her environmental work became part of a broader commitment to democracy, women's rights and opposition to authoritarian government.
entries.work: Maathai established the Green Belt Movement to address environmental decay. She encouraged local women to plant trees in their areas to promote ecological thinking. This initiative eventually expanded into other African nations, resulting in the planting of more than thirty million trees. Her efforts linked environmental care with broader goals like democracy and rights for women.
entries.significance: Maathai's work connected local environmental actions to global issues. Her movement helped protect subsistence resources while advocating for democratic change and female empowerment.

entries.title: Discovering How Quarks Behave Under Strong Interaction Forces
entries.overview: Scientists identified a theory where quarks act like independent particles when they are positioned very close to each other during interactions.
entries.background: The strong interaction binds quarks inside protons and neutrons and also underlies the binding of atomic nuclei. No isolated free quark had been observed, yet experiments required an explanation of why quarks could behave almost independently when probed at very short distances.
entries.work: In 1973, calculations by David Gross, H. David Politzer and Frank Wilczek revealed asymptotic freedom in the theory of the strong interaction. The effective interaction becomes weaker at shorter distances, so closely probed quarks behave approximately like free particles. This short-distance behaviour could coexist with the strong binding that prevents quarks from being observed freely at ordinary scales.
entries.significance: The discovery provided a new way to understand the behavior of the fundamental particles that constitute the building blocks of the atomic nucleus.

entries.title: Developing the Metathesis Method for Organic Synthesis
entries.overview: The laureates explained how metathesis rearranges carbon–carbon bonds and developed catalysts that made this reaction a practical tool for building organic molecules.
entries.background: Chemists build organic substances by rearranging the connections between atoms. In metathesis, groups of atoms exchange places as carbon–carbon double bonds are broken and re-formed. Understanding the sequence of these changes was important for finding compounds that could facilitate the reaction.
entries.work: Yves Chauvin explained the mechanism in 1971, including the role of metal-containing compounds. Richard Schrock developed an effective catalyst in 1990. Around 1992, Robert Grubbs introduced a catalyst that also remained stable in air, making it easier to use. The award therefore joined an explanation of how the reaction proceeds with practical ways to carry it out, rather than crediting all three with one simultaneous invention.
entries.significance: Better control of metathesis gave chemists more effective routes for synthesising organic substances. Its industrial use could make processes more efficient and environmentally favourable, linking an understanding of reaction mechanisms to practical chemical production.

entries.title: Game Theory Analysis of Conflict and Cooperation
entries.overview: These researchers utilized game theory to study how individuals and groups interact, specifically focusing on the conditions required for sustained cooperation and strategic competition.
entries.background: In the mid-twentieth century, social scientists sought deeper mathematical ways to understand why adversaries choose to cooperate or engage in conflict. This period included significant shifts in international relations, trade policies, and economic competition.
entries.work: Robert J. Aumann developed a theory regarding repeated games to identify what allows cooperation to persist over time. Separately, Thomas C. Schelling applied game theory to scenarios where parties interact repeatedly, such as during treaties or trade disputes. Schelling also analyzed strategic commitments to explain how firms compete and how political power is delegated. These individual contributions helped clarify the mechanics of economic conflicts like price wars.
entries.significance: The work expanded mathematical frameworks within the social sciences, providing new tools to examine international trade, political decision-making, and various forms of strategic competition.

entries.title: The Dramatic Works of British Playwright Harold Pinter
entries.overview: Harold Pinter was a British writer whose plays explore the hidden tensions and power struggles found within ordinary conversations and human relationships.
entries.background: Growing up in London's working-class Hackney district, Pinter’s creative perspective was shaped by World War II and prevalent anti-Semitic sentiments. His writing often addresses themes of political oppression and social revolt.
entries.work: In his dramas, Pinter utilizes clear dialogue to reveal underlying issues like gender, class, and power imbalances. He explores how people struggle to communicate within relationships. His theatrical pieces frequently incorporate unpredictable violence and dark humor to unsettle audiences. Through these plays, he examines the precariousness hidden beneath everyday speech and addresses the closed rooms of political oppression.
entries.significance: Pinter's writing is notable for exposing the instability beneath surface-level interactions and for using drama to prompt resistance against established ruling powers.

entries.title: A bacterial cause of many stomach ulcers
entries.overview: Marshall and Warren established the role of Helicobacter pylori in stomach inflammation and many peptic ulcers, opening a way to treat the underlying infection.
entries.background: Ulcers were often approached through explanations involving stress and lifestyle. Warren's observations of bacteria alongside inflamed stomach tissue raised a different possibility: an infection might be contributing to disease. Establishing that connection required evidence beyond simply finding microbes in a sample.
entries.work: Robin Warren observed the bacteria in stomach specimens, and Barry Marshall succeeded in growing the organism in culture. Their work, including studies reported from 1982 onward, connected Helicobacter pylori with gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. Further clinical evidence showed that eliminating the infection could change the course of associated ulcers. The finding brought together microscopic observations, laboratory culture and studies of patients rather than resting on one isolated observation.
entries.significance: For ulcers associated with H. pylori, antibiotic treatment could address an underlying cause. The scope matters: not every ulcer is bacterial, and not every person carrying the bacterium develops ulcer disease.

entries.title: Preventing Military Nuclear Use Through International Monitoring
entries.overview: The agency and its leader worked to stop nuclear energy from becoming weapons while promoting safe, civilian uses of atomic power.
entries.background: The IAEA was established in 1957 to support peaceful nuclear uses without increasing the spread of nuclear weapons. When the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty entered into force in 1970, participating non-nuclear-weapon states accepted IAEA monitoring of their nuclear facilities.
entries.work: The IAEA used technical monitoring and on-site inspections to check compliance with non-proliferation commitments. It exposed North Korean nuclear-weapons development and challenged claims that Iraq had resumed a nuclear-arms programme before the 2003 war. Mohamed ElBaradei, Director General from 1997, worked to strengthen the agency and encourage wider participation in the non-proliferation system through international cooperation.
entries.significance: These efforts aimed to ensure that nuclear energy remains under reliable international control, preventing the expansion of military nuclear capabilities globally.

entries.title: Quantum Optics Theory and Laser Based Precision Spectroscopy Techniques
entries.overview: This prize honors developments in understanding light as quantum packets and creating tools to measure light frequencies with extreme accuracy.
entries.background: Early 20th-century physics described electromagnetic radiation as particles called photons that behave like waves. However, a deep theoretical framework for how these quantum light packets interact was missing until later decades.
entries.work: In 1963, Roy Glauber established the foundation for quantum optics theory. Around 2000, John Hall and Theodor Hänsch developed the frequency comb technique. This method uses laser light containing a series of equally spaced frequencies to measure light wave frequencies with high precision.
entries.significance: These advancements allow scientists to study atomic properties, establish benchmarks for length and time, and determine physical constants using precise light measurements.

entries.title: Mapping How Cells Transfer Genetic Information Using Yeast
entries.overview: Roger Kornberg investigated the molecular mechanics used by eukaryotic cells to copy information from DNA into RNA during protein formation.
entries.background: While scientists mapped how bacteria transfer genetic instructions during the 1960s, the specific process in organisms with distinct cell nuclei remained unmapped until later research.
entries.work: During the first decade of the new millennium, Roger Kornberg studied yeast to uncover the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription. He successfully determined the structural makeup of the enzyme RNA polymerase. Additionally, he produced images that illustrate exactly how an RNA molecule is constructed from a DNA template.
entries.significance: These studies provided a clear view of how genetic instructions are transferred from DNA to RNA within complex cells.

entries.title: Why short-term policy gains may not last
entries.overview: Phelps analysed how economic choices connect the present with the future, particularly through expectations about inflation and decisions about saving and investment.
entries.background: A common view in the 1950s and 1960s treated inflation and unemployment as a stable trade-off. Policymakers seemed able to accept more inflation in exchange for less unemployment. Phelps examined how people form expectations when deciding wages and prices.
entries.work: His analysis linked inflation to both unemployment and expected inflation. In that framework, raising inflation cannot permanently lower unemployment: short-term effects and long-term outcomes differ as expectations adjust. Phelps also studied the trade-off between consuming resources now and investing for future generations. His research considered how saving, education and technological development affect growth and how changes can distribute benefits differently across generations.
entries.significance: The work clarified why policy decisions have consequences beyond their immediate effects. It helped explain the importance of inflation expectations and showed that evaluating investment requires considering future welfare as well as present consumption.

entries.title: Exploring Cultural Interlacing Through Modern Turkish Fiction
entries.overview: Orhan Pamuk received this award for his novels that use new symbols to represent the meeting and overlapping of different cultural traditions.
entries.background: Growing up in an affluent, secular Istanbul family, Orhan Pamuk studied architecture before turning to writing. His narratives focus on the tension found within the borders separating Eastern and Western values.
entries.work: After debuting with Cevdet Bey and His Sons in 1982, Orhan Pamuk achieved international recognition during the 1990s. My Name Is Red, first published in Turkish in 1998, helped establish his reputation. His writing explores identity by examining the similarities and differences between old traditions and modern ways of life, often focusing on the melancholic nature of his home city.
entries.significance: Pamuk's novels provide a way to understand how diverse cultures clash and interlace through the search for identity in a changing world.

entries.title: Discovery of Gene Silencing Through Double Stranded RNA
entries.overview: Researchers found that double-stranded RNA can prevent specific genetic instructions from being used to create proteins, effectively turning certain genes off.
entries.background: RNA molecules perform various roles in cells. While messenger RNA typically carries genetic data from DNA to facilitate protein production as a single-stranded spiral, some RNA exists in a double-stranded format.
entries.work: In 1998, Andrew Fire and Craig Mello studied the roundworm C. elegans. They identified a process called RNA interference. They observed that double-stranded RNA acts to block messenger RNA. This blockage prevents specific genetic information from being converted during protein formation, which results in the silencing of those particular genes.
entries.significance: This discovery revealed how double-stranded RNA serves an important regulatory role within a genome by rendering specific genes inactive.

entries.title: Microcredit Initiatives for Economic and Social Development
entries.overview: Muhammad Yunus and Grameen Bank utilized small, accessible loans to promote self-support and economic growth among the world's most impoverished populations.
entries.background: In 1974, Bangladesh experienced a severe famine. During this period, Muhammad Yunus, an economics professor at the University of Chittagong, sought ways to assist those facing extreme poverty beyond traditional academic teaching.
entries.work: After the 1974 famine, Yunus sought practical ways to help poor people establish small enterprises. His lending initiative expanded through Grameen Bank, established in 1983. The bank offered microcredit: small loans to borrowers whom conventional banks often excluded for lack of collateral. Its approach rested on the belief that even very poor people could manage economic activities when given suitable financial opportunities.
entries.significance: By the 2006 award, Grameen had reached more than seven million borrowers, with over 95 percent of loans going to women or groups of women. The prize recognised efforts to support development from below.

entries.title: Reading the early universe in microwave light
entries.overview: Mather and Smoot used the COBE satellite to measure the thermal spectrum and tiny directional variations of the cosmic microwave background, relic radiation from the early universe.
entries.background: The Big Bang model predicts an early hot universe whose radiation remains detectable as the universe expands and cools. Researchers needed precise measurements of that radiation's spectrum and variations across the sky to test the picture and investigate the origins of cosmic structure.
entries.work: John Mather led the instrument work that measured the background's spectrum, finding an exceptionally close match to the thermal pattern called a blackbody spectrum. This does not mean the radiation comes from a separate dark object in space. George Smoot led the COBE measurements that revealed tiny directional differences in 1992. Those variations offered evidence of early unevenness from which matter could gather under gravity into larger structures.
entries.significance: The measurements strengthened the hot Big Bang account and connected the early universe to the later growth of stars and galaxies. They made precise observations of the microwave background a powerful tool for studying cosmic history.

entries.title: Studying Chemical Processes Occurring on Solid Surfaces
entries.overview: Gerhard Ertl investigated how chemical reactions accelerate when gaseous molecules touch metal surfaces, specifically focusing on the mechanics of surface-level interactions.
entries.background: During the 1960s, understanding how gases interact with solids was vital. Many chemical reactions increase in speed when molecules make contact with a metal surface, necessitating new ways to observe these microscopic events.
entries.work: Using high-purity vacuum techniques originally created for the semiconductor industry, Gerhard Ertl designed methods to observe surface chemistry. He successfully mapped the specific steps of the Haber-Bosch process. This method involves using an iron catalyst to transform atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, a step crucial for creating artificial fertilizer.
entries.significance: Ertl's work provided a detailed map of the chemical transformations that occur during the production of ammonia, clarifying how catalysts function on metal surfaces.

entries.title: Foundations of Theory Regarding Rules for Coordinating Economic Agents
entries.overview: This economic theory examines how to create specific rules and systems to help people coordinate effectively when they lack trust or shared information.
entries.background: In the 1960s, economists began exploring how different market structures function. This research focused on identifying whether certain trading environments or voting procedures allow participants to reach efficient outcomes despite having private information.
entries.work: Leonid Hurwicz pioneered mechanism design in the 1960s. Eric Maskin and Roger Myerson developed its foundations further, studying what rules for markets or collective decisions can achieve when participants have different information. The theory compares possible trading mechanisms, regulation schemes and voting procedures. It asks which arrangements can coordinate participants efficiently, rather than assuming that any market automatically produces a desirable outcome.
entries.significance: This work provides tools to distinguish between effective and ineffective markets, aiding in the identification of efficient regulation schemes and trading mechanisms.
