entries.title: Examining Twentieth Century Life Through Diverse Literary Genres
entries.overview: Doris Lessing received this honor for her extensive writings that analyze human behavior, social conditions, and various historical developments throughout the twentieth century.
entries.background: After moving to London in 1949, Doris Lessing engaged with political movements and campaigns against nuclear weapons. Her diverse career included roles as a journalist, stenographer, and nursemaid before she produced her large body of work.
entries.work: Spanning fifty books, her writing explores different genres and perspectives. In the 1962 novel The Golden Notebook, she examines sexuality, political concepts, and the lives of writers alongside psychological studies. Some of her texts utilize an extraterrestrial viewpoint to depict the end of civilization. Her prose also investigates how people live and interact within a fragmented global society through various lenses.
entries.significance: Her literature provides detailed investigations into the complexities of human existence, focusing on the psychological states and social realities experienced during the modern era.

entries.title: Changing Specific Mouse Genes to Discover Their Functions
entries.overview: Mario Capecchi, Martin Evans and Oliver Smithies established principles for making targeted genetic changes in mice. Researchers could then investigate what happens when a particular gene is disabled or altered.
entries.background: Introducing DNA into an animal was already possible, but changing a chosen gene reliably was a different challenge. It required a way to target that location and pass the resulting modification to offspring.
entries.work: Evans developed cultures of mouse embryonic stem cells in 1981. Such cells could contribute to a developing mouse, including its reproductive cells. Capecchi and Smithies separately developed ways to modify selected genes using homologous recombination, in which matching DNA sequences exchange material. Combining gene targeting with embryonic stem cells made inherited, specific modifications possible. These advances came together during the 1980s; several laboratories produced knockout mice in 1989.
entries.significance: Comparing mice with and without a functioning gene helps reveal that gene's role in development, physiology and disease. The methods became a foundation for experimental models of human illnesses and for investigating possible treatments.

entries.title: Spreading Information Regarding Man-Made Climate Change
entries.overview: This award honors efforts to increase global knowledge about human-caused climate shifts and establishing necessary steps to address these environmental changes.
entries.background: Since 1988, concerns have grown regarding how rising temperatures threaten human life. These changes may trigger conflicts by straining vital resources like drinking water and forcing populations to migrate due to floods or droughts.
entries.work: The IPCC produced four major reports between 1990 and 2007, utilizing research from thousands of experts across many nations to show accelerating warming. Separately, Al Gore used his platform to bring climate issues to political discussions. He wrote the 1992 book Earth in the Balance and later released the 2006 documentary An Inconvenient Truth to increase public awareness.
entries.significance: These efforts brought attention to the urgent need for counter-measures to prevent a global crisis and highlighted how environmental shifts can increase the risk of war.

entries.title: Discovering Giant Magnetoresistance in Ultra Thin Material Layers
entries.overview: Albert Fert and Peter Grünberg identified a phenomenon where tiny magnetic field fluctuations cause significant changes in how electricity flows through very thin materials.
entries.background: When certain materials are stripped down to thicknesses of only a few nanometers, which is just a few atomic layers, their physical properties begin to behave differently than they do in bulk form.
entries.work: In 1988, Albert Fert and Peter Grünberg independently discovered giant magnetoresistance. In structures made from extremely thin layers, changing the magnetic arrangement can produce a large change in electrical resistance. This sensitive response enabled improved electronic read heads, which turn the magnetic patterns stored on a disk into electrical signals. The effect helped make hard drives physically smaller; it did not mean reducing the amount of information they could hold.
entries.significance: This finding allowed engineers to create much smaller hard drives by utilizing how thin layers respond to magnetic changes.

entries.title: Making Living Cells Visible with Fluorescent Proteins
entries.overview: Osamu Shimomura, Martin Chalfie and Roger Tsien turned green fluorescent protein, or GFP, into a widely useful marker for studying living cells and the molecules inside them.
entries.background: A fluorescent protein absorbs light and emits light of another colour. If cells can make such a marker themselves, researchers can observe where particular genes are active or follow proteins to which the marker has been attached.
entries.work: Shimomura isolated GFP from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria in 1962 and investigated its fluorescence. Chalfie showed that the GFP gene could work as a biological marker in other organisms. His team's results, published in 1994, included fluorescent cells in the transparent roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. Tsien explained important features of how GFP fluoresces and developed variants with different colours and improved properties.
entries.significance: These contributions made it possible to track processes that were previously difficult to see inside living cells. Different fluorescent colours let researchers distinguish multiple labelled components, connecting genetic information with visible cellular behaviour.

entries.title: Analyzing Global Trade Patterns and Urban Economic Activity
entries.overview: Paul Krugman developed a theory showing how economies of scale and lower shipping expenses drive trade between similar nations and cause urban growth.
entries.background: Traditional trade theories explained exchange through differences between countries, including their resources and production conditions. They were less suited to explaining extensive trade between similar economies that produce comparable kinds of goods.
entries.work: In 1979, Paul Krugman introduced a model in which economies of scale—lower costs per unit as production expands—help explain trade between similar countries. His research also addressed economic geography: how scale economies and transport costs influence the concentration of production and employment. These ideas connected patterns of international exchange with the reasons economic activity clusters in particular places.
entries.significance: This analysis changed understanding by explaining why modern trade often involves similar industries and how industrial concentration shapes the physical location of economic activity.

entries.title: Literary Exploration of Humanity and Diverse Cultural Perspectives
entries.overview: Jean-Marie Gustave Le Clézio received this honor for writing prose that explores human existence through new poetic adventures and diverse cultural lenses.
entries.background: Le Clézio's family had strong ties to Mauritius, and as a child he travelled from France to join his father in Nigeria. Living among Indigenous peoples in Panama during the 1970s later changed his outlook. These experiences inform writing concerned with relationships between people, nature and history.
entries.work: Since his 1963 debut, Le Clézio has produced over 40 prose works. While his early writings utilized an experimental style, his 1980 book Desert achieved a major breakthrough using flowing prose. His literature focuses on highlighting different cultures and challenging the dominance of Western civilization through descriptions of humanity beyond established societal norms.
entries.significance: His literary contributions provide a way to examine human relationships and the natural world by looking past the superficiality found in contemporary modern civilization.

entries.title: Discovering Viral Links to Cancer and Immune System Disease
entries.overview: Scientists identified how specific viruses integrate into human cells to cause cervical cancer and the immune-weakening disease known as AIDS.
entries.background: Cellular health relies on genes regulating growth and death. When these functions fail, tumors can form. This process may occur when viral genes merge with a host's DNA.
entries.work: In 1983, Harald zur Hausen showed that certain papilloma viruses cause cervical cancer by incorporating their genes into human DNA. Separately, in the same year, Françoise Barré-Sinoussi and Luc Montagnier identified a retrovirus in patients with swollen lymph glands. This virus, named HIV, attacks lymphocytes, which are vital immune system cells.
entries.significance: These discoveries enabled new vaccine development for cervical cancer and provided the basis for much-improved treatment methods for those living with AIDS.

entries.title: Mediating International Disputes and Promoting Global Conflict Resolution
entries.overview: Martti Ahtisaari received this honor for his work resolving various international disputes across multiple continents during a career spanning over thirty years.
entries.background: Born in Viborg in 1937, Ahtisaari experienced displacement after the Soviet Union annexed the town during the 1939–1940 Winter War. He connected those childhood experiences with his later commitment to peace. His career included diplomatic service and Finland's presidency from 1994 to 2000.
entries.work: Ahtisaari became UN Commissioner for Namibia in 1977 and later made a major contribution to the independence process of 1989–1990. He mediated over Kosovo in 1999 and again during 2005–2007. After his presidency, he established the Crisis Management Initiative, which helped negotiate the 2005 agreement ending the long conflict in Indonesia's Aceh province.
entries.significance: His efforts focused on negotiating peace accords and managing crises to address long-standing violent struggles in different parts of the world.

entries.title: Two Ways Symmetry Can Break in Particle Physics
entries.overview: Yoichiro Nambu explained spontaneous symmetry breaking in particle physics. Makoto Kobayashi and Toshihide Maskawa explained a different kind of asymmetry in particle decays, requiring at least three families of quarks.
entries.background: A symmetry means that a transformation leaves the relevant physical description unchanged. Nature raises two distinct questions: how an underlying symmetry can be hidden in the state a system adopts, and why some processes differ when matter and antimatter are exchanged along with a mirror reflection.
entries.work: In 1960, Nambu developed a mathematical account of spontaneous symmetry breaking. This became a central idea in the Standard Model of particles and their interactions. In 1972, Kobayashi and Maskawa proposed a mechanism for the asymmetry observed in kaon decays. Their explanation required more quarks than were then known, organised into three families. Later discoveries and precision measurements supported that framework.
entries.significance: The prize recognised complementary advances in understanding subatomic matter. It distinguished a mechanism that hides an underlying symmetry from an explanation of symmetry violation in particular particle processes.

entries.title: Mapping the Atomic Structure of Cellular Protein Factories
entries.overview: Scientists identified how ribosomes translate genetic instructions into the protein chains necessary for an organism's vital life functions.
entries.background: Cells use ribosomes, large complexes of RNA and proteins, to read messenger RNA and assemble amino acids into protein chains. Revealing how these machines work required locating huge numbers of atoms within a complicated molecular structure.
entries.work: The laureates and their research groups used X-ray crystallography to determine detailed ribosome structures. Yonath began this difficult structural project in the 1970s; Ramakrishnan and Steitz led other major contributions. Their work revealed the architecture underlying protein production and showed how antibiotics attach to bacterial ribosomes.
entries.significance: The structures connected the ribosome's shape with its biological function. They also provided a basis for understanding how antibiotics interfere with bacterial protein production and for designing new medicines.

entries.title: Analyzing Economic Governance in Shared Resources and Organizations
entries.overview: Elinor Ostrom investigated how communities govern shared resources. Oliver Williamson examined why some economic transactions take place within firms rather than through markets, and how each arrangement handles conflicts.
entries.background: An influential view predicted that shared natural resources would be overused unless governments or private owners took control. Meanwhile, explaining economic activity mainly through markets left questions about why organisations exist and where their boundaries should lie.
entries.work: Ostrom's field studies found communities that successfully managed shared forests, pastures and fishing grounds by creating and enforcing rules. Her research showed that collective management can work under suitable conditions. Williamson's work in the early 1970s examined differences between market transactions and internal organisation. He explained why resolving certain conflicts within a firm can cost less than negotiating them through a market.
entries.significance: Together, these separate contributions broadened the study of economic governance. They challenged simple assumptions about shared resources and clarified why different arrangements suit different transactions.

entries.title: Depicting the Landscape of the Dispossessed Through Literature
entries.overview: In 2009, Herta Müller received this honor for using precise language and poetic elements to portray the lives of people facing displacement.
entries.background: Living in Romania as part of the German-speaking minority, Müller experienced life under the Ceaușescu regime. This era of communist rule created a climate of fear and alienation for vulnerable ethnic groups.
entries.work: Müller's prose and poetry explore the psychological effects of dictatorship and persecution. Dismissed as a translator after refusing to cooperate with the Securitate secret police, she became a teacher and author. Her debut, Niederungen, appeared in a censored Romanian edition in 1982, while uncensored copies circulated abroad. Precise, inventive imagery evokes how oppression can alter an individual's inner life and sense of belonging.
entries.significance: Her writing provides a detailed look at the vulnerability of individuals caught within oppressive political systems and the lasting mental traces left by living under a regime.

entries.title: How Telomeres Protect Chromosomes and the Function of Telomerase
entries.overview: Scientists identified how specialized DNA caps protect chromosome ends and discovered the enzyme responsible for building these protective structures.
entries.background: When cells divide, DNA molecules inside cell nuclei must be copied completely without damage. At the ends of chromosomes, protective caps called telomeres exist to prevent the genetic material from breaking down during this process.
entries.work: Blackburn identified a repeated DNA sequence at chromosome ends in the single-celled organism Tetrahymena; the sequence was reported in 1978. In experiments published in 1982, she and Szostak showed that this DNA protected artificial chromosomes introduced into yeast. The cross-species result revealed a broadly shared protective mechanism. In 1984, Greider and Blackburn detected the enzyme later named telomerase, which extends telomeric DNA.
entries.significance: The work explained both how chromosome ends are protected and how their specialised DNA can be maintained. It opened research into chromosome stability, cellular ageing and disease, rather than establishing a simple way to prevent ageing in people.

entries.title: Strengthening International Diplomacy and Global Cooperation Between Peoples
entries.overview: The 2009 prize was given to Barack H. Obama for his attempts to improve worldwide diplomatic relations and support a world without nuclear weapons.
entries.background: Prior to receiving the award, Barack H. Obama advocated for communication across ethnic, religious, and political boundaries. During his early presidency, he sought a fresh start between the West and the Muslim world based on mutual respect.
entries.work: The Nobel Committee highlighted Obama's early calls for dialogue across national and religious divides, nuclear disarmament, and cooperation on global challenges. He had initiated a plan to withdraw U.S. forces from Iraq and supported international action on climate change. The committee also praised his advocacy of human rights and democracy. These were the grounds of an award made near the beginning of his presidency, before a long record of outcomes could be assessed.
entries.significance: The award highlighted his early efforts to foster cooperation between different populations and his commitment to addressing major global challenges like climate change and nuclear disarmament.

entries.title: Developments in Optical Fibers and Digital Image Sensors
entries.overview: These discoveries enabled rapid long-distance data transmission and the creation of digital images through light-sensitive semiconductor circuits.
entries.background: Glass fibres could guide light, but early fibres lost too much of it for long-distance telecommunications. A separate challenge was converting a pattern of light into electrical information that could be stored and processed as an image.
entries.work: In the 1960s, Charles Kao showed that sufficiently pure glass could reduce transmission losses enough to make long-distance fibre communication practical. His analysis guided the development of suitable fibres. In 1969, Willard Boyle and George Smith conceived the charge-coupled device, initially as an electronic memory. In imaging applications, light creates electrical charge in a grid of cells; that charge is transferred and read out to reconstruct the image.
entries.significance: Kao's work helped establish optical telecommunications. The CCD became a major technology for digital photography and scientific imaging, showing how semiconductor circuits could record light electronically.

entries.title: Developing Methods for Joining Carbon Atoms via Palladium Catalysis
entries.overview: Scientists created new ways to link carbon atoms together using palladium as a catalyst to synthesize various organic compounds.
entries.background: Organic substances, which are many chemical compounds containing carbon, are abundant in nature. Creating these substances through chemical methods is vital for both scientific research and industrial production processes.
entries.work: In the late 1960s, Richard Heck developed reactions to bind carbon atoms. During the mid-1970s, Ei-ichi Negishi developed similar carbon-linking reactions. By the end of the 1970s, Akira Suzuki also developed these coupling methods. All three used palladium as a catalyst to facilitate these cross couplings without the metal becoming part of the final organic product.
entries.significance: These individual advancements provided new chemical tools for synthesizing complex organic substances needed in scientific and industrial applications.

entries.title: Analyzing Markets with Search Frictions and Labor Impediments
entries.overview: This research examines how difficulties in finding matches between buyers and sellers influence economic outcomes like wages, unemployment levels, and job vacancies.
entries.background: In many markets, employers and job seekers do not connect instantly. This search process consumes time and resources, creating frictions that prevent perfectly efficient market results.
entries.work: Peter Diamond developed a theoretical framework for searching markets. Dale Mortensen and Christopher Pissarides created theories specifically applying these concepts to the labor market. Their models demonstrate how economic policies and regulations influence wages and vacancies. These mathematical frameworks also extend to analyzing other sectors, such as housing markets.
entries.significance: These models provide tools to understand how various economic policies and regulations impact unemployment rates and the movement of workers and goods.

entries.title: Mapping Power and Individual Resistance Through Narrative Fiction
entries.overview: Mario Vargas Llosa received this award for his writing that explores how people resist, revolt, or face defeat within various power structures.
entries.background: During the 1960s, a period of rapid development in Latin American literature known as El Boom occurred. This era featured significant creative growth across the continent's literary traditions.
entries.work: Mario Vargas Llosa produced an extensive body of work including novels, plays, essays, and journalism. His writing utilizes rich language across diverse genres, such as historical novels, thrillers, and autobiographical books. These narratives focus on mapping structures of power and depicting the struggles of individuals. While he also engaged in political activity as a presidential candidate in 1990, his primary contribution lies in these varied literary forms.
entries.significance: His literary contributions provide detailed imagery regarding the relationship between human beings and the social forces that govern their lives.

entries.title: Development of the Medical Process Known as In Vitro Fertilization
entries.overview: Robert Edwards developed human in vitro fertilisation, or IVF: fertilising an egg in laboratory culture, allowing early embryo development, and transferring an embryo into the uterus.
entries.background: Infertility can arise for several reasons, including blocked Fallopian tubes that prevent eggs and sperm from meeting. IVF offered a route around some of these barriers, but required understanding egg maturation, fertilisation and the conditions needed for early development.
entries.work: Edwards investigated how human eggs mature and how sperm become capable of fertilisation. Working with gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe, he combined laboratory research with techniques for collecting mature eggs from ovaries. Fertilisation took place in culture dishes, despite the familiar phrase test-tube baby. In 1978, Louise Brown became the first child born following IVF. The work required successful embryo transfer as well as fertilisation outside the body.
entries.significance: The achievement established an effective treatment approach for many forms of infertility and transformed reproductive medicine. It enabled pregnancies that would otherwise have been difficult or impossible, without guaranteeing success for every patient.

entries.title: The Non-violent Struggle for Human Rights in China
entries.overview: This award honors the long-term, peaceful efforts of an individual to promote basic civil liberties and democratic reforms within the Chinese political system.
entries.background: In 1989, student protests occurred in Tiananmen Square. Following these events, China maintained a one-party system. Liu Xiaobo later used his background in literature and philosophy to advocate for constitutional freedoms regarding speech, assembly, and press.
entries.work: After earning a doctorate in 1988, Liu participated in the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and was imprisoned. He later spent three years in a labour camp for criticising the one-party system. In 2008, he co-authored Charter 08, a manifesto calling for gradual democratic reform. Arrested that December, he received an eleven-year prison sentence in 2009. He rejected the accusation that peaceful political opposition amounted to undermining the state.
entries.significance: The work highlighted demands for Chinese authorities to uphold Article 35 of their own constitution, which guarantees citizens rights such as freedom of speech and association.

entries.title: Experiments Regarding the Two-Dimensional Material Graphene
entries.overview: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov demonstrated that graphene—a sheet of carbon atoms only one atom thick—could be isolated and studied experimentally, opening a new field of materials research.
entries.background: Graphite is built from layers of carbon arranged in hexagonal patterns. The challenge was obtaining and investigating an individual layer. Such an extremely thin crystal raised questions about stability and about how electrons would behave within it.
entries.work: In 2004, Geim and Novoselov reported experiments on graphene. Their work made this two-dimensional material available for exploring unusual physical behaviour. Graphene combines strength with very small thickness, conducts heat and electricity well, and transmits most visible light. Its tightly connected atomic sheet also acts as a barrier to gases such as helium; describing it as dense refers to that barrier, rather than to a heavy bulk material.
entries.significance: Graphene offered both a test bed for fundamental physics and possibilities for new electronic devices and materials. The prize recognised experimental access to its properties, rather than promising that every proposed application would become practical.

entries.title: Discovering Order Without Repetition in Quasicrystals
entries.overview: Dan Shechtman discovered an ordered atomic structure that did not repeat periodically. The finding forced scientists to widen their definition of a crystal.
entries.background: Traditional crystallography treated a crystal as a regularly repeating arrangement of atoms. That rule limits the rotational symmetries a crystal can display. An ordered diffraction pattern with a forbidden symmetry therefore appeared to contradict established theory.
entries.work: In April 1982, while visiting the U.S. National Bureau of Standards, Shechtman examined a rapidly cooled metal alloy using an electron microscope. Its electron diffraction pattern showed an arrangement that could not be explained by an ordinary repeating crystal. He checked the observation rather than dismissing it as an error. The resulting discovery established quasicrystals: solids with long-range order but without a periodically repeated atomic unit.
entries.significance: Quasicrystals showed that order does not require periodic repetition. The discovery changed how solid structures are classified and opened research connecting crystallography, materials science and mathematical descriptions of nonperiodic patterns.

entries.title: Analyzing Cause and Effect Within the Macroeconomy
entries.overview: This research provides methods for studying how unexpected events and changes in economic policy influence various aspects of a nation's overall economy.
entries.background: Economists sought to understand how fluctuations in interest rates, taxes, and oil prices impact production, unemployment, inflation, and investment. This involves examining how different policy shifts and sudden economic shocks trigger specific consequences.
entries.work: In 2011, Thomas J. Sargent and Christopher A. Sims were recognized for empirical research on macroeconomical cause and effect. Sargent developed techniques to analyze how permanent policy restructurings affect the economy and how businesses and households adjust expectations. Separately, Sims created a method to study how central bank interest rate changes influence inflation and growth, alongside analyzing the economic impact of rising oil prices.
entries.significance: These methods allow researchers to examine the relationship between specific economic policies and their resulting effects on key indicators like inflation, investment, and production levels.

entries.title: Poetic Imagery and Reality in the Work of Tomas Tranströmer
entries.overview: Tomas Tranströmer used brief, clear images to provide new ways of perceiving reality through his poetry.
entries.background: Starting in the 1950s, this writer utilized a style rooted in everyday life. His creative approach focused on simplicity and often drew inspiration from both musical elements and the natural world.
entries.work: The poet's writing features original and sharp imagery. Following a stroke in 1990 that affected his speech, his later poems transitioned into an even more condensed and concentrated format. This technique allows readers to focus closely on the text. His verse maintains its connection to ordinary existence while using translucent descriptions to reveal deeper aspects of the surrounding world.
entries.significance: His poetic method enables readers to find wonder within mundane settings by utilizing precise, concentrated imagery to access a fresh perspective on reality.

entries.title: Understanding How Immune Systems Detect and Respond to Microorganisms
entries.overview: Scientists identified how specific receptors detect germs and how certain cells trigger the body's natural defenses against bacteria and viruses.
entries.background: The immune system utilizes two distinct lines of defense, known as innate and adaptive immunity. Before these discoveries, the specific mechanisms by which the body recognizes invading microorganisms remained unclear.
entries.work: Steinman identified dendritic cells in 1973 and, in subsequent studies, showed their exceptional ability to activate T cells. Hoffmann's 1996 experiments showed that the Toll gene was essential for fruit flies to defend themselves against fungal infection. In 1998, Beutler's work with mice identified a related receptor system needed to respond to bacterial lipopolysaccharide. The discoveries connected recognition of microbial signals with the activation of immune defences.
entries.significance: These findings revealed how receptors identify pathogens to activate innate immunity and how dendritic cells initiate adaptive immune responses.

entries.title: Women's Rights and Participation in Building Peace
entries.overview: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, Leymah Gbowee and Tawakkol Karman were honoured for nonviolent work connecting women's safety and political participation with the pursuit of peace.
entries.background: War and repression can expose women to violence while excluding them from decisions about their country's future. The committee emphasised that lasting peace requires women to participate in political life and peace processes on equal terms.
entries.work: Gbowee organised women across Christian and Muslim communities in Liberia, mobilising public pressure to end the war and later encouraging participation in elections. Sirleaf won Liberia's 2005 presidential election and took office in 2006 as Africa's first democratically elected woman president. The committee credited her with consolidating peace and strengthening women's position. In Yemen, journalist Karman founded Women Journalists without Chains and campaigned for freedom of expression, democracy and women's rights, becoming a prominent figure during the 2011 Arab Spring.
entries.significance: The three recipients represented different forms of public action: grassroots organising, national leadership and journalism. The award stressed women's agency in shaping peace, rather than viewing them only as people needing protection during conflict.

entries.title: Distant Supernovae Reveal Accelerating Cosmic Expansion
entries.overview: Two independent teams found evidence that the expansion of the universe had begun accelerating, overturning the expectation that gravity would be slowing it down.
entries.background: To investigate expansion history, astronomers needed both distances and redshifts. Type Ia supernovae provide a way to estimate distances from their brightness, while redshift records how much the expanding universe has stretched their light.
entries.work: Saul Perlmutter led the Supernova Cosmology Project. Brian Schmidt led the High-z Supernova Search Team, in which Adam Riess played a central role. In 1998, the teams reported that distant supernovae were fainter than expected in a decelerating universe. Comparing brightness with redshift indicated that these explosions were farther away than the expected expansion history allowed. The result pointed to cosmic acceleration, rather than simply tracking individual stars moving through space.
entries.significance: The finding transformed cosmology and focused attention on whatever drives accelerated expansion, commonly described as dark energy. It established a major observational constraint while leaving the underlying cause open to investigation.

entries.title: Revealing How Cell Receptors Receive and Relay Signals
entries.overview: Robert Lefkowitz and Brian Kobilka explained the nature and workings of G-protein-coupled receptors, a large family of proteins that help cells respond to chemical signals.
entries.background: Hormones such as adrenaline can change a cell's behaviour without entering it. Researchers therefore suspected that cell surfaces contained receptors, but identifying these scarce proteins and understanding how they transmitted a signal was difficult.
entries.work: Beginning in 1968, Lefkowitz used radioactive tracers to investigate hormone receptors. His research helped identify and isolate the beta-adrenergic receptor. In the 1980s, Kobilka identified the gene encoding this receptor. Its similarity to a light-sensitive receptor in the eye helped reveal a much larger family. In 2011, Kobilka and colleagues captured the receptor in an activated complex, showing how it connects an outside signal to machinery inside the cell.
entries.significance: The work connected molecular structure with cellular communication. These receptors participate in many physiological responses and are major targets for medicines, making their mechanisms important for both basic biology and drug development.

entries.title: Developing Stable Matching Theory and Practical Market Design
entries.overview: Lloyd Shapley developed theories of stable matching, and Alvin Roth used matching theory to help design practical markets. Stability means no pair would both prefer to leave their assigned matches for one another.
entries.background: Finding optimal ways to bring different players together is a fundamental economic problem. Achieving stability means ensuring that no two agents would choose one another over their current assigned partners.
entries.work: From the 1960s, Lloyd Shapley used Cooperative Game Theory to study various matching methods and identify ways to achieve stability. Starting in the 1980s, Alvin Roth applied these theoretical results to observe how markets function. Through laboratory experiments and empirical studies, Roth showed that stability is vital for successful matching. He also created systems for pairing organ donors with patients, school children with schools, and doctors with hospitals.
entries.significance: The research provides a framework for designing organized systems to match participants in complex real-world markets.

entries.title: Merging Folk Tales and History Through Hallucinatory Realism
entries.overview: The 2012 prize honored an author for using hallucinatory realism to blend traditional oral stories, historical events, and modern social problems.
entries.background: Growing up in a farming family in Shandong Province, Mo Yan worked as a cattle herder before joining the army. His early writing followed the literary rules of the ruling regime, but he later developed more independent storytelling methods.
entries.work: Mo Yan writes novels, essays and short stories. He draws on older Chinese literature and oral traditions to address contemporary issues. His works include Red Sorghum, The Garlic Ballads and Life and Death Are Wearing Me Out. Blending the everyday with fantastic elements, his narrative style brings folk traditions, historical experience and modern social tensions into the same imaginative world.
entries.significance: Mo Yan became an internationally recognized author by creating a unique way to connect China's folk history with the realities of modern society.

entries.title: Reprogramming Mature Cells Back to an Immature State
entries.overview: Scientists discovered that specialized adult cells can be reverted to a versatile state where they can develop into many different cell types.
entries.background: Early biological thought held that once cells became specialized during development, they could not return to their original, immature form. This belief suggested the process of cellular differentiation was one-way and permanent.
entries.work: In 1962, Gurdon replaced the nucleus of a frog egg with the nucleus from a tadpole intestinal cell. The resulting development showed that a specialised cell's nucleus retained the instructions needed to produce other cell types. In 2006, Yamanaka identified a small set of genes whose activity could reprogramme mouse skin cells into pluripotent stem cells, capable of developing into different kinds of body cells.
entries.significance: The discoveries showed that cellular specialisation need not be irreversible. Nuclear transfer and gene-based reprogramming provided different ways to investigate how cell identity is maintained and changed, opening new approaches to studying development and disease.

entries.title: The European Union's Role in Promoting Peace and Democracy
entries.overview: The European Union received the prize for its contribution to peace, reconciliation, democracy and human rights through more than six decades of European cooperation.
entries.background: European integration developed after devastating wars between neighbouring countries. Later challenges included the division of Europe during the Cold War, democratic transitions in southern Europe, and violent conflicts following Yugoslavia's breakup.
entries.work: The Nobel Committee highlighted reconciliation between France and Germany and the strengthening of democracy in Greece, Spain and Portugal. It also pointed to enlargement after the Cold War, which brought Central and Eastern European countries into the union. In the Balkans, the committee credited European integration with encouraging reconciliation after war. Its assessment emphasised the EU's stabilising role during economic hardship and social unrest.
entries.significance: The award recognised a long institutional process of replacing rivalry with cooperation. Its rationale was that shared institutions and democratic commitments had helped reduce the risk of renewed conflict among member states. This was the committee's assessment of the union's contribution, rather than a claim that every European conflict had been resolved.

entries.title: Controlling and Measuring Individual Quantum Systems
entries.overview: Serge Haroche and David Wineland independently developed methods for investigating individual quantum systems while preserving the delicate quantum behaviour they wanted to study.
entries.background: Quantum theory already explained many experiments, but precise control of a single particle posed a special difficulty. Interaction with its surroundings or with a measuring device can destroy the quantum properties under investigation. Researchers needed ways to isolate particles and probe them carefully.
entries.work: Wineland used electric fields to trap charged atoms, or ions, and light to cool, control and measure them. Haroche used the complementary approach: trapping photons between highly reflective mirrors and sending atoms through the cavity to investigate the light. Their experiments allowed researchers to manipulate individual systems and examine the interaction between matter and light with exceptional control.
entries.significance: The techniques made fragile quantum states experimentally accessible and supported work toward quantum information processing and more precise clocks. The achievement was controlled measurement of individual systems, extending an already experimental science into a previously difficult regime.

entries.title: Developing Multiscale Computer Models for Complex Chemical Systems
entries.overview: Scientists created computer methods to predict how molecules change during chemical reactions by merging two different types of physics calculations.
entries.background: Predicting chemical reactions is difficult because atoms rearrange into new molecules. While advanced quantum mechanics can describe reaction sites, calculating entire large molecules requires simpler, less complex classical mechanics approach.
entries.work: In the 1970s, Martin Karplus, Michael Levitt, and Arieh Warshel developed multiscale models for computers. Their method combined advanced quantum mechanics calculations for specific reaction sites with simpler classical mechanics for the remaining parts of a molecule. This allowed researchers to use computational power to simulate how atoms move and change places during chemical processes.
entries.significance: This work enabled the use of computers to calculate the paths of chemical reactions by applying different physical rules to different parts of a molecular system.

entries.title: Empirical Analysis of Asset Price Movements and Market Efficiency
entries.overview: Eugene Fama, Lars Peter Hansen and Robert Shiller developed evidence and methods for understanding asset prices, including why short-term changes are hard to predict and what longer-term patterns reveal.
entries.background: Prices respond to information, expectations and risk. Explaining their movement requires more than observing that they rise or fall: economists need statistical tests that distinguish competing accounts of how markets work.
entries.work: Beginning in the 1960s, Fama and collaborators found rapid responses to new information and little short-term predictability. Shiller's work in the early 1980s showed price fluctuations too large for a simple dividend-based model and identified longer-horizon predictability. Hansen developed the Generalized Method of Moments in 1982, providing a powerful way to test economic models against data. His applications revealed difficulties for standard asset-pricing theories.
entries.significance: Their separate contributions established central tools and questions in empirical finance. Fama's results influenced index investing; Shiller stimulated behavioural explanations; Hansen strengthened model testing. The prize recognised a research programme, rather than a reliable formula for predicting any particular future price.

entries.title: Mastery of the Contemporary Short Story Form
entries.overview: Alice Munro received this prize for her skill in writing short stories that capture complex human experiences and deep moral struggles.
entries.background: Growing up in small Canadian towns, Munro began writing during her teenage years. She later worked as a library clerk and bookstore owner before focusing entirely on her literary career starting in the late 1960s.
entries.work: Munro focuses almost exclusively on the short story genre. Her narratives use small-town settings to explore themes of moral conflict, relationship difficulties, and the connection between memory and reality. Using subtle techniques, she demonstrates how minor events can significantly alter a person's life. She manages to fit the intense complexity usually found in novels into only a few pages of text.
entries.significance: Her writing shows that brief stories can contain epic depth, effectively illustrating the lasting weight of seemingly insignificant moments through nuanced storytelling.

entries.title: Discovering How Cells Move Molecules Using Vesicle Transport Systems
entries.overview: Scientists identified the internal machinery that regulates vesicle traffic, which is a major transport system used by cells to move various molecules.
entries.background: Cells produce many different molecules that must reach specific locations. To travel, these substances are grouped into tiny sac-like structures called vesicles. These sacs carry materials internally and transmit signals from the cell surface to other cells.
entries.work: During the 1970s, Schekman studied yeast cells with transport defects and identified genes needed for different steps of vesicle traffic. In the 1980s and 1990s, Rothman explained how vesicles recognise and fuse with the appropriate target membranes. Südhof's studies of nerve cells during the 1990s revealed how vesicles are prepared for the precisely timed release of signalling molecules.
entries.significance: These discoveries revealed how the machinery regulating vesicle traffic functions to ensure molecules and signals arrive at their proper cellular destinations.

entries.title: Efforts to Eliminate Chemical Weapons Through International Monitoring
entries.overview: The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons works to ensure that stockpiling and producing chemical weapons is stopped through global oversight.
entries.background: The Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993 established an international framework to prohibit chemical weapons and verify their destruction. Two decades later, chemical attacks during Syria's civil war gave the committee an additional reason to support the organisation's work.
entries.work: The organisation monitors compliance with the 1993 convention by performing inspections to verify rules are followed. It has successfully overseen the destruction of numerous stockpiles. While aiming for universal elimination, the group also pressures states that have not ratified the treaty. The Norwegian Nobel Committee noted that the United States and Russia had not yet destroyed their large chemical arsenals during this period.
entries.significance: The work serves as a potential template for other disarmament treaties by attempting to achieve the total removal of weapons of mass destruction.

entries.title: Explaining Particle Mass Through the Higgs Field
entries.overview: François Englert and Peter Higgs received the prize for a theoretical mechanism explaining how elementary particles acquire mass through interaction with a field present throughout space.
entries.background: A successful account of particle interactions had to explain why some elementary particles have mass while others, such as photons, do not. The mechanism allows an underlying symmetry of the equations to be hidden in the physical state of the field.
entries.work: In 1964, Englert and Robert Brout developed this idea independently of Higgs. A field could give mass to particles that interact with it; the Higgs boson is an excitation of that field, rather than a tiny object that distributes mass to other particles. In 2012, the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider discovered a new particle whose properties supported its identification as a Higgs boson.
entries.significance: The discovery supplied crucial evidence for a central component of the Standard Model. The prize joined a decades-old theoretical explanation with a major experimental confirmation, while further measurements continued to investigate the particle's detailed properties.

entries.title: Seeing Cellular Detail Beyond Conventional Light Microscopy
entries.overview: Eric Betzig, Stefan Hell and William Moerner developed approaches that use fluorescent molecules to resolve details too close together for conventional optical microscopy.
entries.background: Diffraction limits how sharply a traditional light microscope can distinguish neighbouring objects. The laureates overcame this practical barrier by controlling which molecules emit light, extracting more information than an image of all glowing molecules at once provides.
entries.work: Hell proposed stimulated emission depletion microscopy in 1994 and demonstrated the approach in 2000. One beam excites fluorescence while another suppresses it around a very small remaining region; scanning this region builds an image. Betzig and Moerner, working separately, laid foundations for single-molecule methods. These switch on only a sparse selection of fluorescent markers at a time, locate them, and combine repeated images. Betzig applied this approach in 2006.
entries.significance: Super-resolution microscopy brought molecular-scale organisation within reach of optical imaging, including studies in living cells. It lets scientists investigate where biological molecules are and how they behave, while distinguishing contributions that arose through different experimental routes.

entries.title: Analyzing Market Power and Regulation Through Economic Theory
entries.overview: Jean Tirole studied how companies with significant market influence affect society and developed methods for designing effective industrial regulations.
entries.background: When a small group of firms dominates a market without oversight, prices may rise unfairly and new competitors might be blocked from entering the industry.
entries.work: Since the mid-1980s, Jean Tirole has developed a coherent account of market power and regulation. Using game theory and related methods, he established a framework for designing rules suited to different circumstances. Applications ranging from banking to telecommunications showed why effective regulation depends on the particular information, incentives and competitive conditions within an industry.
entries.significance: His work provides a structured way to understand how to regulate powerful firms to prevent negative social consequences in different market environments.

entries.title: Exploring Memory and Life During the German Occupation
entries.overview: Patrick Modiano received this prize for using memory to recreate elusive human lives and reveal the realities of life under Nazi rule.
entries.background: During World War II, Paris was under German occupation. Modiano uses this historical setting to examine themes of identity, guilt, and oblivion within everyday urban environments.
entries.work: Since his 1968 debut, Patrick Modiano has written stories centered on the city of Paris. He draws from interviews, newspaper articles, personal notes, and his own experiences to investigate difficult questions. His writing focuses on uncovering how people lived through the occupation, using the art of memory to bring ungraspable destinies to light through grounded, historical narratives.
entries.significance: His literary work serves to uncover the life-world of the German occupation, focusing on the complex intersections of history and individual human experience.

entries.title: Discovering the Brain's Internal Navigation and Positioning System
entries.overview: Researchers identified specific brain cells that act as a biological GPS, allowing humans and animals to understand their physical location and navigate through space.
entries.background: Understanding how living beings orient themselves in their surroundings is vital for survival. Scientists sought to uncover the biological mechanisms within the brain that enable creatures to track movement and find paths between different locations.
entries.work: In 1971, O'Keefe recorded nerve-cell activity while rats moved around a room. Particular hippocampal cells fired at particular locations, providing a kind of internal map. In 2005, May-Britt and Edvard Moser identified grid cells in a nearby brain region. Each cell became active at multiple locations forming a hexagonal grid across the environment. Their subsequent work explored how these and other cell types cooperate in navigation.
entries.significance: These discoveries revealed the existence of specific cells that constitute a functional positioning system within the brain's center.

entries.title: Global Struggles For Children's Rights And Educational Access
entries.overview: Two activists were recognized for their distinct efforts to protect young people from exploitation and ensure every child can attend school.
entries.background: In the Swat Valley, the Taliban movement began destroying girls' schools in 2008. Meanwhile, many children faced forced labor and slavery for economic profit through various exploitative systems.
entries.work: Yousafzai's diary for BBC Urdu in 2009 described life under Taliban rule and defended girls' education. She survived a Taliban gunman's attack in 2012 and continued campaigning, including a speech at the United Nations in 2013. Satyarthi founded the Save the Childhood Movement and GoodWeave, which certifies carpets made without child labour. By 2014, he and colleagues had helped free 83,000 children from slavery. He also led a worldwide march against child labour in 1998.
entries.significance: The march helped spur an International Labour Organisation convention against child exploitation and hazardous work. Yousafzai's advocacy brought international attention to girls' education. Their separate campaigns connected children's freedom from exploitation with access to schooling.

entries.title: Developing Efficient Blue Light Emitting Diodes Using Gallium Nitride
entries.overview: Researchers created efficient blue light-emitting diodes (LEDs) by utilizing a specific semiconductor material, which allows for the production of bright white light.
entries.background: Red and green LEDs existed before efficient blue versions became available. Blue light was the missing component for practical white LED lighting, whether combined with other coloured LEDs or used to excite a phosphor that converts some of it into other colours.
entries.work: During the 1980s and 1990s, Akasaki and Amano worked together at Nagoya University while Nakamura pursued a separate programme at Nichia. They overcame difficult problems in using gallium nitride semiconductors to make efficient blue LEDs. The resulting devices made bright white LED lamps practical, including designs that combine a blue LED with a light-converting phosphor.
entries.significance: This invention enabled the creation of bright, energy-saving white light sources, changing how light is produced for various uses.

entries.title: The Molecular Systems That Repair DNA
entries.overview: Tomas Lindahl, Paul Modrich and Aziz Sancar explained different repair mechanisms that maintain genetic information despite chemical damage and errors during DNA copying.
entries.background: DNA is a durable store of information, but it is not chemically unchanging. Its components can deteriorate spontaneously, ultraviolet light can damage it, and replication can insert mismatched bases. Cells therefore need repair systems that recognise different kinds of problems.
entries.work: Lindahl's research from the 1970s revealed enzymes involved in removing and replacing damaged DNA components. Sancar worked out how proteins repair damage such as that caused by ultraviolet light. Modrich investigated mismatch repair, which corrects copying errors. His bacterial studies showed how methylation helps distinguish the original strand from the strand needing correction. In 1989, his group reconstructed that repair process using purified components.
entries.significance: The discoveries revealed DNA maintenance as an active collection of molecular processes. They helped explain why defects in repair can contribute to cancer and informed investigations of ageing and possible treatments, while distinguishing several different pathways rather than a single universal repair mechanism.

entries.title: Analyzing Consumption Patterns and Their Link to Poverty and Welfare
entries.overview: Angus Deaton investigated how people spend money on goods and services, exploring the connections between individual consumption habits and broader societal economic development.
entries.background: Understanding how spending relates to income and savings is necessary for creating effective economic policies. This research focuses on how price changes and income levels influence the way individuals purchase essential products and services.
entries.work: After earning his doctorate in 1974, Angus Deaton researched how consumption depends on prices and its relationship to savings. He demonstrated that data regarding what people consume can be used as a tool to study welfare, poverty levels, and economic development. His work examines the specific ways individual spending patterns reflect the larger economic health of a society.
entries.significance: Deaton's analysis provides methods to use consumption data to evaluate poverty and human welfare, offering a way to measure economic progress through actual spending behavior.

entries.title: Documentary Novels Exploring Life Within the Soviet Union and Belarus
entries.overview: Svetlana Alexievich won this prize for creating a collection of many different perspectives regarding human suffering and bravery in modern history.
entries.background: Growing up in Belarus, Alexievich studied journalism in Minsk. Her professional work criticizing political regimes in the Soviet Union and later Belarus caused her to live frequently in several European countries.
entries.work: In her documentary novels, Alexievich uses interviews to build a collage of various individual voices. This technique blurs the line between journalistic reporting and fiction. Through her five-part series, Voices of Utopia, she depicts personal experiences during and after the Soviet Union era. Her writing focuses on how individuals lived through these major political shifts.
entries.significance: Her books serve as a monument to courage by capturing the diverse, personal accounts of people living under specific political systems.

entries.title: New Therapies for Parasitic Infections and Malaria
entries.overview: Researchers identified new ways to treat diseases caused by worms and single-cell parasites, including malaria, river blindness, and elephantiasis.
entries.background: Many infectious diseases are spread by insects. These include malaria, which causes high fevers, as well as river blindness and lymphatic filariasis, which cause corneal damage and chronic swelling.
entries.work: Ōmura isolated and cultured soil bacteria with promising biological activity. Campbell tested these cultures and found a substance effective against parasites. The active agent, avermectin, was purified and chemically modified to produce ivermectin, which became important against river blindness and lymphatic filariasis. Separately, during the 1970s, Tu investigated traditional remedies and extracted artemisinin from sweet wormwood. This compound acts against malaria parasites.
entries.significance: These discoveries provided effective treatments for roundworm-related infections and established drugs based on artemisinin that have improved health and survival for millions.

entries.title: Civil Society Mediation During Tunisia's Democratic Transition
entries.overview: Tunisia's National Dialogue Quartet was recognised for helping political opponents find a peaceful route through a crisis threatening the democratic transition after the 2011 revolution.
entries.background: Political assassinations and social unrest brought the transition close to collapse in 2013. The Quartet formed that summer to mediate among competing forces, providing a channel for negotiation when ordinary political processes were failing.
entries.work: Its four members were the Tunisian General Labour Union, the Tunisian Confederation of Industry, Trade and Handicrafts, the Tunisian Human Rights League and the Tunisian Order of Lawyers. Together they brought labour, business, human-rights and legal organisations into the mediation effort. Their dialogue helped Islamist and secular movements cooperate and contributed to a constitutional settlement that made parliamentary and presidential elections possible.
entries.significance: The committee credited the Quartet's collective role in reducing confrontation and advancing pluralistic government. The prize highlighted civil society's capacity to support political compromise across deep divisions. Its rationale concerned achievements in that transition, rather than a guarantee that Tunisia's subsequent political development would remain democratic.

entries.title: Evidence of Mass Through Neutrino Type Switching
entries.overview: Scientists discovered that neutrinos change between three different types, a process which proves these tiny particles possess physical mass.
entries.background: Modern physics relies on the Standard Model, which historically assumed that the three types of elusive neutrinos were massless particles. This fundamental scientific framework required a significant update after new experimental evidence emerged.
entries.work: In 1998, the Super-Kamiokande collaboration, with Kajita in a leading role, reported evidence that neutrinos produced in the atmosphere changed type on their way to its underground detector in Japan. The Sudbury Neutrino Observatory collaboration, led by McDonald, studied neutrinos from the Sun in Canada. Its first results in 2001 showed that missing electron neutrinos had changed into other types. Together, these experiments established neutrino transformation and its implication that neutrinos are not all massless.
entries.significance: These findings showed that the Standard Model is incomplete because it lacks the mass property of neutrinos, necessitating revisions to existing physical theories.

entries.title: Designing and Synthesizing Tiny Molecular Machines
entries.overview: Scientists created tiny chemical structures where individual parts move against each other to act as the world's smallest machines.
entries.background: To build a functioning machine, components must possess the ability to move relative to one another. This work focused on using molecules as the fundamental building blocks for such mechanical movements.
entries.work: In 1983, Sauvage developed a way to link two molecular rings into a catenane, allowing them to move relative to each other. In 1991, Stoddart developed a rotaxane with a molecular ring threaded onto an axle-like structure. In 1999, Feringa constructed a molecular motor that rotated in one direction through cycles of light-driven change and thermal relaxation. The motion required energy input, rather than occurring perpetually on its own.
entries.significance: The work established building blocks for controlling molecular motion. Researchers can use these principles to investigate new materials, sensors and possible energy-storage systems, although particular applications require further development.

entries.title: Economic Theories Regarding Incomplete Contracts and Agent Monitoring
entries.overview: This research examines how legal agreements function when parties cannot predict every future event or fully observe each other's specific actions.
entries.background: In any economy, contracts help people cooperate and manage uncertainty. However, it is often impossible to write a document that covers every possible future situation or tracks every movement of a worker.
entries.work: During the late 1970s, Bengt Holmström studied how company owners should structure agreements for executives when their actions are hard to monitor. In the mid-1980s, Oliver Hart created theories regarding incomplete contracts, focusing on how decision-making rights should be assigned when a contract cannot specify every potential eventuality.
entries.significance: These studies provided frameworks used in designing institutional structures, creating laws, and managing the governance of modern corporations.

entries.title: New Poetic Expressions Within The American Song Tradition
entries.overview: Bob Dylan received the 2016 literature prize for creating new poetic expression within the American song tradition, drawing on folk music and a range of literary influences.
entries.background: Bob Dylan moved to New York City in 1961. His songwriting draws from modernism and beatnik poetry influences, building upon a long-standing history of American folk music traditions.
entries.work: Since his 1962 debut, Bob Dylan has composed lyrics involving themes of religion, love, and political protest. His writing utilizes polished rhymes and surreal imagery to convey meaning. While focusing on music and lyrics, he also produced prose works like Chronicles. His songwriting often incorporates elements from his personal life and experiences with social struggles into the musical compositions he performs.
entries.significance: Dylan's work introduced unique poetic textures to popular song formats, blending traditional folk roots with modern literary influences and imagery.

entries.title: Discoveries Regarding How Cells Process Components for Reuse
entries.overview: Yoshinori Ohsumi identified genes and mechanisms behind autophagy, the process by which cells break down and recycle some of their own components.
entries.background: Autophagy was already known, but its molecular machinery remained poorly understood. Cells deliver material for degradation to specialised compartments: lysosomes in animal cells and the vacuole in yeast. Recycling becomes especially important when nutrients are scarce.
entries.work: In the early 1990s, Ohsumi designed experiments that made autophagy visible in yeast. By studying yeast strains in which the process failed, he identified genes required for it and investigated the steps they control. This experimental approach turned a difficult-to-observe cellular process into one that could be analysed genetically and mechanistically.
entries.significance: His findings established a foundation for understanding how cells maintain themselves and respond to nutrient shortages and infection. They also opened investigations into the involvement of autophagy in hereditary disorders, neurological disease and cancer. The prize recognised the mechanisms of cellular recycling, rather than the first observation that cells can digest their own material.

entries.title: Efforts to End Longstanding Civil War in Colombia
entries.overview: Juan Manuel Santos led negotiations to terminate a conflict between the Colombian government and Marxist guerrillas that lasted over five decades.
entries.background: For fifty-two years, Colombia experienced intense warfare involving rebels, paramilitary groups, and the state. This struggle resulted in hundreds of thousands of deaths, mostly civilians, and displaced millions of people from their homes.
entries.work: After becoming president in 2010, Santos pursued a negotiated settlement. Formal talks with FARC began in 2012 and produced an agreement in August 2016. Voters narrowly rejected it in a referendum, after which Santos sought a broad dialogue to preserve the process. The Nobel announcement recognised his efforts amid that uncertainty. A revised agreement was subsequently signed in November and ratified by Congress, with strong emphasis on the rights and participation of victims.
entries.significance: The process sought to replace decades of armed violence with a political settlement that included the voices of those impacted by the war.

entries.title: Topological Discoveries Regarding Phases of Matter
entries.overview: Researchers identified how mathematical topology explains how matter changes states and exists in unusual phases when subjected to extremely low temperatures.
entries.background: Matter typically exists as solids, liquids, or gases. However, at very cold temperatures, substances can enter unique states like superconductivity or superfluidity, which require new descriptions.
entries.work: In the early 1970s, David Thouless and Michael Kosterlitz applied topology to describe phase transitions in thin layers. Later, Thouless explained the quantum Hall effect regarding electrical conductivity shifts. During the 1980s, Duncan Haldane used these mathematical concepts to explain the magnetic properties found in specific chains of atoms.
entries.significance: These theoretical discoveries provided a way to understand topological phases and transitions, potentially aiding future developments in electronic components and new materials.

entries.title: Developing Methods for High Resolution Imaging of Biological Molecules
entries.overview: Jacques Dubochet, Joachim Frank and Richard Henderson developed methods that made cryo-electron microscopy a powerful way to determine the structures of biological molecules preserved in frozen water.
entries.background: Electron microscopes use electron beams instead of light to image tiny molecules. However, these machines operate in a vacuum where water evaporates, and the electron beams themselves can destroy biological structures.
entries.work: In the early 1980s, Dubochet developed rapid freezing that traps molecules in water without forming distorting ice crystals. Between 1975 and 1986, Frank developed methods for combining faint two-dimensional images into three-dimensional reconstructions. Henderson showed how low electron doses and mathematical analysis could limit radiation damage while recovering structural detail. In 1990, he produced a detailed three-dimensional molecular structure using electron microscopy.
entries.significance: These techniques allow for high-resolution structure determination of biomolecules, providing knowledge useful for the development of various pharmaceuticals.

entries.title: Analyzing How Human Psychology Influences Economic Choices and Markets
entries.overview: Richard Thaler explored how psychological traits, such as limited self-control and feelings of fairness, affect the way individuals make financial decisions.
entries.background: Many economic models assume that people make consistently rational decisions. Thaler investigated systematic ways actual choices depart from that assumption, including the effects of fairness, limited rationality and difficulty exercising self-control.
entries.work: Richard Thaler applied psychological insights to analyze economic decision-making. His research focused on three specific areas: why people do not always act completely rationally, how notions of fairness and reasonableness play a role, and the effects of a lack of self-control. By examining these human traits, he investigated how individual choices influence broader market functions.
entries.significance: These findings provided new perspectives for economic research and policy by incorporating real-world psychological factors into the study of financial behavior.

entries.title: Literary Achievements in Novels of Emotional Depth and Restraint
entries.overview: Kazuo Ishiguro received this honor for writing novels that explore the hidden gaps within our perceived connections to the world through powerful emotional storytelling.
entries.background: Growing up in a Japanese family residing in Great Britain influenced the perspectives found in his writing. His earlier stories were set in Japan, while later narratives explored diverse genres like science fiction and fantasy.
entries.work: In 1989, Ishiguro published The Remains of the Day, focusing on an English butler's feelings for a housekeeper during the World War II era. His prose utilizes restrained language to depict dramatic events. His various works frequently examine themes involving lifelong deception, the passage of time, and memory, uncovering deep emotional truths beneath surface-level interactions.
entries.significance: Ishiguro’s writing uses controlled linguistic styles to reveal the underlying instability in human relationships and our sense of connection to the surrounding world.

entries.title: How genes and proteins keep a daily biological clock
entries.overview: Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash and Michael Young uncovered molecular feedback mechanisms that let organisms maintain roughly daily rhythms and adapt them to the cycle of day and night.
entries.background: Biological clocks influence sleep, metabolism and other functions in many plants and animals. Earlier fruit-fly experiments had identified mutations in a gene called period that disrupted daily rhythms, but the machinery behind the timing remained unclear.
entries.work: In 1984, Hall and Rosbash, working together, and Young independently isolated the period gene. Hall and Rosbash subsequently showed that its protein, PER, changes in abundance over the day. Their work supported a feedback loop in which accumulating PER inhibits the activity of its own gene. Young identified additional components that help PER function and regulate the timing of the cycle.
entries.significance: The discoveries explained how a recurring rhythm can emerge from interactions between genes and proteins. They established principles of cellular timekeeping that extend beyond fruit flies, rather than showing that every living cell has an identical clock.

entries.title: Efforts to Achieve a Treaty Prohibiting Nuclear Weapons
entries.overview: This international organization works to highlight the devastating human impact of nuclear warfare and promotes a legal ban on these weapons.
entries.background: ICAN was founded in 2007 to build public and governmental support for a nuclear-weapons ban. Its initiators believed nuclear-armed states were failing to fulfil disarmament commitments under the Non-Proliferation Treaty. The campaign drew inspiration from earlier movements against nuclear weapons and landmines.
entries.work: Operating through partners in over one hundred countries, the Geneva-based group participated in planning inter-governmental conferences. These meetings focused on the humanitarian disasters resulting from nuclear use. Their actions helped lead to a 2016 United Nations General Assembly resolution to begin negotiations for an international legal prohibition. In 2017, 122 UN member states voted to support a treaty against developing, stockpiling, or using such weapons.
entries.significance: The campaign's efforts contributed to a global vote supporting a treaty to prohibit nuclear weapon development and use, though many nuclear-armed and NATO nations did not support it.

entries.title: Listening to colliding black holes with LIGO
entries.overview: Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne helped make the first direct detection of gravitational waves possible: tiny changes in distance caused by ripples in spacetime.
entries.background: General relativity predicted these waves, but their effect on Earth is extraordinarily small. A detector must distinguish the stretching and squeezing of space from vibrations, thermal motion and other sources of noise.
entries.work: Weiss analysed those noise sources and developed a laser interferometer design that compares the lengths of two perpendicular arms. Thorne helped establish the theoretical foundations, including what astronomical sources should produce detectable waves. Barish led the construction effort and the collaboration needed to turn the experiment into a working observatory. In 2015, the LIGO collaboration detected waves from two merging black holes using instruments at two widely separated sites.
entries.significance: The observation tested a central prediction of relativity and opened a new way to study objects that are difficult to observe with light. The prize recognized three leading contributors within a much larger scientific and engineering collaboration.

entries.title: Creating New Proteins Through Controlled Genetic Selection
entries.overview: Scientists utilized the biological process of evolution to design specific proteins and antibodies for use in modern medicine and manufacturing.
entries.background: Natural evolution allows species to adapt to changing environments over time. Researchers applied these same principles of genetic change and selection to engineer proteins that address human chemical challenges.
entries.work: In 1993, Frances Arnold performed the first directed evolution of enzymes, which speed up chemical reactions. George Smith developed phage display in 1985, using a bacteria-infecting virus to evolve new proteins. Gregory Winter used this same phage display method to perform the directed evolution of antibodies.
entries.significance: These methods enable more eco-friendly production of chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Specifically, these techniques helped create medications for autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis and renewable fuels.

entries.title: Bringing climate and ideas into models of economic growth
entries.overview: William Nordhaus and Paul Romer separately expanded growth economics to account for two forces that standard models left outside their explanations: environmental damage and the creation of knowledge.
entries.background: Economic activity affects the climate, which in turn affects the economy. Technological progress can raise productivity, but it also requires people and firms to invest in developing new ideas. Understanding long-term growth therefore requires more than tracking capital and labour.
entries.work: Nordhaus developed models linking economic activity, carbon emissions, climate change and their economic consequences, allowing researchers to compare policy choices such as carbon taxes. Romer’s 1990 model explained how incentives shape innovation. A central distinction is that an idea can be used by many people without being used up, even though creating it is costly and access to it may be restricted.
entries.significance: Their frameworks made climate policy and technological innovation part of the analysis of growth itself. They provide tools for examining policy trade-offs; the results still depend on assumptions about damages, incentives and future developments.

entries.title: Narrative Imagination Representing Boundary Crossing Through Encyclopedic Passion
entries.overview: Olga Tokarczuk received this award for her writing style, which uses a vast range of knowledge to depict the movement between different worlds.
entries.background: After studying psychology in Warsaw, the Polish author began writing fiction. Her literary interests grew while reading extensively in a school library during her youth. Her debut novel appeared in 1993.
entries.work: Tokarczuk writes novels that explore tensions between opposites like nature and culture or reason and madness. Using perspectives inspired by maps, she connects small-scale stories to large-scale realities. Her 2014 historical novel, The Books of Jacob, details the life of the 18th-century sect leader Jacob Frank while presenting a wide view of an overlooked period in European history.
entries.significance: Her storytelling technique illustrates how crossing boundaries serves as a fundamental way of living by connecting diverse cultural and historical elements.
