entries.title: New Principles for Treating Cancer via Immune System Regulation
entries.overview: Scientists found a way to treat cancer by preventing certain proteins from acting as brakes that stop immune cells from attacking tumor cells.
entries.background: Cancer remains one of the world's most significant health challenges, causing millions of deaths annually. To combat it, researchers looked for methods to activate the body's natural defenses against tumors.
entries.work: In 1992, Tasuku Honjo identified a protein on immune cells and studied its function to reveal it acts as a brake on the immune system. During 1994–1995, James Allison investigated a known protein that also serves as an immune brake. He realized that releasing this brake could allow immune cells to attack tumors, developing this idea into a new therapeutic approach.
entries.significance: These discoveries established a new principle for cancer therapy by stimulating the body's inherent ability to target and destroy tumor cells.

entries.title: Care and justice for survivors of wartime sexual violence
entries.overview: Denis Mukwege and Nadia Murad were recognized for confronting sexual violence used as a weapon in armed conflict, through medical care, survivor testimony and demands for accountability.
entries.background: In the Democratic Republic of Congo, armed groups have used rape to terrorize communities during prolonged conflict. In Iraq in 2014, Islamic State attacked the Yazidi minority and subjected women and girls, including Murad, to sexual enslavement.
entries.work: Mukwege founded Panzi Hospital in Bukavu in 1999, initially to address maternal health needs. He and his team became known for treating survivors of sexual violence, including repairing severe injuries and supporting recovery. Murad escaped captivity and spoke publicly about the crimes committed against her community. As an advocate and United Nations goodwill ambassador, she called for survivors to be heard and perpetrators brought to justice.
entries.significance: The award connected treatment and recovery with the political and legal struggle to end sexual violence in war. It recognized survivors as witnesses and advocates, while directing attention to crimes that are often hidden by stigma and impunity.

entries.title: Trapping with light and amplifying ultrashort laser pulses
entries.overview: Arthur Ashkin developed optical tweezers, while Donna Strickland and Gérard Mourou developed a way to generate extremely intense, ultrashort laser pulses. These were two different advances in controlling light.
entries.background: Light carries momentum and can exert forces on small objects. Intense laser pulses also offer powerful ways to process matter, but simply amplifying a short pulse can damage the material used to amplify it.
entries.work: Ashkin used focused laser beams to trap and move tiny particles. In 1987, he demonstrated that living bacteria could be trapped without being harmed, opening biological applications of optical tweezers. In 1985, Strickland and Mourou introduced chirped pulse amplification: stretch a pulse in time to reduce its peak power, amplify it, then compress it again to obtain a much more intense short pulse.
entries.significance: Optical tweezers made it possible to manipulate and investigate microscopic biological systems. Chirped pulse amplification enabled powerful laser systems used in research and precise material processing, including corrective eye surgery. The prize joined these distinct uses of laser light, without attributing both techniques to all three recipients.

entries.title: The Development of Rechargeable Lithium Ion Battery Technology
entries.overview: Scientists created rechargeable batteries using lithium to store electricity by moving ions through materials with molecular-scale spaces.
entries.background: Finding ways to store electrical energy is a major challenge for the global energy supply. Lithium is an ideal element for this process because it easily releases electrons during chemical reactions.
entries.work: In the 1970s, Stanley Whittingham created a cathode using titanium disulphide to hold lithium ions. In 1980, John Goodenough developed a cobalt oxide cathode that provided higher voltage. In 1985, Akira Yoshino built a battery using a petroleum coke anode. This carbon material also contains spaces for lithium ions, resulting in the first commercially viable lithium-ion battery design.
entries.significance: These technological advancements enabled the widespread use of portable power in modern electrical equipment, such as electric cars and mobile phones.

entries.title: Testing specific ways to reduce poverty
entries.overview: Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer helped transform development economics by testing particular interventions in real communities, rather than treating poverty as one indivisible problem.
entries.background: A programme can sound promising yet fail to help the people it targets. Comparing participants with nonparticipants may also mislead, because the two groups can differ before a programme begins. Researchers needed stronger evidence about cause and effect.
entries.work: Kremer and colleagues pioneered school-based field experiments in Kenya in the 1990s. Banerjee, Duflo and collaborators extended this approach across education, health and other areas. Random allocation to intervention and comparison groups helps distinguish a programme’s effect from pre-existing differences. For example, studies in India found that tutoring aimed at pupils who were falling behind improved learning, revealing a problem that simply adding classroom resources could miss.
entries.significance: The approach made it possible to compare practical policies and investigate why they work. Its results concern particular interventions and settings; applying them elsewhere requires attention to local conditions, rather than assuming one experiment supplies a universal cure for poverty.

entries.title: Exploring Human Experience Through Linguistic Ingenuity in Literature
entries.overview: The 2019 prize honors Peter Handke for using creative language to examine the edges and unique qualities of being human.
entries.background: After studying law, Peter Handke left his university studies following the 1966 release of his first novel. He chose to move away from the era's common focus on political or community-driven writing styles.
entries.work: Writing across various formats including novels, essays, and screenplays, Peter Handke seeks new ways to express personal discoveries. His diverse bibliography includes dramatic works and notebooks. Notably, he authored A Sorrow Beyond Dreams following his mother’s death. Through different literary forms, he focuses on capturing the specific details of human existence and the periphery of life.
entries.significance: His writing serves as a major influence in post-Second World War Europe by providing fresh linguistic tools to describe individual experiences.

entries.title: The molecular switch that lets cells respond to oxygen
entries.overview: William Kaelin, Peter Ratcliffe and Gregg Semenza uncovered a system that changes gene activity when oxygen becomes scarce, helping cells adjust their metabolism and the body improve oxygen supply.
entries.background: Oxygen is needed to extract energy efficiently from food. Tissues experience changing oxygen levels, and one response is increased production of erythropoietin, a hormone that promotes the formation of oxygen-carrying red blood cells. The link between oxygen and gene activity was unclear.
entries.work: Semenza identified the gene-regulating complex HIF. Ratcliffe showed that the oxygen-sensing response operates in many tissues. Kaelin’s work on the VHL tumour-suppressor protein connected it to oxygen regulation, and Ratcliffe linked VHL to HIF degradation. The Kaelin and Ratcliffe groups then showed how oxygen-dependent chemical modification allows VHL to mark a HIF component for destruction. When oxygen falls, HIF can accumulate and activate adaptive genes.
entries.significance: The discoveries explained a fundamental physiological response and provided targets for drug development. They are relevant to anaemia and to tumours, which can exploit oxygen-response mechanisms to support their growth.

entries.title: Resolving the Longstanding Border Conflict Between Ethiopia and Eritrea
entries.overview: Abiy Ahmed Ali received this honor for initiating a resolution to the border dispute with Eritrea and working toward international cooperation.
entries.background: Following a 2002 arbitration ruling, Ethiopia did not accept the decision regarding disputed territory. This led to sixteen years of a frozen state characterized by neither war nor peace between the neighboring nations.
entries.work: After becoming Prime Minister in April 2018, Abiy Ahmed Ali accepted the previous legal ruling. In September 2018, he and Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki signed a peace agreement. Additionally, Abiy Ahmed Ali released political prisoners, removed press censorship, and increased female representation in government roles, such as appointing a female Minister of Peace.
entries.significance: His actions broke a long-term diplomatic deadlock. At the time of the award, Ethiopia faced significant challenges regarding internal ethnic conflicts and the implementation of democratic processes.

entries.title: Reconstructing the universe and finding a world around another Sun
entries.overview: James Peebles helped turn cosmology into a quantitative account of the evolving universe. Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz discovered the first known planet orbiting a star similar to the Sun.
entries.background: The microwave background preserves evidence of the early universe, but interpreting it requires physical models. Detecting planets around other stars poses a different challenge: a planet is faint beside its much brighter host star.
entries.work: From the 1960s onward, Peebles developed theoretical tools for understanding the early universe, its background radiation and the formation of cosmic structure. His work helped establish the modern cosmological framework in which ordinary matter is a small part of the total. In 1995, Mayor and Queloz detected 51 Pegasi b by measuring periodic Doppler shifts in its star’s light, revealing motion caused by the orbiting planet.
entries.significance: Peebles supplied foundations for interpreting observations within models that include dark matter and dark energy; he did not discover all those components alone. The planetary discovery established an important new path for studying worlds beyond the Solar System.

entries.title: Developing Precise Genetic Scissors for Editing DNA Sequences
entries.overview: Scientists created a precise way to edit genomes by repurposing a bacterial immune mechanism to cut specific DNA segments during biological processes.
entries.background: All living organisms rely on genes made of DNA sections to control life processes. Researchers sought ways to manipulate these genetic instructions with high precision using molecular tools found in nature.
entries.work: In 2012, Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna developed a method for high-precision genome editing. They utilized the immune system of a bacterium, which functions by cutting viral DNA into pieces. By extracting and simplifying the molecular components of these genetic scissors, they made the CRISPR/Cas9 tool generally applicable to different organisms.
entries.significance: This technique provides tools for new scientific discoveries, improved crops, and potential new methods for addressing genetic diseases and cancer.

entries.title: Designing auctions when bidders have different information
entries.overview: Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson explained how auction rules and incomplete information influence bidding, then helped design auctions for resources such as radio-spectrum licences.
entries.background: An auctioned asset can have a value that bidders estimate differently. The person with the most optimistic estimate may win but overpay: the winner’s curse. When several related items are sold, buying one can also change the value of others.
entries.work: Wilson analysed auctions with uncertain common values, explaining why rational bidders may bid cautiously. Milgrom developed a broader theory combining common values with values specific to individual buyers, and examined how auction formats affect outcomes. Together they developed practical formats for selling interrelated spectrum licences. US authorities first used one of these formats in 1994, allowing bidding across multiple licences in successive rounds.
entries.significance: The work connects economic theory to the design of public institutions and markets. Better auction rules can improve the allocation of scarce resources and the information available to bidders, with consequences for buyers, sellers and public revenue.

entries.title: The Universal Themes in the Poetry of Louise Glück
entries.overview: Louise Glück received this award for writing poetry that uses simple, clear language to connect specific personal experiences to broader human existence.
entries.background: Glück draws inspiration from classical mythology and the long-standing tradition of English-language poetry. Her creative process involves examining recurring themes such as family life, childhood, various relationships, and death.
entries.work: In her collections, Louise Glück uses precise and clear language that avoids complex poetic formalities, often opting for everyday spoken words. She connects personal memories and individual experiences to universal concepts. By integrating classical motifs and myths into her writing, she bridges the gap between private life and the shared human condition through an austere and unmistakable poetic voice.
entries.significance: Her writing style allows readers to find commonality in individual struggles by transforming specific, private moments into themes that apply to everyone.

entries.title: Finding the virus behind unexplained bloodborne hepatitis
entries.overview: Harvey Alter, Michael Houghton and Charles Rice identified hepatitis C virus and established its role in liver disease, enabling blood screening and the development of antiviral treatments.
entries.background: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. Hepatitis A is usually spread through contaminated food or water, whereas hepatitis B can spread through blood. Even after tests for these viruses became available, many transfusion recipients developed hepatitis from an unidentified cause.
entries.work: Alter and colleagues demonstrated that the unexplained transfusion-associated disease involved another infectious agent and showed it was a virus. Houghton’s team identified genetic material from that virus in 1989, allowing it to be named and tested for. Rice then used an engineered viral RNA genome to show in 1997 that hepatitis C virus alone could cause hepatitis, resolving a crucial question about causation.
entries.significance: Together, the studies connected clinical observations, molecular identification and experimental proof. They made donated blood much safer and provided the basis for effective drugs. The achievement concerned identifying a specific cause of disease, rather than treating all hepatitis as a single infection.

entries.title: Efforts to Combat Hunger and Prevent Food as a Weapon
entries.overview: The World Food Programme received this award for fighting global hunger, improving conditions in conflict zones, and opposing the use of starvation during warfare.
entries.background: Established in 1961 by the United Nations General Assembly and FAO, the organization works amid conflict and food insecurity. Severe hunger affected more than 100 million people in 2019. The COVID-19 pandemic subsequently intensified hunger during 2020.
entries.work: In 2019, the World Food Programme delivered emergency food aid across 88 countries. Beyond immediate relief, the organization focused on long-term goals by increasing local food production and addressing specific nutritional requirements for infants and women. These activities aim toward the United Nations' objective of removing poverty and hunger through voluntary funding from governments and private donors.
entries.significance: The work addresses how food scarcity affects stability in war-torn regions, specifically targeting the prevention of using starvation as a tool of combat.

entries.title: Why black holes can form, and what lies at our galaxy’s centre
entries.overview: Roger Penrose established that black-hole formation is a robust prediction of general relativity. Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez led independent teams that found compelling evidence for a supermassive black hole in the Milky Way.
entries.background: Early mathematical descriptions left open whether black holes required unrealistic symmetry. Observers faced a different problem: an object that traps light must be studied through its effects on surrounding matter, and dust obscures the centre of our galaxy.
entries.work: In work published in 1965, Penrose developed mathematical methods showing that gravitational collapse can lead to a singularity under general conditions within Einstein’s theory. Beginning in the 1990s, Genzel and Ghez’s teams tracked stars near Sagittarius A* using increasingly precise observations. The stars’ orbits revealed a very large mass confined to a remarkably small region.
entries.significance: The theoretical result made black holes credible consequences of relativity rather than mathematical curiosities. The stellar measurements provided strong observational evidence for the compact central object. A mathematical prediction and an astronomical detection are distinct contributions, not interchangeable proofs.

entries.title: Developing New Methods Using Small Organic Molecules as Catalysts
entries.overview: In 2000, researchers created a method of catalysis using small organic molecules to speed up chemical reactions without being consumed in the process.
entries.background: Chemists require catalysts, which are substances that accelerate chemical reactions while remaining separate from the final product, to effectively build complex molecules for various uses.
entries.work: Working independently in 2000, Benjamin List and David MacMillan demonstrated ways to use small organic molecules as catalysts. List showed that the amino acid proline could drive an asymmetric carbon-bond-forming reaction. MacMillan designed organic catalysts that also favoured one mirror-image product over the other. This control of molecular handedness is called asymmetric organocatalysis: it can strongly favour the desired form rather than necessarily producing both forms equally.
entries.significance: This technique supports pharmaceutical research and offers a way to make chemical processes more environmentally friendly by using organic molecules to direct molecular construction.

entries.title: Analyzing Cause and Effect Using Natural Experiments in Economics
entries.overview: These researchers developed ways to study cause and effect by using unexpected events or policy changes to observe how different groups respond.
entries.background: In the social sciences, determining true cause and effect is difficult. Researchers often face questions where they cannot control who participates in a specific program or policy change being studied.
entries.work: David Card used natural experiments to study how immigration, education, and minimum wages affect labor markets, finding that higher minimum wages do not always decrease employment. In 1994, Joshua Angrist and Guido Imbens identified what causal conclusions are possible when individuals cannot be forced or prevented from joining a studied program.
entries.significance: This work provided new methods for analyzing causal relationships and offered evidence-based insights into how specific economic policies influence the workforce.

entries.title: Exploring Colonialism and Refugee Experiences Through Literary Prose
entries.overview: Abdulrazak Gurnah received this award for writing about how colonialism affects people and the difficult lives of refugees caught between different cultures.
entries.background: Growing up in Zanzibar, Gurnah experienced the 1960s when political persecution against those of Arab descent forced many to flee. This history of displacement informs his focus on individuals navigating the gap between continents.
entries.work: In his novels, Gurnah depicts a culturally diverse East Africa. His writing explores the disruption experienced by refugees without using simple explanations. He tracks individual lives with a commitment to truth, often presenting bleak realities through an unbending lens. These stories illustrate the consequences of colonial history on human movement and cultural identity.
entries.significance: His literature provides a detailed look at the intersection of colonial legacy and the struggles faced by those seeking new homes across different worlds.

entries.title: The molecular gates that turn heat and pressure into signals
entries.overview: David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian identified ion channels that respond to temperature or mechanical force, explaining how physical stimuli can begin electrical signals in cells.
entries.background: Feeling a hot surface or a light touch requires a conversion from the outside world into nerve activity. Scientists knew that sensory nerves carried signals, but the identity of key molecular sensors remained uncertain.
entries.work: Julius used capsaicin, the substance responsible for chilli peppers’ burning sensation, to find a gene encoding TRPV1, a channel also activated by painful heat. Patapoutian’s team studied cells that produced an electrical response when poked. By disabling candidate genes, they identified Piezo1 in 2010 and then a related channel, Piezo2. Further experiments established roles for Piezo channels in sensing mechanical force, including touch and body position.
entries.significance: These discoveries connected sensations to identifiable proteins in cell membranes: when the channels open, ions move and electrical conditions change. They also provided starting points for studying other physiological processes that depend on temperature and mechanical forces, rather than explaining sensory perception only at the level of whole nerves.

entries.title: Protecting Freedom of Expression Through Independent Journalism
entries.overview: Two journalists received this award for their work defending free speech and reporting on abuses of power within their respective countries.
entries.background: In the Philippines, democratic norms faced threats from increasing authoritarianism and state-led violence. Simultaneously, in Russia, journalists faced significant danger while investigating government corruption, human rights violations, and military actions following the Soviet Union's dissolution.
entries.work: Maria Ressa co-founded Rappler in 2012. By the time of the award, she and its journalists had exposed abuses in President Duterte’s anti-drug campaign and documented how social media spread disinformation and harassment. Dmitry Muratov co-founded Novaya Gazeta and served as its editor for most of the period from 1995 to the award. It investigated corruption, electoral fraud and human-rights abuses despite the murders of colleagues, including Anna Politkovskaya.

entries.title: Modeling Earth's Climate and Understanding Complex Disordered Systems
entries.overview: Scientists developed methods to model Earth’s climate and identify patterns within complex, disordered systems ranging from tiny atoms to large planets.
entries.background: Earth’s climate and many physical materials are complex systems defined by randomness and disorder. Researchers sought ways to predict global warming and understand how fluctuations behave in chaotic environments.
entries.work: In the 1960s, Syukuro Manabe modelled how radiation and atmospheric circulation interact, showing how increased carbon dioxide warms Earth’s surface. Klaus Hasselmann linked short-term weather variability to longer-term climate and developed methods to distinguish human influences from natural variability. Separately, Giorgio Parisi developed a theory of disordered systems, notably spin glasses: materials whose magnetic interactions compete so that not every local preference can be satisfied. His work uncovered mathematical structure behind this apparent disorder.
entries.significance: Manabe and Hasselmann laid foundations for climate prediction and identifying human-caused warming. Parisi’s distinct work supplied methods for understanding complex systems, with applications extending beyond physics into fields such as biology and machine learning.

entries.title: Developing Efficient Methods for Connecting Molecular Building Blocks
entries.overview: Scientists created techniques to snap chemical components together rapidly and efficiently, allowing for the construction of increasingly complex molecules.
entries.background: For a long time, attempting to build intricate molecular structures was an expensive process that required significant amounts of time. Researchers sought more effective ways to join these tiny building blocks.
entries.work: Barry Sharpless promoted click chemistry: reliable reactions that join molecular building blocks efficiently. In 2002, he and Morten Meldal independently developed the copper-catalysed azide–alkyne reaction. Carolyn Bertozzi pursued a related but distinct problem: reactions that work in living systems without disrupting their chemistry. Because copper could harm cells, she developed copper-free reactions for labelling biological molecules, allowing researchers to track them in living systems.
entries.significance: Click chemistry simplifies the construction and linking of molecules in research and materials development. Bioorthogonal chemistry makes it possible to follow biological processes within living systems and supports research into more precisely targeted treatments. The biological methods were not simply the copper-catalysed reaction applied unchanged to cells.

entries.title: Why useful banks can be vulnerable to destructive runs
entries.overview: Ben Bernanke, Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig explained why banks matter to the economy and why their failure can turn financial problems into a much deeper crisis.
entries.background: Savers want access to their money, while businesses and households often need loans that last for years. Banks bridge that mismatch by pooling deposits and making longer-term loans, but they cannot instantly recover every loan if everyone demands cash at once.
entries.work: Diamond and Dybvig’s theoretical work showed how this useful role also makes banks vulnerable to self-fulfilling runs: fear of failure can prompt withdrawals that cause failure. Their framework explains how deposit insurance can reduce that risk. Diamond also analysed banks’ role in monitoring borrowers. Bernanke used historical and statistical research to show that banking failures helped deepen and prolong the Great Depression by damaging the supply of credit.
entries.significance: The work established why protecting the banking system is more than rescuing individual firms. It informs financial regulation and crisis policy, while explaining the economic costs of losing the relationships and information through which banks allocate credit.

entries.title: Reading ancient DNA to uncover lost branches of human history
entries.overview: Svante Pääbo developed methods for studying genomes from extinct human relatives, revealing both their relationship to modern humans and episodes of interbreeding between populations.
entries.background: Ancient DNA breaks into short fragments, undergoes chemical damage and becomes mixed with microbial or modern human DNA. Recovering an authentic genome therefore requires methods that distinguish scarce ancient material from contamination.
entries.work: Pääbo and his collaborators refined these techniques and published a first Neanderthal genome sequence in 2010. DNA from a small bone found in Denisova Cave revealed another previously unknown hominin group, the Denisovans. Comparisons with present-day human genomes showed that Neanderthals and Denisovans contributed genetic material to ancestors of some living populations after migrations out of Africa.
entries.significance: The work established palaeogenomics as a way to investigate human evolution directly through genetic evidence. It showed that our history includes interaction between different human lineages, not simply one lineage replacing all others. Some inherited variants still affect physiology, including immune responses, linking ancient population history with biological differences today.

entries.title: Civil society documenting abuses and defending human rights
entries.overview: Ales Bialiatski, the Russian organization Memorial and Ukraine’s Center for Civil Liberties were recognized for defending the right to criticize power and recording abuses that authorities sought to conceal.
entries.background: Their work developed amid authoritarian repression, the legacy of Soviet state violence and armed conflict. The award treated independent documentation and the protection of basic rights as essential parts of peace and democracy.
entries.work: Bialiatski founded Viasna in Belarus in 1996 to help detained protesters and their families; it developed into an organization documenting repression and torture. Memorial preserved evidence of Soviet-era persecution and investigated later abuses, including during the Chechen wars. The Center for Civil Liberties, founded in Kyiv in 2007, promoted the rule of law and documented unlawful detention and other abuses, expanding its work on war crimes after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
entries.significance: The prize honoured one individual and two organizations, not three governments. At the time of the award, Bialiatski was imprisoned and Memorial faced forced dissolution. entries.title: Testing entanglement and turning it into a resource
entries.overview: Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger tested the unusual correlations between entangled particles and helped develop experimental methods for quantum information science.
entries.background: Bell’s inequalities set limits on correlations in theories where outcomes are fixed by local hidden properties. Quantum mechanics predicts that entangled systems can exceed those limits. Testing the difference required carefully controlled measurements on separated particles.
entries.work: Clauser and collaborators carried out a landmark photon experiment in 1972 that violated a Bell inequality. Aspect’s experiments in the early 1980s strengthened the evidence, including by changing measurement settings while photons were in flight. Zeilinger and colleagues developed increasingly sophisticated entangled-photon experiments, including quantum teleportation, which transfers a quantum state between systems using entanglement together with ordinary communication.
entries.significance: The experiments ruled out broad classes of local hidden-variable explanations and made entanglement a practical resource for research. They helped establish foundations for quantum networks, computing and cryptography. Entangled correlations do not allow a controllable message to travel faster than light, despite their striking departure from everyday expectations.

entries.title: The Discovery and Synthesis of Tiny Quantum Dots
entries.overview: Scientists developed methods to create nano-sized particles called quantum dots, which exhibit unique physical behaviors when matter shrinks to incredibly small dimensions.
entries.background: When grains of matter reach nano-dimensions, quantum phenomena emerge. Understanding how the size of these tiny particles influences their properties was a central challenge in particle physics and chemistry.
entries.work: In 1981, Aleksey Yekimov produced size-dependent quantum effects in colored glass using copper chloride nanoparticles. Louis Brus proved in 1983 that such quantum effects exist in particles floating freely in fluid, noting smaller particles absorb blue-shifted light. In 1993, Moungi Bawendi created nearly perfect quantum dots with smooth surfaces and specific sizes using an easy-to-use production method.
entries.significance: These tiny particles are now utilized in LED lamps, computer and television screens, and for mapping biological tissue.

entries.title: Understanding Long-term Changes in Women's Labor Market Participation
entries.overview: Claudia Goldin used historical evidence to explain how women’s employment and earnings changed in the United States, showing why economic growth alone does not eliminate gender differences.
entries.background: Historically, female employment levels have shifted significantly. In the nineteenth century, the transition from farming to industrialism caused a decline in the number of married women working.
entries.work: Goldin reconstructed long-term patterns from historical records. Married women’s participation fell as production moved from farms into industrial workplaces, then rose with the growth of the service sector. She linked these changes to institutions, expectations and social norms concerning family responsibilities. Her research also showed how modern earnings differences can widen after the birth of a first child, even among men and women with similar education and occupations.
entries.significance: The research connects long-run economic change with decisions about education, work and family. It explains why increasing women’s educational attainment does not automatically close earnings gaps, and why the timing and organization of work matter alongside formal access to employment.

entries.title: Innovative Plays and Prose Expressing Deep Human Emotions
entries.overview: Jon Fosse received this award for creating plays and prose that use simplified language to communicate complex, unspoken feelings.
entries.background: The contemporary theatre landscape has been shaped by new ways of presenting drama. Jon Fosse contributes to this tradition through a wide range of writing, including novels, poetry, essays, and children's books written in Nynorsk.
entries.work: Writing in Nynorsk, Jon Fosse utilizes a radical reduction of both dramatic action and language. His creative process focuses on using simple, everyday terms to represent intense human emotions such as powerlessness and anxiety. Through these stark images, he depicts a loss of orientation. Despite a generally negative outlook in his writing, his works also incorporate elements of humor, warmth, and a specific type of vulnerable simplicity.
entries.significance: Jon Fosse acts as a major innovator in modern theatre by finding ways to give a voice to things that are otherwise difficult to express.

entries.title: Making laboratory-produced mRNA more useful for vaccination
entries.overview: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman discovered how chemical changes to RNA building blocks could reduce unwanted inflammatory responses and improve protein production, removing major obstacles to mRNA vaccines.
entries.background: Messenger RNA carries instructions that cells can use to make proteins. Vaccination can supply mRNA encoding a viral protein so the immune system learns to recognize it. Early laboratory-made mRNA, however, could provoke strong inflammatory reactions and was inefficient at producing the intended protein.
entries.work: In 2005, Karikó and Weissman showed that modifying certain nucleoside bases greatly reduced inflammatory activation in immune cells. In studies published in 2008 and 2010, they demonstrated increased protein production from modified mRNA and investigated why this occurred. These findings addressed how cells recognize and respond to introduced RNA.
entries.significance: The discoveries were crucial foundations for the effective mRNA vaccines developed against COVID-19, alongside advances such as lipid delivery systems. The aim is to reduce an unwanted response to the RNA while enabling an immune response against the encoded viral protein, not to switch off the immune system generally.

entries.title: Advocating for Human Rights and Women's Equality in Iran
entries.overview: Narges Mohammadi received this honor for her long-term efforts to oppose female oppression and support universal human freedoms within the Iranian theocracy.
entries.background: Since 2003, after joining the Defenders of Human Rights Center, Mohammadi has operated within a regime characterized by strict religious rule. This period included widespread protests in autumn 2022 following the death of Mahsa Jina Amini.
entries.work: Mohammadi supported imprisoned activists and campaigned against executions, torture and sexual violence by the state. By the October 2023 award announcement, she had been arrested thirteen times and received sentences totalling decades in prison and 154 lashes. From Evin prison she supported the protest movement that followed Mahsa Jina Amini’s death in 2022, continuing to challenge repression despite her own imprisonment.
entries.significance: Her actions turned her into a symbol for freedom, highlighting the ongoing struggles for democracy and equality despite severe personal consequences and state retaliation.

entries.title: Experimental Methods for Generating Ultra-Short Light Pulses
entries.overview: Scientists developed ways to create extremely brief flashes of light, known as attosecond pulses, which allow researchers to observe how electrons move within matter.
entries.background: Electronic movements drive the energy exchanges between light and matter and are fundamental to life. Because these motions occur in hundreds of attoseconds, capturing them requires specialized experimental techniques to observe such rapid changes inside atoms or molecules.
entries.work: In 1987, Anne L’Huillier observed many high-frequency overtones when infrared laser light passed through a noble gas. Her studies helped explain how such light could be combined into extremely brief pulses. In 2001, Pierre Agostini produced and measured a train of pulses lasting about 250 attoseconds each. Ferenc Krausz’s team separately isolated a single pulse of about 650 attoseconds. A single attosecond is one billionth of one billionth of a second.
entries.significance: These tools enable real-time observation of predicted electron phenomena. Such methods may eventually help advance fields like medical diagnostics and electronics.

entries.title: Predicting protein shapes and designing new proteins
entries.overview: David Baker developed computational methods to design proteins, while Demis Hassabis and John Jumper transformed the prediction of protein structures from amino-acid sequences.
entries.background: Proteins are chains of amino acids that fold into three-dimensional shapes. Their shapes help determine what they do, from catalysing reactions to transmitting signals. Two related challenges are predicting the shape of an existing sequence and choosing a sequence that will produce a desired new shape.
entries.work: In 2003, Baker’s team designed and experimentally verified a protein with a structure unlike those found in nature, demonstrating a route to creating new proteins through computation. In 2020, Hassabis, Jumper and their team presented AlphaFold2, an AI system that achieved a major improvement in structure prediction. It subsequently enabled predictions on an enormous scale.
entries.significance: Protein design opens possibilities for new medicines, sensors and materials. Structure prediction helps researchers investigate how existing proteins work. Predicted structures remain models with varying confidence, rather than experimental measurements of every protein or every state it can adopt.

entries.title: How institutions shape prosperity and persist over time
entries.overview: Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson investigated how political and economic institutions influence prosperity, and why arrangements that benefit a ruling elite can persist despite wider economic costs.
entries.background: Countries differ greatly in income, and those differences cannot be understood simply by comparing their resources. Rules governing property, participation and political power shape who can invest, innovate and benefit from economic activity.
entries.work: The researchers examined institutional differences established under European colonial rule and their long-term consequences. They distinguished arrangements focused on extracting resources for a narrow elite from institutions offering broader participation and protection of economic rights. Their theoretical work explained why elites may resist reforms that threaten their power, and how conflict and commitments between groups can contribute to institutional change.
entries.significance: The research placed institutions and political power at the centre of development economics. It supplies evidence and frameworks for explaining persistent income differences, rather than a claim that one factor determines every country’s fate or that institutional reform automatically guarantees prosperity.

entries.title: Poetic Prose Exploring Historical Trauma and Human Fragility
entries.overview: Han Kang received this honor for using intense, poetic writing to examine historical wounds and the delicate nature of human existence.
entries.background: Starting her career in 1993 as a poet, Han Kang transitioned into writing short stories and novels. Her literary tradition involves exploring the intersections between the living and the deceased, as well as the bond between soul and body.
entries.work: Through works such as The Vegetarian, Human Acts, and We Do Not Part, Han Kang utilizes an experimental prose style. She investigates invisible social rules and historical traumas while highlighting how vulnerable life is. Her writing focuses on the connection between physical bodies and the spirit, establishing her as a modern innovator in contemporary prose through these specific narrative techniques.
entries.significance: Her contribution involves developing a unique way to address painful history and the fragility of being alive through innovative, rhythmic language.

entries.title: Tiny RNAs that regulate how genetic messages are used
entries.overview: Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun discovered microRNA and explained how these short RNA molecules can control protein production after a gene has already been copied into messenger RNA.
entries.background: Many different cell types share essentially the same DNA but use different sets of genes. Regulation does not end when DNA is transcribed: cells also control what happens to the resulting RNA messages and how much protein they produce.
entries.work: Studying developmental timing in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, Ambros found that the lin-4 gene produced a short RNA rather than a protein. Ruvkun showed that lin-4 regulated protein production from lin-14 after its messenger RNA had been made. Comparing their results revealed matching sequences through which the small RNA could interact with its target. They published these findings in 1993; later work established that microRNA regulation is widespread.
entries.significance: The discovery revealed a previously unknown layer of gene control. It explained how small, non-protein-coding RNAs can help coordinate development and cell function, with implications for understanding diseases in which gene regulation goes wrong.

entries.title: Efforts to Achieve a Nuclear Weapon Free World
entries.overview: Nihon Hidankyo works toward eliminating nuclear weapons by sharing personal accounts regarding the humanitarian devastation caused by atomic bombings.
entries.background: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 killed vast numbers of people immediately, with many more dying later from burns and radiation injuries. Survivors, known as Hibakusha, faced lasting health and social consequences that were long neglected.
entries.work: In 1956, various local Hibakusha associations and victims of Pacific nuclear tests established Nihon Hidankyo. This grassroots organization pursues two goals: advocating for the social and economic rights of all Hibakusha and preventing future nuclear catastrophes. The group utilizes personal witness statements to conduct educational programs focused on the devastating human consequences following the use of such weapons.
entries.significance: The movement brings attention to the previously ignored fate of survivors while promoting the motto 'No more Hibakusha' through direct testimony.

entries.title: Foundational Discoveries Enabling Machine Learning with Artificial Neural Networks
entries.overview: Scientists created mathematical networks that mimic brain structures to store information and learn patterns from data, providing the basis for modern artificial intelligence.
entries.background: Artificial neural networks draw inspiration from how biological neurons function. These systems use nodes with varying values to process information, modeling how many small parts influence a larger system's behavior.
entries.work: In 1982, John Hopfield invented a network designed for saving and recreating patterns using physics-based models. Later, between 1983 and 1985, Geoffrey Hinton applied statistical physics tools to develop the Boltzmann machine. This specific invention allows a system to learn how to identify characteristic features within datasets. These individual developments provided important foundations for modern machine learning technologies.
entries.significance: These inventions allow computers to perform complex tasks like analyzing images and classifying or generating visual content by recognizing essential patterns within data.

entries.title: Designing crystals with useful spaces inside
entries.overview: Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi developed metal–organic frameworks, porous crystals whose internal spaces and chemical properties can be designed by choosing their building blocks.
entries.background: A material can be useful because of its empty spaces as well as its solid structure. To capture, separate or store particular molecules, chemists need frameworks with suitable cavities that remain accessible and behave predictably.
entries.work: Robson demonstrated a pioneering framework design in 1989, linking metal ions with organic molecules to form an extended structure. Kitagawa showed that gases could enter and leave such frameworks and developed ideas about their flexibility. Yaghi advanced the creation of stable frameworks and the systematic adjustment of their structures. Together, these contributions established methods for building families of porous materials rather than discovering only one useful substance.
entries.significance: MOFs offer ways to tailor materials for gas storage and separation, chemical reactions and water capture from air. These applications are at different stages of research and use; the prize recognized the underlying molecular architecture, rather than showing that every proposed application has already been widely deployed.

entries.title: Understanding the Mechanisms Behind Long Term Economic Growth
entries.overview: Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt explained how technological innovation can sustain long-term economic growth, while also displacing established products and creating conflicts over change.
entries.background: For much of human history, economies frequently experienced periods of stagnation. Researchers sought to understand why the last two centuries shifted toward a pattern of lasting, self-sustaining growth rather than periodic decline.
entries.work: In the 1990s, Joel Mokyr used historical records to show that innovation requires scientific understanding and societies open to change. Separately, in 1992, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt developed a mathematical model for creative destruction. This model describes how new, superior products displace older ones, creating conflicts that must be managed to ensure progress is not hindered.
entries.significance: The research explains conditions that support repeated innovation and the competitive pressures it creates. Sustained growth here means a long-term process, not an economy without recessions or a guarantee that every innovation benefits everyone equally.

entries.title: Literary Achievement in Central European Prose Traditions
entries.overview: László Krasznahorkai received this honor for his expansive body of work that explores themes of apocalyptic terror and the enduring strength of art.
entries.background: His writing exists within a specific Central European creative lineage. This tradition often utilizes the grotesque and the absurd to examine difficult subjects through a lens of pessimism, unpredictability, and dark humor.
entries.work: Krasznahorkai crafts prose using long, winding sentences to create a flowing linguistic style. His notable novels include Satantango, The Melancholy of Resistance, War & War, Baron Wenckheim's Homecoming, and Herscht 07769. Additionally, his travels through China and Japan provided inspiration for works such as Seiobo There Below.
entries.significance: His writing provides a unique perspective on apocalyptic themes while maintaining a connection to established regional literary styles through its distinct structural and tonal qualities.

entries.title: The immune cells and gene that help prevent attacks on the body
entries.overview: Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi explained important mechanisms of peripheral immune tolerance: how immune responses are restrained so that the body’s defences do not damage its own tissues.
entries.background: Protection against infection requires powerful immune cells, but some can recognize the body’s own components. Eliminating dangerous cells during development is not the only safeguard; regulation is also needed among immune cells circulating in the body.
entries.work: In 1995, Sakaguchi identified a population of regulatory T cells that suppress harmful immune responses. In 2001, Brunkow and Ramsdell linked severe autoimmune disease in mice to mutations in the Foxp3 gene and connected its human counterpart to a related disorder. In 2003, Sakaguchi showed that this gene governs the development of the regulatory cells, joining the cellular and genetic findings into a common explanation.
entries.significance: The discoveries revealed an active system for maintaining tolerance rather than simply a passive failure to react. They support research into controlling autoimmunity, improving transplant acceptance and countering immune suppression in cancer, where the desired direction of treatment can differ.

entries.title: Promoting Democratic Rights and Political Transitions in Venezuela
entries.overview: Maria Corina Machado received this prize for her continuous efforts to support democratic rights and seek a peaceful shift from dictatorship to democracy in Venezuela.
entries.background: Venezuela has faced expanding authoritarianism, where the right to vote and express opinions is under threat. This historical setting involves a regime that tightened its grip on power despite widespread opposition mobilization and documentation of election results.
entries.work: After founding the Atenea Foundation in 1992 and Súmate in 2002 to monitor elections, Machado entered the National Assembly in 2010. Following her 2014 expulsion from office, she helped form the Soy Venezuela alliance in 2017. During the 2024 presidential election, she supported Edmundo Gonzalez Urrutia after being blocked from running herself, helping to document evidence that the opposition won.
entries.significance: Her actions highlight the struggle for elective government and political representation, which serve as foundations for peace both within individual nations and between different countries.

entries.title: Quantum tunnelling and discrete energies in an electrical circuit
entries.overview: John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis demonstrated that the collective state of a superconducting electrical circuit can display quantum tunnelling and quantised energy levels, extending observable quantum behaviour beyond individual particles.
entries.background: Quantum tunnelling allows a system to cross an energy barrier that classical physics would prevent it from crossing. Large systems usually lose readily observable quantum behaviour, so showing these effects in an engineered circuit required careful control and measurement.
entries.work: In 1984 and 1985, the researchers studied a superconducting circuit containing a Josephson junction. Its collective state could remain trapped with current flowing but no voltage. They demonstrated escape from that state by quantum tunnelling, detected by the appearance of a voltage. They also measured discrete energy levels, showing that the circuit absorbed energy in particular amounts. The macroscopic tunnelling concerned this collective circuit state, not merely electrons crossing the junction’s insulating layer.
entries.significance: The experiments established a controllable macroscopic system exhibiting two central quantum properties. They helped create foundations for technologies that use superconducting circuits as quantum devices, including quantum computing and sensing.

entries.title: Amplifying molecular handedness
entries.overview: Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai discovered chemical mechanisms that amplify a preference for one molecular mirror image, connecting asymmetric catalysis with self-reinforcing reactions.
entries.background: Many molecules exist as two mirror-image forms, called enantiomers, which can interact differently with biological systems. Producing mainly one form matters in chemical manufacturing. Researchers also wanted to understand how a small initial imbalance between mirror images could grow into an overwhelmingly one-sided mixture.
entries.work: Kagan showed that the balance of mirror images in a catalyst need not transfer proportionally into its product. Certain catalyst combinations behaved differently, allowing a greater asymmetry in the product. Soai then developed an asymmetric autocatalytic reaction: its product helped catalyse the formation of more of itself. A slight initial excess could consequently reinforce itself through successive reaction cycles. This demonstrated a laboratory mechanism for greatly amplifying molecular handedness, without establishing the exact chemical history of early life.
entries.significance: These findings gave chemists ways to understand and optimise asymmetric reactions. They also provided an experimental model for investigating the emergence of molecular handedness; Soai’s artificial reaction is distinct from the chemistry used by living organisms.

entries.title: Economic policy built from individual decisions
entries.overview: Robert Hall and Michael Woodford were recognised for connecting stabilisation policy with the decisions of households and firms, including how expectations influence consumption and economic activity.
entries.background: Older macroeconomic models relied heavily on statistical relationships between large economic totals. Their performance during changing conditions raised questions about how reliable those relationships were. A model built from individual choices could instead examine how people respond when policy, prices, income expectations or borrowing conditions change.
entries.work: Hall derived a benchmark in which changes in consumption depend on new information about future circumstances. Predictable departures can then reveal conditions such as borrowing constraints. Woodford developed a New Keynesian framework connecting forward-looking consumption, firms’ price-setting and interest-rate policy. Prices do not adjust instantly, so changes in demand can affect production. Together these contributions helped link central-bank actions and communication with the behaviour of households and businesses inside explicit economic models.
entries.significance: The resulting frameworks provide tools for examining interest-rate decisions and economic shocks. Their usefulness comes from stated behavioural assumptions and mechanisms, not from a promise that every household behaves identically or that policy outcomes can be predicted without uncertainty.

entries.title: Classical voices in new literary forms
entries.overview: Anne Carson was recognised for an inventive body of work that brings classical literature into contemporary writing, crossing the boundaries between poetry, essays, translation and other forms.
entries.background: Carson’s work grows out of both classical scholarship and the possibilities of present-day language. Ancient texts become partners in writing about love, grief and memory. Rather than separating translation, criticism and poetry, her books often combine those activities, allowing voices from different periods to interact.
entries.work: In Autobiography of Red, Carson reimagines material from a Greek myth as a modern verse narrative about Geryon. Nox approaches mourning through an accordion-fold work combining images, letters and texts, alongside a translation of Catullus. Other books juxtapose writers across centuries or use multiple short forms rather than a single continuous narrative. These examples illustrate the Swedish Academy’s emphasis on formal invention: the prize concerns an entire authorship, not one book or a single historical discovery.
entries.significance: Carson makes engagement with the classical tradition an active means of creating new literature. Her work asks readers to move between genres and perspectives, and demonstrates how a book’s arrangement and physical form can participate in its meaning.

entries.title: Switching nerve cells with light
entries.overview: Peter Hegemann, Georg Nagel and Karl Deisseroth were recognised for light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, which let researchers control selected nerve cells using light.
entries.background: Understanding a brain circuit requires more than observing which cells are active. Researchers need to change the activity of chosen cells and measure the consequences. Closely intermingled neurons make that difficult. A light-sensitive protein from an alga offered a new experimental way to obtain such control.
entries.work: Hegemann investigated how Chlamydomonas responds to light. Working with Nagel, he identified channelrhodopsins: proteins that allow charged ions across a cell membrane when illuminated. Nagel’s experiments characterised their function in other cells. Deisseroth and colleagues introduced channelrhodopsin into neurons and used blue light to trigger electrical activity. His group subsequently controlled selected neurons in living mice using optical fibres. Combining genetic targeting with precisely timed illumination established optogenetics as a tool for investigating neural circuits.
entries.significance: Experiments could now test how particular cell populations contribute to behaviour and bodily functions. The method transformed neuroscience research and has motivated clinical investigations, but experimental control of neurons is not itself a general treatment for psychiatric disorders.

entries.title: International law as a means of peace
entries.overview: Navi Pillay was recognised for efforts to promote peace through international law, including work strengthening legal accountability and institutions concerned with grave human-rights abuses.
entries.background: The Nobel Committee presented the award as support for resolving conflict through law rather than force. International tribunals need workable legal principles and institutions able to apply them. Pillay’s career connected opposition to apartheid in South Africa with the development of international criminal and human-rights law.
entries.work: Pillay defended opponents of apartheid before serving on South Africa’s High Court and at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. She later served at the International Criminal Court and as United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. The committee highlighted her contribution to tribunal work recognising that rape and sexual violence can constitute international crimes, including genocide. These were judicial and institutional achievements involving courts and colleagues, not laws created by one individual acting alone.
entries.significance: The award linked peace with accountability and protection for victims of violence. It also expressed the committee’s support for international legal institutions under pressure; that rationale should be distinguished from treating every contested legal or political question as settled.

entries.title: Catching cosmic neutrinos in Antarctic ice
entries.overview: Francis Halzen was recognised for scientific leadership behind IceCube and the detection of high-energy neutrinos from space, opening an additional way to investigate powerful cosmic processes.
entries.background: Distant cosmic objects accelerate particles to enormous energies, but their workings are difficult to observe. Neutrinos can carry information from those environments because they interact so rarely with matter. That same property makes detection difficult: an observatory needs an exceptionally large volume in which to catch rare interactions.
entries.work: Halzen proposed using Antarctic ice as the detection medium and led the international effort that developed IceCube. Light sensors embedded throughout a cubic kilometre of ice record flashes associated with neutrino interactions. The array was completed in 2011, and its observations established the presence of high-energy neutrinos arriving from beyond the solar system. The award recognises Halzen’s decisive contributions within a collaboration of researchers and engineers, rather than treating the observatory as a solo invention.
entries.significance: IceCube supplied an astronomical messenger beyond ordinary light. Its observations let researchers investigate extreme particle-producing environments through neutrinos, while the source and interpretation of individual events remain subjects for continuing scientific investigation.
